Research into the human brain network has yielded substantial insights, yet a crucial question remains largely unanswered: what is the complete correlation configuration of the brain network? To address this gap, this study employed cutting-edge technology to create a comprehensive functional brain network through high-resolution EEG data, which was subsequently analyzed using advanced techniques for complex data analysis. The outcome revealed a highly organized and revealing correlation matrix with intriguing patterns and properties that could shed light on the fundamental nature of brain function and the source of cognitive disorders. Furthermore, this study employed advanced image analysis techniques to identify subtle abnormalities in brain correlation and connective tissue, which may enable the early detection of brain changes and disorders at their inception. The outcome of this research is expected to open up new avenues for understanding the human brain and developing groundbreaking diagnostic methods and treatments for a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transformation, representing a link between 
complex Schr$\ddot{o}$dinger operators and Gaussian polynomials on phase space, 
can be extended into a Clifford algebra-complemented variant. This adaptation leverages 
the association of Euclidean space's Clifford algebra with its vector space, utilizing 
the elements of the Clifford algebra as coefficients to generalize the transformation. 
As a result, a Taylor isomorphism arises, characterizing a one-to-one correspondence 
between Segal-Bargmann spaces for the generalized and classical cases. Furthermore, 
it has been demonstrated that the generalized transformation preserves the positive definite 
hermitian property. Additionally, calculations involving the norm and inner product 
in the Segal-Bargmann space, formulated via the generalized transformation, were 
carried out and found to align with their corresponding expressions in the classical 
instance. Lastly, exploration of the generalized transformation's connection to 
Clifford analysis was also initiated.

We establish that a class of Gaussian fields possess the property that the expectation of a functional of the field's trajectory conditioned on its values at distinct spatial points is equal to the expectation of the same functional for a field that is conditioned on those points and then averaged over all possible realizations of the relevant secondary field. In the specific context of Gaussian fields, this relationship provides a justification for the strategy of first conditioning the field and then taking the expectation over all possible secondary fields, thereby allowing us to construct non-trivial examples of fields for which the secondary field may be specified non-randomly. As a consequence, this approach can be employed to derive the exact distribution of the path of a Bessel process upon conditioning on its initial values, thereby synthesizing a random variable whose squared magnitude is exponentially distributed with parameter one, along with an independent uniform variable on the interval $[0,1)$. Similarly, we utilize our method to derive the joint distribution of the times of entry and exit for Brownian motion in a specific region shaped like an elongated ellipse. Finally, by conditioning on the field's values at two distinct points, we are also able to establish that the distribution of the inverse of a multiple independent and identically distributed random variable is a generalized inverse Gaussian distribution, thereby synthesizing a random variable whose squared magnitude is exponentially distributed with parameter one and a variable whose distribution is a mixture of the variables 1/\sqrt(t) and 1/\sqrt(1-t) with coefficients 1 and

This research demonstrates the effectiveness of a ground-and-sky sensor network in monitoring environmental changes by leveraging data from ultra-wideband (UWB) radios to construct a comprehensive spatial awareness system. By fusing the received UWB radio signals with the network's sensor data and spatial information, our approach generates an overarching understanding of the surrounding environment. This novel method facilitates the creation of a real-time, 3D spatial framework by using the information transmitted among UWB radios, ground sensors, and aerial sensors. Furthermore, our approach allows for the seamless integration of this environment-aware system into a mobile robot, thereby enhancing its navigation capabilities and spatial mapping abilities. This contribution not only offers a practical solution for building a novel type of sensor network but also explores the foundational principles and the emerging opportunities associated with using UWB radio signals in statistical content-based sensing applications.

After a decade of groundbreaking deep underground experiments that have significantly advanced our understanding of neutrinos, the next generation of comprehensive and highly sensitive explorations is ready to begin. The focus will be on a pioneering design for the massive LArTPC detector DUNE, which is set to lead the way in ongoing efforts to gain even more insight into neutrino properties. DUNE's groundbreaking design combines state-of-the-art technology with an enormous target mass, paving the way for unparalleled precision in multiple areas of neutrino research. In this chapter, the underlying scientific objectives and the numerous potential scientific breakthroughs enabled by DUNE's underground and near-site experiments will be presented. Additionally, the competing design concepts and development stages of the detector will be discussed in detail.

A crucial element in the reconstruction of hadronic decays of heavy bosons, especially in LHC experiments, is the accurate identification of top quark characteristics. The process of mapping these characteristics from their proton-proton collision data is complex and influenced by various systematic uncertainties. In an effort to address this issue, a novel approach was developed, specifically a set of algorithms designed to analyze the patterns of top quark appearances, known as top tagging. Similar to the interpretation of particle collision data in the Standard Model, this top tagging algorithm faces the problem of attributing responsibility to individual input features for classifying events as top-rich or not. Inspired by the SHapley Additive exPlanations method, which assigns values to input variables for classification results, this analysis introduces the use of Shapley values in top tagging. The analysis utilizes Shapley values on three distinct top tagging datasets derived from top quark pp collisions at 13 TeV. The analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of enhanced top tagging algorithms over traditional ones. Furthermore, this analysis demonstrates the potential use of analytical methods in quantifying the impact of individual features on the model's decision-making process.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for virtual organizations, requirement necessity, semantic enlargement, and evaluation. The document draws upon previous research in VO semantics and semantic web technologies to propose and evaluate new virtual organization features.

To accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) training, techniques such as importance sampling, off-policy learning, and experience replay have been utilized. While experience replay proves particularly beneficial in deep RL, its standard implementation can sometimes hinder training by emphasizing rare events over common ones. This is because the approach measures policy performance based on the expected value, which can lead to increased variance and hinder the learning process. To address this shortcoming, a new variance-reducing approach to experience replay has been proposed, which utilizes a more stable estimate of the task reward. By minimizing variance in reward estimates, the proposed method enhances the efficiency of off-policy RL algorithms and promotes policy enhancements. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this novel approach not only accelerates RL training but also facilitates policy improvements compared to existing methods, while showcasing robustness across a range of RL and transfer learning scenarios.

Two new techniques, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization, have recently been proposed to analyze path integrals with odd Grassmann variables in the context of topological gauge theories and spin liquids. This research investigates the equivalence between these two methods and provides a proof of their compatibility. Furthermore, it shows that these two mechanisms produce identical results in the specific application of the $Q$-matrix formalism, commonly used in the study of topological spin liquids and quantum chaos.

Recently, there has been significant interest in using hidden state variables to make predictions about future motion patterns. However, most existing approaches overlook the fact that motion is multi-faceted and temporal in nature. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called MoDeRNN, which incorporates a dynamic graph neural network to uncover detailed motion characteristics. By automatically discovering co-related spatial relationships, the model captures the inherent structure of the environment and models the evolution of future motion patterns. The model's core consists of an adaptive graph module and a node-specific dynamic RNN module, which together enable the modeling of both spatial and temporal dimensions. Through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we propose a quantitative metric to evaluate predictive models, revealing interesting spatial relationships that can't be captured by conventional methods.

This research focuses on addressing memory safety issues in the next-generation web platform, particularly when interacting with web content written in WebAssembly. Our investigation aims to compare memory safety features in various languages and APIs, culminating in an experimental framework that uses JavaScript to safely manage memory in WebAssembly applications alongside Rust's existing memory management. The introduction of a new abstract data type in JavaScript enables the creation of a lifetime-based approach to memory safety, complemented by performance-correct exception points. These exceptions points, implemented in both Rust and JavaScript, allow for predictable memory handling by combining the benefits of monomorphic (Rust) and polymorphic (JavaScript) type checks. The paper outlines memory abstraction, lifetime rules, and exception point guidelines, accompanied by performance measurements and case studies. The proposed approach was successfully prototyped and tested in the Uno runtime environment.

This research explores neutrinoless double-beta decay, confirming the major components involved and examining the phenomenon within the framework of the Standard Model. A new theory, called the collider scale interaction theory, has been developed to explain this process through high-energy collisions between particles. The theory models the decay process as the combination of four lepton interactions, resulting in a combined mass of zero. The strength of these interactions, represented by coupling constants, determines the likelihood and timeframe of the decay process. The researchers have established relationships governing these coupling constants between particles and neutrinos, and have used them to create a relationship chart. The theory also predicts consequences for particle behavior in experiments and advanced technologies, and the researchers have used theoretical calculations and simulation methods to create charts illustrating how neutrinoless double-beta decay interacts with other particle processes. The theory provides a framework that can be tested and validated through high-energy particle experiments involving complex particle interactions.

A novel method using polar subcodes has been developed to accelerate belief transmission list (TL) decoding for binary memoryless channels. This method assembles a transmission list comprising several codewords, transmits them through the channel, and receives them as a single bundle. Upon reception, successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding is performed using the bundle as a single symbol, yielding a prospective list of probable messages. Subsequent iterative CRC checks and filtering of the transmission list yield a refined list, potentially including only a single message, thereby enhancing decoding efficiency. Experimental data for binary phase shift keying (BPSK) channel transmission using 128 symbols and 32 subcodes reveals a 25.6% decrease in decoding failure rate compared to conventional SCL decoding. Furthermore, simulation results indicate a 24.5% decrease in latency and up to 2.5 dB in received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement relative to SCL decoding. This method is adaptable to variety of channel codes.

Images from space telescopes often get distorted by the telescope's optical issue, but we can use various techniques to rectify this. Normally, images are corrected through a process called deconvolution, but some galaxies have objects that appear out of focus due to a specific issue with the Hubble Space Telescope's lens. These particular galaxies have multiple images that become more sharp when their shapes are known and used to correct for the lens's effect, but combining them requires a precise calculation to produce a clear image. This calculation, known as a demagnification, is typically given for each position but varies according to direction, making it challenging to correct the distortion in the image. This issue is addressed with a new method that uses a parameterised expression to describe the lens's effect with varying position, allowing for overall correction of the image's distortion. Demagnification values obtained from the analysis are provided for different positions in the Hubble Space Telescope's field of view, allowing for a standard correction procedure for the lens's effect. This correction is then demonstrated to improve the deconvolution process of the images by reducing discontinuities and improving the accuracy of the results.

The fracture initiation in a crystalline material is accurately modeled by a sudden jump in its potential energy and is characterized by infinite volume and surface tension. The stress concentration at the material imperfection can be calculated by a linear elastic analysis before the fracture initiation. The perfect fracture initiation in a infinite perfect crystal is feasible only if the crack is expanding into a new phase space characterized by infinite lower energy levels. The sudden change in potential energy during fracture is given by the difference in new and old equilibrium states across the new phase space. The stress at the material imperfection before the fracture can be determined by a non-linear elastic analysis under the conditions of equilibrium prevailing in the old phase space. The analysis shows that the fracture stress in polycrystalline metals such as copper and iron is significantly lower than their corresponding single crystal counterparts. The empirical relationship between the fracture stress and the inverse of the average grain size in metals such as copper and iron is confirmed through numerical simulations of the fracture initiation in an infinite perfect crystal across a new phase space. The simulation results for the fracture stress agree with the corresponding experimental values, while considering a finite number of energy levels that sufficiently represents the material behavior.

We establish connections between the Armendariz-Kim-Shieh self-avoiding walk exploration, the L\'evy-Brownian Gaussian free field, and multiple SLE curves driven by the output of the Cauchy process, which is also represented as the inverse of the two-matrix model's partition function or as the eigenvalue distribution of a unitary matrix in complex Boltzmann gas. This outcome builds on previous findings of Dub\'edat and Dub'edat-Shieh linking the field to a single SLE curve driven by the Watson distribution. This reference point enables a detailed analysis of the conformal loop ensemble's asymptotic properties, which are linked to the four-point correlation functions of the underlying Gaussian free field. This study also results in comprehensive findings on the asymptotic properties of the four-point correlation functions of the multiple SLEs linked to the Armendariz-Kim-Shieh walk and the Watson curve.

This research presents an alternative proof of the partial regularity criterion for solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with periodic initial conditions, specifically those defined by the L_4(t,L_2(\mathbb{T}^3)) norm.

Although the concept was initially developed for evaluating linear timing relationships, it can also be applied to fundamental quantum computations within linear duration frameworks.  In this study, we explore the intersection of quantum calculations with duration expressions by leveraging Groenewald's initial work on the topic.  We demonstrate that for the specified context, any observation of the system leads to the conclusion that the calculated probability is zero, given the absence of the diagonal matrix element.  We then establish that, in this particular setting, the no-cloning theorem naturally prevents normalization; in other words, it asserts that the calculated probability is zero.  A detailed example illustrates the process, followed by a discussion of additional findings and potential limitations in linear duration contexts.

A decentralized system based on block-chains has numerous advantages, key among them being the assurance of genuineness, the integrity and immutability of data. This capability is highly beneficial in the realm of Internet of Things, comprising IoT-devices such as sensors and actuators which are prone to malfunctions. By means of external parties known as oracles that supply additional information and by means of smart contracts, a mechanism for ensuring the authenticity of data from these unreliable sources, this problem can be rectified. In this paper, a comprehensive framework for implementing such a blockchain system is explored along with a real-world application of this technology in a network for food supply.

The diverse forms of life on our planet are inhabited by various cell types, which exhibit a wide range of complex shapes. Traditionally, modeling cellular structures has been an intricate task due to their non-repeating, non-periodic characteristics. The emergence of deep neural networks has led to significant breakthroughs in shape synthesis, but their limitations remain apparent when working with biomedical data. Our approach leverages conditional neural processes to create novel, detailed cell models from trained patterns. Our method enables the creation of cells with spatial features and morphologies not previously observed during training. Our research focuses on reconstructing and generating human red blood cell models. The models we develop demonstrate cellular resilience during adverse conditions and have a level of accuracy when compared to scanning electron microscope images.

Document accessibility has become a critical issue in contemporary information systems. Users who encounter physical and cognitive disabilities require accommodations that enable them to access digital content without compromise. A recent surge in the production of digital content from diverse authors and sources has exacerbated this challenge, prompting a necessity for accessibility solutions. In response to this demand, various systems have been developed to mitigate accessibility problems by recording, tracking, and ensuring document usability standards. A novel among these is EAGLE, an innovative solution based on the XACML access control framework, which ensures that digital content complies with ISO 23000-3. This research provides an overview of the subject, delves into the current methodologies used in accessing electronic documents, and presents a cutting-edge approach by integrating XACML with the XSL-FO template, thereby guaranteeing that adaptable and accessible document formats are applied to enable print-challenged users to read digital content comfortably.

While BERT's masked language modeling has achieved impressive results on numerous NLP tasks, it still has some limitations in its universal nature. This limitation arises from its reliance on looking leftward when processing sequences during both masked and masked LM tasks. This makes it difficult to model right-to-left languages and leads to inconsistent results when evaluating task-dependent context. To address these issues, we propose an effective yet efficient universal autoregressive language pretraining method that overcomes BERT's limitations. This method enhances the XLNet's autoregressive objective with an extensive array of ordered permutation representations, thereby improving the model's right-to-left modeling capabilities and achieving these improvements without elevating memory demands. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method performs better in various tests, including right-to-right language modeling, and task-dependent context evaluation. Furthermore, our findings indicate that our method can surpass BERT's results in numerous NLP tasks such as machine reading comprehension, question answering, and natural language inference.

The primary technique for detecting exoplanet atmospheres relies on analyzing transit depth, but its accuracy can be compromised by stellar activity. Highly active M-dwarfs are the primary targets for this method, which has led to the development of a new strategy to improve detection by considering stellar evolution models. These models can also inform the development of a new method for identifying active periods and predicting the composition of exoplanet atmospheres, particularly in M-dwarf stars. However, the presence of strong magnetic fields, rotational periods, and activity levels make it challenging to achieve reliable results with current technology. We investigated the impact of stellar activity on a proposed technique for identifying exoplanet atmospheres, which relies on analyzing transit spectra at low resolution through binary models of the Sun and M-dwarfs. We considered various atmospheric compositions, escape velocities, and non-radial stellar activity patterns, which led to the development of a new approach using high-resolution spectroscopy to distinguish between planets and stellar activity. This method, which combines escape velocity and the study of spectral shapes, offers significant advantages and could be applied retroactively to existing data, particularly in cases where the signal-to-noise ratio is high and the dominant spectral features are broad. Additionally, the technique is feasible with current technology, which typically offers resolutions between 10,000 to 25,000.

We investigate the formation of three- and four-dimensional metric geometries with constant curvature on Riemannian manifolds, including those with singularities. This corresponds to the resolution of the Hamiltonian constraint in general relativity and the discovery of conformal metrics with constant scalar curvature and specific weight constraints. Our research is based on the inverse mean curvature flow, which can be used to construct these metrics locally, provided certain mild conditions on the Riemannian manifold are met. These conditions are: the presence of a complete non-constant curvature factor, local conformal completeness, a specific curvature constraint, and the non-existence of certain closed Gomory-Riemannian surfaces. If these conditions are satisfied, we can develop conformal metrics with constant scalar curvature and the specified weight constraints through the inverse mean curvature flow, which in turn allows us to solve the Hamilton constraint in Einstein's theory of general relativity and identify new four-dimensional geometries with constant curvature, including Schwarzschild and de Sitter spaces, as well as a class of singular hypersurfaces called Edmonds' bodies.

Research into neurobiology and bio-inspired robotics suggests that fast and agile movements of certain animals may be better understood by studying their behavior on multiple surfaces, including solid surfaces and those surrounded by fluid. In order to enhance our understanding of the neural control and locomotion principles found in these animals, scientists conducted a similar experiment on terrestrial creatures that excel at movement, specifically centipedes, in a environment surrounded by water. This study found that a species of centipede, when forced to move across a water interface, switched from using traditional leg movement patterns to a more complex and energetic gait, one that allowed for forward movement while using fewer leg movements. It was observed that this new gait, characterized by its high cost of movement, provided the creature with greater stability while walking near the water interface and crossing over into a new area without touching the ground.

Numerical models play a vital role in forecasting the potential risks associated with an asteroid impact that generates a large tsunami, such as one that travels over land and predicts which areas will be affected. Current numerical models are limited by their rigid approach, assuming the Earth's interior and surface behave in a predetermined manner. In order to develop adaptable and accurate tsunami simulation models that can simulate an asteroid of any composition and size, we recommend a multi-physics approach. This methodology divides an asteroid into separate sections, applying different material behaviors according to variables such as temperature, pressure, and volume. By employing this multi-physics method and incorporating additional algorithms, such as mass conservation and energy transfer, we can develop more reliable and flexible asteroid impact simulation models. Our proposed framework allows users to incorporate various material models and algorithms easily, thereby facilitating rapid experimentation and a deeper understanding of an asteroid's behavior during an impact. Ultimately, this approach can aid in reducing uncertainty and generating more accurate forecasts for a wide range of asteroid compositions and sizes.

Recent near-infrared photometry from the JWST NIRCam program known as CEERS, provides highly accurate stellar mass and star-forming rate measurements in the pre-explosion stage of SN1000A's host galaxy, which spans a massive 1.6 x 10^11 solar mass range. Furthermore, by stacking the CEERS galaxy's photometry, we've uncovered a 2.0 microMpc^-1 slope in the galaxy distribution at 0.2 z 0.4, confirming the prevalence of massive, starburst galaxies in the distant universe. Data also suggests that galaxies which appear dim in optical or near-infrared, are actually experiencing intense, extremely short-lived starburst activity within massive, irregularly shaped galactic disks influenced by external material such as intergalactic gas. Observations indicate that these rare galaxies are unusually large and have relatively low stellar masses but are capable of producing up to 20 percent of their total stellar mass through highly efficient, extremely short-lived starburst events which are rapid, intense and fuelled by external material. Furthermore, according to predictions grounded in current understanding, it's expected that these highly efficient, ultra-luminous starbursts will be infrequently observed in galaxies which are near peak bursts but will be present in very early or late stages of these events, due to a limited observing window. A modified gravity theory in seven dimensions has been introduced, based on the Gaussian framework, to model a spin-1 field mimicking the Standard Model's U(1) symmetry. The resulting portal interactions and primary vertices give rise to a seven-dimensional field equation with curvature terms linked to a cosmological constant, yielding an extra dimension beyond the standard four dimensions. The additional dimension radius, \(R\), affects tree-level processes in a manner analogous to a non-minimal U(1) coupling. Furthermore, the presence of a non-minimal spin-1 coupling has a impact on chiral symmetry breaking in processes such as \(K\rightarrow\pi e^+e^-\) and \(B\rightarrow\rho \pi e^+e^-\) decays.

This research extends two existing studies to derive an infinite sequence of Euler polynomial coefficients for blocked discs in a channel with two dimensions and a slit. Building upon previous findings by Boukhaufa and Serrano, our work derives an alternate sequence of coefficients for a 2D blocked disc in a channel, paralleling their 1D discovery. Additionally, similar to the contributions of Boukhaufa and Serrano, our calculations yield two infinite sequences of Euler polynomial coefficients for blocked discs in a three-dimensional channel with two dimensions and a slit.

Recent studies indicate a peculiar, yet unexplained phenomenon where ENSO-related variations in global precipitation tend to vanish at extremely low and elevated elevation levels. In this study, an advanced rating system for precision is developed, and an extensive analysis of precipitation data reveals not only the restoration of these variations but also the emergence of contrasting patterns above and below 500m in elevation. A notable, reversed enhancement of precipitation is observed at high altitudes in response to the intense 1997 El Ni\doingo\odo event, and long-term patterns appear to be heavily regulated by subtle, periodic variations in global precipitation over land and sea. A complex, interdependent relationship is discovered between seasonal climate patterns, and these variations are found to strongly impact and fluctuate with the occurrence of our four distinct seasons.

To examine the dynamic light scattering (DLS) response of bending modulated planar epoxy films during non-affine elastic deformation, a laboratory-based experimental approach was developed.  The epoxy film, initially intact, was subjected to a non-affine regime of large strains via a periodic 3D-bent silicon rib, and this multi-scale technique led to a continuous strain monitoring method.  The intensity variation observed in the light scattering signal was found to be in perfect sync with the modulus loss curve obtained through nanoindentation, and this correlation was also similar to that reported in literature for polymers.  In contrast to affine behavior, this observed light scattering response appears to be an effective method for detecting non-affine elastic deformation in solids, and combining this approach with light scattering may offer a new way to analyze complex materials.

This research investigates the influence of behavioral adaptations in a polluted environment on population dynamics using mathematical single-species models integrated with an age structure. We establish models based on optimal control theory, which considers various factors like habitat toxicity, nutritional constraints, environmental rehabilitation, foraging activities, and how different agents respond to these factors. We explore model solutions under two key assumptions - optimal and actual behaviors - and provide comprehensive analyses, including asymptotic models and numerical simulations. This comprehensive approach aims to provide accurate representations of population models with diverse agent responses to environmental toxins.

A new approach to incorporating the weakening property into existing formal systems is developed by adapting the concept of hypersequents from the cut-elimination procedure in natural deduction. This approach extends the already established methodology used in proof-theory. We focus on a specific class of formal systems known as subsingle-negation-lambda and an even more restricted class known as relativized subsingle-negation-lambda. Both of these classes become the foundation for investigating the computational complexity properties of Weakening and Reduction Hypersequent Substitutional Logics, as earlier methodologies relied heavily on them. Our study explores the trade-offs between the efficiency of propositional operations, the level of undecidability, and the inclusion of the weakening rule in these formal systems. We discover that incorporating the weakening rule results in a significant increase in computational complexity but can lead to more nuanced undecidability conclusions. We show that the weakening rule has a limited impact on the undecidability of certain hypersequent logics, indicating that these particular cases were already known to be undecidable. In turn, this discovery allows us to simplify haskell implementations of certain hypersequent logics that incorporate the weakening rule.

This study introduces HyperExpan, an innovative knowledge expansion system for named entity classification that learns in a hyperbolic space. By leveraging the Minimax Hyperbolic Center Loss, HyperExpan optimizes an entity's central representation and adapts it for knowledge expansion. Notably, HyperExpan can integrate with existing models, including models trained in Euclidean spaces, making it highly versatile. Evaluations conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate that HyperExpan consistently outperforms previous methods, further showcasing its superiority by showcasing improved classification performance alongside enhanced understanding of the entity hierarchy.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the impact of electric fields on the interaction between molecular dimers within the S66 dataset, consisting of 66 dimers. These dimers consist of dimers formed from atoms that have a multipole expansion up to the $q=4$ order and a non-bonding distance of more than 3.5 Å, ensuring that physics is dominated by electrostatics. Monopoles and dipoles were found to influence dimers holding a charge of zero, while dimers with a dipole moment applied a large attractive force to other dimers with a similar orientation of dipoles. A specific pattern was noticed, where dimers with large dipoles were found to influence interactions the most, despite their smaller size. Furthermore, dimers with quadrupole moments were found to have little effect compared to the influence of electric fields, due to the smallness of their contribution. A good agreement was found between calculations conducted via a highly accurate method and those conducted via a more computationally efficient method, with a correlation coefficient of 0.96 obtained. An analysis was also conducted to establish the zero-field monopole convergence properties of the computational method employed, finding the maximum error to be around 57 milimeV for monopole interactions. An explanation is provided as to why certain dimers showed a discontinuity, due to a change in the direction of polarization occurring.

The advent of Industry 4.0 has seen a surge in the use of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence across manufacturing systems. Despite their pros, these approaches often raise concerns about unpredictability and job loss in the media. This research aims to shed light on another aspect of these models that has been understudied: their lack of statistical clarity. By combining an industry-wide dataset with an analysis of the predictions' patterns, this work investigates the effect of job rank, reveals the level of job awareness among models, and determines the optimal size of training samples for optimal results. Our findings demonstrate that models of different sizes fail to provide consistent outcomes until the training sample exceeds a certain threshold, after which the size of the training sample has minimal impact on the prediction accuracy.

This paper introduces a framework for assessing the reliability of control systems by leveraging a logical formulation of a cyber-physical system's behavior, captured with a specific time-dependent logical operator. The proposed approach analyzes a CP system's robustness using a set-enriched temporal logic, examining the effects of feedback and time on the system's performance. This conceptual framework is Enriched STL, a language that expands regular STL by incorporating feedback into temporal logic observations. The analysis utilizes a measurable model, which accounts for disturbances and feedback, to evaluate the CP system's reliability over a specified time period and define robustness relative to a specific performance metric. This study demonstrates the practical application of the proposed approach using a classic cart-pendulum system.

Data collection on human activities like running, climbing stairs, biking, and rowing has been enhanced by wearable technology, featuring high-resolution accelerometers. This paper presents a novel framework for identifying concealed underlying measurement patterns produced by instrument malfunctions or external factors, such as accidental detachment from the wearer or interference from external sounds. The proposed model is an extended version of the widely used generalized linear model and is initially validated in a simulated environment before applying it to real-world data sets involving running and rowing activities. The proposed shadow model demonstrates improved accuracy in predicting the underlying measurement pattern with fewer errors compared to existing models.

We're focusing on a specific nonlinear diffusion equation on a compact, connected Riemannian manifold M, with boundary, where diffusion occurs throughout the manifold and not just on its boundary. This type of equation is significant in mathematics literature, particularly for Chaplygin top dynamics and polar top dynamics. It has been established that a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition is associated with a unique solution for this diffusion equation. This article investigates the relationship between the rate of convergence and the norms involved, specifically examining how the solution's approximation varies based on the diffusion parameters and the manifold's geometry. This work relies heavily on analysis and proof of specific mathematical inequalities.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus, specifically those of kpc-scale, exhibit a faint radio signal. Previous investigations into these sources, involving a calculation of their average radio emission, indicated that their radio luminosity displays a negative relationship with distance when analyzing 22 AGN, displaying a three-decade range of radio signal variability. In contrast, our research explores a different method by studying the characteristics of individual sources within specified angular size bins. By utilizing high-sensitivity radio data from ATCA, we calculated the average flux density of 287 mJy/arcsec^2 and 50 mJy/arcsec^2 from sources measuring less than 5" or more than 18", respectively, without observing a correlation between flux density and angular size within our data set. In addition, our research reveals an absence of relationships between source properties such as optical and X-ray brightness. We hypothesize that small-sized sources may exhibit characteristics similar to larger-sized sources, thereby causing their average properties to converge at distant observation angles.

Statistical modeling, an advanced aspect of formal language and quantitative modeling, offers a unified theoretical framework to analyze and identify complex patterns within noisy data, specifically in areas such as text classification, speech recognition, and software security. This research introduces abstract concealed models (ACMs), a type of probabilistic model that incorporates the inherent uncertainty of real-world data, as the foundational type system for addressing uncertainty in statistical modeling. By treating ACMs as a monadic carrier over the category of sets, it provides a comprehensive definition of security for high-level programming languages, encompassing data-dependent access control and information flow confidentiality. Additionally, we develop a specific type of ACM, known as the abstract error-tracing concealed model, which offers a precise definition of quantitative data flow analysis. This work sets the groundwork for integrating ACMs with programming languages, an area we will explore in future research.

This research explores the underlying principles of nonlinear physics, assuming that the inherent randomness leads to emergent phenomena that are irreversible and have a global impact. It postulates the existence of irreducible, locally undetermined entities and develops the concept of statistical nonlocality as a means to address these uncertainties globally. This idea is applied to physically meaningful models, one of which is the Turner model representing organ evolution. We demonstrate that the Turner model's nonlocality is a natural consequence of its dynamic consistency, as it reduces to local randomness in the absence of meaningful global influences. Additionally, this research examines the statistical nonlocality of the Czarnecki model, proposing a modified approach that takes into account the model's inherent irreducibility and is consistent with its dynamically meaningful properties.

We introduce an advanced scattering-based model, Flexible Scattering Phenomenology (FSP), built upon the Wilsonian effective action framework. It integrates all relevant higher-order corrections into a single, unified approach. FSP offers several key benefits, including the decoupling of theoretical and phenomenological calculations and the versatility to include or exclude specific higher-order terms as needed. We demonstrate the practical application of the FSP formalism through two benchmark scenarios, dark matter annihilation in fixed mediation channels and in fixed cross-section models. The introduction of the FSP formalism paves the way for more accurate and precise event-level simulations that can be used in concurrent phenomenological studies to determine the viability of specific models.

This paper presents the development of a unified framework for thermodynamic analysis of a blackbody in the presence of the Casimir effect. Initially, the total electric field of a blackbody is constructed by summing contributions from photons and electromagnetic fluctuations caused by the Casimir effect. Subsequently, a comprehensive expression for the blackbody radiation energy density is derived, formulated as a sum of two terms: one accounting for photon energy and the other accounting for electromagnetic fluctuations. This expression is proven to adhere to the conservation principle of energy. Furthermore, a detailed analysis is provided of how the Casimir effect influences key thermodynamic properties, such as internal energy, entropy, pressure, and temperature. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the Casimir effect displaces the temperature of a blackbody both vertically and horizontally. This displacement of temperature is a direct consequence of the Casimir effect.

This study proposes a privacy concept for location data, utilizing a log-loss metric, which measures the discrepancy between an individual's location and the predicted location for their social contacts. Since location data is often subject to restrictions, we investigate a limited privacy setting where the privacy-preservation mechanism doesn't know the individual's actual location, only the locations of their friends. To achieve this, we develop two location-predictation mechanisms - one based on a hierarchical model and the other on a hierarchical generalized linear model. To evaluate the proposed privacy concept, we employ a method called mean absolute error, which provides an unambiguous measure of location privacy when the underlying distribution is normal. However, when the underlying distribution isn't normal, the privacy score is only relatively stable and not fully consistent. To address this issue, we propose an alternative approach based on the deviation from normal distribution. Furthermore, we develop a method to calculate the expected value of the location loss, thereby establishing a definition of expected location privacy. Our investigation reveals that the expected location privacy is a more stable measure than the actual location loss. Moreover, we establish an inequality linking the expected location privacy and the maximum possible restriction of the privacy-preservation mechanism. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed location privacy concept, we conduct simulations with real-time traffic data.

The task of reconstructing a mobile object's pose in three-dimensional space when using point cloud data from an external reference, is key in fields such as manufacturing, robotics and computer vision. In this study, a novel approach to three-dimensional pose estimation utilizing Deep Learning concepts is introduced. By transforming raw point cloud data into a shape-preserving, Normal Distribution Transform representation via principal component analysis, the proposed method bypasses cumbersome orientation mapping requirements commonly found in Deep Learning solutions for this problem. In addition to this, the proposed method employs a Transformer-based ensemble model for feature extraction, enabling the method to avoid unreliable surfaces, such as those found on occluded mobile objects. Furthermore, this method leverages historical data for improved accuracy, by modeling the expected point cloud, given the object's current state. In a further development of this approach, a new method for evaluating the method's reliability, using LiDAR and IMU sensor data, is introduced. Experiments demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance in both simulated and real-world scenarios.

A key objective in neuroimaging analysis involves mapping functional brain connections across individuals. Recent research suggests that these connections should not be viewed as fixed entities but rather dynamic aspects of brain function. However, defining a functional brain link at a group level does not necessarily mean it exists for each individual. Therefore, we must develop models that accurately reveal the existence or absence of a connection for every single participant, without relying on assumptions from a prior distribution. By applying a probabilistic framework to data from 1,200 participants without any prior assumptions, our findings indicate that functional brain connections are widespread throughout the brain and follow a principle of'shortest path'. Notably, our results show that these connections are consistently strong in areas responsible for attention, and we further demonstrate that our approach enables the accurate prediction of an individual's resting-state brain activity based on their age, gender, and cognitive ability, all while maintaining statistical reliability.

In a single-hop beeping network connecting $n$ agents, each node receives a distinct beeping signal from a central leader and uses this to establish a personal identifier. However, the current method for assigning names at a central location may lead to an efficient technique called \emph{power-saving naming}. This naming convention allows agents to create their own unique identifiers using local signals from a central leader and then share their findings with other agents through an efficient \emph{leader-coordinated initialization} process. This new approach leads to a more decentralized and efficient process, enabling name creation and initialization to be completed in a reduced number of steps, specifically $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$, and thus saving significant amounts of energy while using minimal power to achieve optimal results, specifically $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{1/2})$. This new method overperforms by achieving nearly double the number of steps required to save nearly three and a half times the amount of energy compared to a current best technique known as double-covered naming, achieving savings of around fifty percent while using fifty percent more energy than a current best technique known as sequence naming.

Recent research into NLP using code-mixed text has been driven by the widespread use of multiple languages in social media platforms across North and South America, particularly in areas like romance, English, and Spanish. However, existing models have yet to effectively utilize word embeddings in code-mixed text. A primary challenge in developing universal word embeddings lies in decoding word embeddings that function across languages while preserving linguistic characteristics. To address this limitation, we have devised Transition point based Dynamic and Relative positional representation for code-mixed languages (PESTO), which employs transition patterns to create language-specific positional representations. The experimental results demonstrate that PESTO outperforms state-of-the-art models on data from social media platforms for three different code-mixed language pairs: Rom-Rst, Qn-Ar, and Qn-Qd. The success of PESTO has prompted us to conduct an in-depth analysis of transition patterns to explore their semantic significance. Notably, our approach also creates novel word embeddings that maintain linguistic characteristics during code-mixed text. The data, models, and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/akshaj1999/PESTO-Transformer-Based-LM.

The superconducting properties of hydrogen rich compounds are significantly impacted by vibrations in the presence of electron-phonon interactions. At high pressures, the convergence of energy levels of certain energy levels (van Hove singularities) influences this impact. It activates an unusual effect known as the change in density of states where the total density of states of a material exhibits a discontinuity due to the convergence of these energy levels. It has been observed that in the H3B4 family of compounds, this impact leads to the alteration of isotope effects and critical pressures required for superconductivity. It was observed that the H3S compound exhibits a critical pressure of 155 GPa, whereas its isotopes DS (-H, -F, -Cl) display increased critical pressures of 165, 160, 155 GPa respectively. This phenomenon is attributed to the alteration of energy levels due to vibrational frequencies at specific pressures that trigger the change in density of states.

In fast-paced online multi-player environments with dynamic objects, both motion prediction and planning require efficient handling of up-to-date spatial data. Our novel approach introduces a motion planning system that utilizes Proximity Grids, a low-compute cost representation of static and moving objects in a spatially-aware environment. At critically-synched time-steps, this method ensures both latest object positions and optimal motion paths are accounted for. We developed an iterative solver for our grid-based system, informed by advanced path-finding techniques such as the jitters algorithm. To further improve efficiency, we utilized the midpoint axis-alignment cross product method for rapidly identifying nearest-neighbor objects within the grid. Our spatially-aware motion planning system significantly outperforms existing methods and maintains real-time capabilities even with low computational overhead. We demonstrate this technique in a mobile game titled "Racing Through The Markets".

This research introduces an efficient visual relocalization technique based on geometric information and machine learning features that can rapidly establish relationships between a device's current image and a database of pre-recorded map, all while minimizing computational time. We train a neural network to generate feature maps that can accurately localize camera perspectives. These feature maps enable cameras to track distinctive landmarks and determine their position in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, a surface feature mapping approach allows us to construct a database of features that can accurately capture camera movements in three-dimensional space and efficiently match new images with existing features, all while minimizing computational time. We tested the technique in real-time conditions by simulating outdoor scenarios and found that it successfully localized the camera's position in nearly 90% of cases with only a single image reference.

In a multiuser MIMO network, simultaneous data transmission to multiple users is enabled by MIMO, but this introduces interference between users, necessitating careful user pairing. This study addresses the problem of simultaneously determining the best user pairs and transmission parameters, including precoders and power levels, by minimizing errors in channel state estimation under limited feedback constraints. A novel algorithm, the group-based LASSO method, is developed to achieve this, differentiating itself from existing sparse coding techniques such as Dictionary Learning, which does not involve feedback. Unlike other methods that rely on individual sparse coding, the proposed algorithm incorporates regularization on group levels to optimize multiple parameters as a whole. Notably, the proposed approach outperforms conventional MIMO systems by avoiding interference between users and yields better results than feedback-free methods without sacrificing the benefits of MIMO.

The logical function semifield of a tropical curve is generated by the functions with restricted behavior on the finite sets of points, and it has a finite basis composed of elementary functions and functions such as division. Our proof demonstrates that the set of logical function semifields is finitely generated and closed in the space of tropical semifields. This discovery led to the invention of a compact version of the logical function semifield, and it was also extended to the logical function ring.

This paper investigates data-driven functions derived from model-based approaches called Q-procedures. Q-procedures are characterized by forming a convex set of parametric models based on a given estimation method and a non-increasing function. This research makes two key contributions. Firstly, it identifies necessary conditions for a data-driven function to produce a consistent estimate of a true model. Secondly, these conditions are applied to specific situations, demonstrating the consistency of popular procedures such as the reduced-basis Q-procedure and the variational Q-procedure. Notably, this paper's results imply the consistency of certain data-driven methods for parametric models that were previously unproven, including models for relative entropy regularization, the H1-regression, and variational Bayesian linear regression.

Building on Fox's biquadratic invariant, which he calculated through the componennt formal group, we show that its expansion, the Fox-Hartenstein invariant, results in a three-order characteristic of Vassiliev invariants. Notably, the Vassiliev invariant, in the field of rational numbers, does not equal zero, whereas the Fox-Hartenstein invariant does when the field is real. Additionally, we establish a relation between this new invariant and the LP invariant. Furthermore, we utilize cohomology of braid groups to formulate a multiplicative modification of the LP invariant, which holds the property of being Vassiliev of the third order. Alongside this, we find that the LP invariant displays an inverse relationship with the Fox-Hartenstein invariant and that their compositions conform to a specific trace equation. Alongside these findings, we also prove that the LP invariant, when the field is rational, does not satisfy a specific homomorphism equation yet satisfies it when the field is real.

Even though certain iron-based superconductors exhibit spin and orbital orderings, the iron-based superconductor LiFeAs remains stable under extreme pressure and has unique properties that set it apart from other iron-based compounds, making the study of its orbital ordering and its relationship with superconductivity all the more compelling. In this study, we used x-ray diffraction to analyze LiFeAs at various temperatures and pressures, examining the orbital ordering's impact on its structure. LiFeAs's lattice shows no change upon cooling below its superconducting critical temperature of 18 Kelvin, regardless of whether it's under high pressure or not. In contrast, similar experiments on LiFeAs under extreme pressure and in the presence of magnetic field did not yield any observable nematic deformation. These findings suggest that, unlike other iron-based compounds, LiFeAs does not exhibit orbital ordering or nematicity. As a result, LiFeAs's unconventional superconductivity may have an entirely different origin, potentially linking it to its unique properties without requiring orbital ordering.

This research investigates how adjustments in the two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) will be influenced by findings from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and other instruments, such as the International Linear Collider (ILC) and gravity wave detectors, like the Cosmic Observatory (ICO). Recent findings, including data from the LHC Run 2 experiments, are taken into account. To compare theoretical predictions with experimental data, the SAMUEL program is used. By adjusting the parameters of the model, accurate predictions can be made about a wide range of phenomena, such as Higgs boson properties, additional physics beyond the standard model, and precision measurements of vector boson interactions. The study also examines how these adjustments might be received, incorporating feedback from various studies. It highlights the significance of accurately measuring precise properties of the Higgs boson to distinguish 2HDM, while non-accelerator detections, like gravity wave or neutrino oscillations, are taken into account for consistency.

This research introduces a novel approach to neural education, where a neural network is taught by an ensemble of particles that harness the principles of evolutionary processes, in tandem with an algorithmic procedure that leverages self-organizing strategies. Our proposed method holds the advantage of overcoming data scarcity, and we demonstrate its efficacy through its application in a simulation of bird migration. Furthermore, this technique enables the development of a neural network capable of tackling complex high-level challenges by breaking them down into manageable low-level tasks, thereby facilitating the creation of a neural controller that achieves a global objective. In addition, our method allows for the establishment of a neural network-based system that fosters collaborative relationships between various procedural agents working towards a common goal. Our abstract concludes with a discussion of the methodology's potential applications in educational settings focused on systemic self-organization and autonomous systems.

We analyze the dynamics of relativistic chiral gauge theories across multiple dimensional spaces. These theories include massless QCD and both unitary and non-unitary techni-Yang-Mills models. A specific test we use to detect anomalies involves volume regularization. This test confirms that the standard anomaly matching conditions are accurate in six dimensions. Additionally, we apply this method to a theory with an unorthodox symmetry group, specifically $SU(1,2)$, which has unique properties. Unlike conventional $SU(N)$ theories, this model features negative Dynkin indices associated with $SU(2)$ subgroups inside $SU(2)$, leading to distinct anomalies and dimensional regularization behaviors when reduced to lower dimensions. Most significantly, we derive anomalies in theories with a non-unitary symmetry, a long-known phenomenon in techni-Yang-Mills theory.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the steady Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we explore the relationship between input forces and resulting flow patterns in dimension 3 or higher. This work shows that the steady Navier-Stokes equation becomes unstable when certain flow patterns are considered, resulting in the equation being classified as poorly defined in certain mathematical frameworks. Conversely, we found that the steady equation remains stable when these specific flow patterns are absent, utilizing specific mathematical frameworks known as Besov spaces.

In antiferromagnetic materials with significant magnon-electron interactions, the response to temperature can be remarkably vibrant. When subjected to a magnetic field, the low-energy magnon states undergo a characteristic downward shift in frequency in addition to compression, which ultimately results in the splitting of the Mott-like gap into two distinct peaks. Interestingly, the high-temperature realm of these materials can be accurately modeled using the manchester coupling model for slight magnon-hole interactions; however, a more significant shift towards more complex models with increasing temperatures is anticipated. On the other hand, when interactions involving quadruplets of magnons play a crucial role, the model of fully-pairing magnons reveals intriguing consequences, such as the occurrence of both shift and compression in a broad temperature range alongside the emergence of'magnon-polaritons' with distinct characteristics.

This research paper proposes two sets of modifications to enhance the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptography system. Currently, this system uses a specific Goppa codes matrix to encrypt and decrypt messages, but it suffers from several security shortcomings. To counter these issues, we've developed two different approaches: Firstly, we replace the Goppa codes matrix with a generalized Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem codes matrix in the encryption process. Secondly, we substitute the traditional decryption method involving Berlekamp-Massey decoding for a new approach using the syndrome sequence and the Fourier transform, as proposed by Refs. [25, 26]. Our experiments reveal that the modified system offers superior resistance to several commonly used attack methods, while also achieving increased non-linearity and minimizing the occurrence of weak keys.

Pre-training large language models with massive datasets has yielded impressive
results, yet recent findings indicate that word segmentation influences the model's
performance. To address this, we introduce Dict-BERT, a pre-training approach that
integrates a dictionary-based word segmentation task into the traditional BERT
process, alongside other enhancements. Specifically, we merge dictionary and
dictionary-encoded word hidden states, and employ a novel learning strategy for
the Dictionary Embedded Mask Token with a paired sentence. Experimental outcomes
confirm that word segmentation affects the model's performance, and Dict-BERT surpasses
BERT and other competitive models, such as WordLevel-BERT and ELMo, achieving a 0.66%
absolute F1 score improvement on the 14B Chinese WeChat corpus without any task-
specific optimizations.

We develop a novel method to compute the volume of the minimal spanning acycles in a minimal spanning acycle ensemble. This framework has far-reaching implications for studying the topological properties of random simplicial complexes as they evolve from a minimal state. Notably, our results reveal that a minimal spanning acycle ensemble exhibits a phase transition at a critical threshold where it transitions from a simple, topologically consistent state to a complex, topologically rich state. Moreover, our framework allows us to demonstrate that minimal spanning acycles in a generic random 2-complex exhibit continuous topological variations as the number of elements in the ensemble increases. Conversely, when the ensemble is non-generic, we observe discrete topological variations. In addition, our analysis extends to other types of random simplicial complexes, including random d-complexes for d >= 3, showing that their minimal spanning acycle ensembles exhibit similar behavior.

In an environment where Educational Data is highly valuable and closely kept, a new category of attacks on privacy has been proposed, known as Pragmatic Privacy Attacks. These can compromise user privacy even when the data is secured through Federated Learning, which is used in hybrid edge-cloud scenarios. By applying such attacks, an adversary can create uncertain conditions that force an edge device to compromise user confidentiality without being aware of it, which may result in the adversary gaining access to sensitive user information. Our research shows that these type of attacks can have a significant impact on education-based datasets, which are particularly vulnerable. To address this threat, a novel method to detect and prevent such attacks has been developed, which involves monitoring edge device behavior to identify and block attacks, making it a proactive solution. Our research found that when implemented properly, this method can effectively prevent an adversary from carrying out such attacks and reduce confidence in the attack's effectiveness, which was found to be up to 10% after our research was carried out.

We propose a new theoretical framework for $B$-meson decays into baryons and hypothetical "dark baryon-antibaryon" pairs. This study focuses on the initially unknown branching fractions for such decays. Utilizing the QCD sum rules through the light-cone world, we calculate the differences in light-cone operator product expansion for baryon and antibaryon transitions from the $B$ meson to the $D$ meson, thereby determining the ratio of these fractions. We also derive the amplitude for the specific decay process $B^+ \to n \bar{n} \eta'$ and obtain estimates for the branching ratios of several $B$-meson decays into baryons and dark antibaryons, such as those involving proton-antiproton and lambda-antilambda transitions.

This work introduces a simulated game scenario that challenges players to defend a city from fictional, airborne and cyber-based assaults. The game rules and strategies developed can be applied to real-world situations where cities are under attack, prompting policymakers and city administrators to make informed decisions when allocating resources for emergency situations.

Researchers have discovered the existence of black stars across various gravity theories. In the current study, we have found and analyzed the black star solutions for the $R^n$ static metric, initially considered in the context of the Einstein field equations. These black star solutions can also be applied to the modified $f(R)$ gravity, yielding similar results to those obtained with Einstein's theory. Additionally, we have investigated the phase transitions of these black stars into Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes and developed relevant conditions in terms of mass and radius. Since these black stars and related cosmological solutions exist within a finite volume, indicating the universe is enclosed in a cavity, we have conducted an extensive analysis into its implications. These findings show that, in this universe, there are black holes and stars existing alongside a cosmological constant, leading to a thermodynamic interpretation with novel properties. Specifically, we have observed that certain black holes demonstrate a Hawking--Page transition towards a new state, exhibiting a significant thermal behavior, whereas others exhibit thermal behavior only when confined to the cavity through Casimir energy. Moreover, we have found that these systems, when bounded by the cavity, show negative heat capacity, displaying atypical thermodynamic characteristics.

In the context of label noise, the performance of supervised learning models can be compromised, particularly when dealing with a large amount of mislabeled data. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a ranked aggregation approach for data retrieval, which utilizes batch sampling and group-based loss to prioritize the most reliable data for training. To facilitate data retrieval, a initial model is first developed and used to assign labels to the data; subsequently, the proposed approach calculates a reliability score for each data sample based on the predicted labels and returns the top-ranked subset to retrain the model. Notably, the framework is versatile and can be applied to various ranking models, in addition to handling diverse types of label noise. To demonstrate its efficacy, a case study is presented, focusing on the creation of a Dutch corpus for scientific articles; given the vast amount of data with likely label noise, the application of ranked aggregation for data retrieval yields substantial improvements in performance.

Current graph neural networks excel at various tasks but require significant time and resources to train due to their inherent complexity. To training efficiencies, some methods limit data accessibility or restrict data labels, but we then encounter issues in discovering optimal node representations. In this research, we identify the potential of pseudo-node labels derived from graph structure and data, and present a method to obtain these labels with minimal effort. This method is combined with self-attention mechanisms and adapted for use with both node and edge pseudo-labels. We conduct experiments on numerous benchmark graphs across various tasks, and achieve improved results compared to existing solutions.

The analytical equation for the radiated power of a charged particle undergoing
a curved trajectory at a constant velocity in a plasma wave is found to have a
direct proportionality relationship with the plasma wave's amplitude. This equation
also reveals a direct proportionality relationship between the radiated power and
the square of the electron beam's transverse deflection amplitude. Given the large
amplitude of the plasma wave (approximately 30 micrometers) in the AWAKE Experiment
setup, the generated radiated power is anticipated to be substantial, potentially
resulting in the experiment's equipartitioning limit being achieved. To achieve the
required electron-stopping distance in the AWAKE Experiment setup within 100 meters,
the analytically predicted transverse electron energy developed due to the curved path
would be in the gigaelectronvolt range, which is consistent with the AWAKE Experiment
specifications.

To ensure the confidentiality of users contributing to machine learning, the field of differentially private machine learning has become crucial. However, applying this principle to decision tree learning can be complex, particularly when dealing with features that use categorical data. In this research, we present three algorithms for privately learning decision trees, using data that has been horizontally partitioned, on features with either discrete or continuous values. Our first algorithm validates the exactness of the algorithm in a private CART analysis while showcasing compromised accuracy. In contrast, our second algorithm utilizes a modified version of the CART algorithm that incorporates the lazy DP technique to yield better results. Additionally, we propose a new method called the lazy local PDNT algorithm, which calculates decision trees locally without revealing the structure, while ensuring that the derived tree bears no information about any individual user and exhibits minimal width. Furthermore, we introduce an improved algorithm called semi-sparse PDNT, which utilizes semi-sparse techniques combined with the CPSET method from the lazy local PDNT to enhance tree width and efficiency. Our findings from experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that the semi-sparse PDNT algorithm outperforms the other methods in most cases. Notably, the algorithm achieved an impressive 100-fold decrease in tree width compared to one of our primary methods while maintaining a tree accuracy of over 98 percent.

A novel approach is introduced for estimating probability measures via minimized R\'enyi distance, leveraging the characteristics of the associated divergence that remains consistent under various transformations and constraints. By incorporating a proximal optimization method inspired by Bregman mechanics into the traditional Gaussianization technique, we develop an efficient algorithm capable of handling constrained and regularized model choice problems. We demonstrate the devised algorithm's efficacy in the context of heteroscedastic, Poisson, and weighted log-normalization transformations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's ability to incorporate diverse constraints into its operations.

Network modeling through Chain Event Networks requires rigorous evaluation to identify the most effective framework. This involves defining frameworks based on event partitions and then calculating the associated parameters. Existing studies have focused on constructing networks using frequency-based methods, but selecting the best framework remains an unresolved issue. Our research tackles this challenge by developing a Bayesian framework selection approach within the Bayesian Maximum A Posteriori framework. We utilize both traditional and non-parametric priors to calculate the framework's likelihood and score. This enables the selection of the most effective framework by minimizing a scoring function. Our proposed method is applied to both simulated and real-world data, showcasing its superiority over a competing method. Additionally, we utilize the Bayesian framework to estimate parameters and assess uncertainty in network models.

In the context of minimal norm solution retrieval within convex analysis, a robust time-evolving process based on Damped Inertial Mechanics with vanishing Tikhonov regularization is proposed. This process guarantees that as time approaches infinity, it will converge towards the minimal norm solution, even in the presence of noisy data, thanks to a specially designed momentum term and Tikhonov regularization that cancels out data errors. A comprehensive stability and robustness analysis is performed, revealing the influence of regularization parameters and momenta on the error terms. A numerical demonstration is presented, showcasing the effectiveness of this algorithm in recovering minimal norm solutions from under-determined linear equations.

In the field of distributed robotics, the 'unpredictable shifts' phenomenon has significant implications for the behavior of robots. On a two-dimensional plane, a group of robots is placed along a line, with each robot possessing a limited movement range. The wall at one end is actuated by a finite-state automaton, generating a random path. While following the path allows the robots to stay closest to the wall, the automaton's movements can produce complex patterns. However, the 'unpredictable shifts' phenomenon is missing from this setup, as the automaton's patterns often become predictable when analyzed using a suitable reference system. We introduce a task where robots are placed along a line segment and must maintain their position along this segment. The wall at one end is driven by an infinite-cycle finite-state automaton, whose pattern is unknown and definitively unpredictable. Our research proves that, in this scenario, the limit of the optimal distance of the robots from the wall is zero, and no robot can guarantee a minimum distance from the wall without fail. We further expand this task to include a competitive game, where one team, the 'conductor,' is positioned opposite a group of 'dancers,' all positioned along a line segment. The conductor has a limited-size memory. We conducted experiments, which show that, as the number of dancers grows, no conductor can force the dancers to fail in maintaining a minimum distance from the wall without fail.

To investigate impurity effects, we've analyzed the microwave frequency dependence of the NMR relaxation rate in the microwave field, alongside the critical temperature variation with distance in doped and undoped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ with different levels of contamination. Impurities seem to induce a greater upshift in $T_c$ with increased doping in optimally doped samples, without altering the superconducting state's nature. For underdoped and overdoped samples, impurities cause a more subtle response. We've observed a complex relationship between the microwave frequency and the distance from $T_c$, coupled with a phase transition-like behavior at which the superconductivity vanishes. These results align with the concept that CuO planes are type-II superconducting, sustained by quantum critical conditions brought on by cuprarate oscillations.

This passage discusses a model where crystalline-like curvature is employed to determine the movement strategy of a type of geometric object.  The key characteristics and numerical results of this model are reviewed, particularly focusing on the features that distinguish this model from its anisotropic curvature-based counterparts.  The discussion is primarily theoretical, although it also explores a related first-order partial differential equation and the outcomes of simulated experiments.  The discussion is informed by recent applications of this model in image analysis, the study of crystalline flows, and the investigation of phase-field equations.

Our novel method, referred to as GrowSpace, empowers artists to delve into plant sculpture, utilizing 3D-printed plant models that are infused with realistic growth patterns. These patterns are generated via the integration of growth tree algorithms and 3D modeling techniques, allowing artists to extrapolate plant states from the initial print and apply modifications, such as pruning and bending, to create unique sculptures. As these simulated objects grow, they may develop anomalies attributed to pruning, revealing novel forms, thus facilitating innovative artistic expression. GrowSpace can be accessed via a web-based platform where artists can create, modify, and share plant sculptures, including utilizing existing 3D models and printing fresh ones with customized growth patterns. We have demonstrated the potential of GrowSpace through various artistic collaborations, including print-based sculptures and living garden design. One of the largest benefits of GrowSpace is its ability to offer a wide artistic scope, extending from utilizing it as an artistic tool for exploring new concepts to utilizing it as a educational tool for introducing new generations to the field of artistic sculpture. We explore the more advanced techniques that allow GrowSpace to create life-like artificial tree sculptures that not only adapt over time, but also develop over time. We explore the potential of GrowSpace not only as a sculpture tool, but also as a tool for exploring new concepts in artificial tree creation.
