We define a notion called an outer algebra in a frame polynomial setting, where a polynomial's support shares a subcollection with a given frame polynomial. This concept aligns with the idea of outer order in a poset, seen in order theory. Our work, involving partial circle matroid determination, utilizes this concept and its associated outer algebra dimension. We demonstrate that a partial circle matroid with a ground set of size three or less is uniform if and only if its frame polynomial's associated outer algebra has dimension one. Additionally, our findings reveal that a partial circle matroid's ground set is a forest if and only if its associated outer algebra's framework is one-dimensional in every base. This leads to an extension of our previous research on outer order in integer partitions. We also establish general non-restricted matroid framework conditions for outer algebras based on a different approach.

Research into uncertainty within artificial intelligence has been ongoing for several decades, and one significant challenge in natural language processing is predicting its own reliability. Current advances in uncertainty modeling have been largely explored in tasks involving the interpretation of audio, and our study focuses on incorporating uncertainty into dialogue state monitoring via automatic speech recognition. We utilize the Word Confusion Networks to assess the uncertainty in ASR outputs and find that the divergence between language models and acoustic models provides a effective measure of uncertainty. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that incorporating uncertainty information enhances the effectiveness of DSMT, a system that monitors dialogue states, and outperforms using outputs from WFST-based ATOM.

We derive explicit formulas for calculating the total Eisenbud-Yekuteli invariants,
which gauge the presence of torsion in virtual structures defining t-structures on
derived categories of coherent sheaves on curves. This is accomplished via two approaches:
one grounded in algebra, which applies techniques for counting standard modules in
homological algebras, and another, more geometric, which leverages the concept of
t-structures generated by exceptional objects and the moduli of stable objects.
Furthermore, we obtain an explicit formula for the torsion suppression threshold in
Eisenbud-Yekuteli invariants which separates the contributions of torsion from those
of virtual structures. These findings have implications for a curve equipped with a
weighting, where the total Eisenbud-Yekuteli invariants can be split into components
reflecting Gromov-Witten invariants with specified point interactions based on the
weighting. This decomposition is central to the recent construction of local DT-invariants,
which ultimately enabled the proof of DT-Giveous-Witten conjecture for curves.

Lippert, Pommerehne, and Pchelin \cite{ppp15}, introduced a novel universal structure known as LPP-frames. This specific type of frame enables creating quantifier free defining formulae for classes that exhibit the property of delta-consistency. Initially, LPP-frames were proposed for classes containing only atomic sentences. An extension and generalized version of LPP-frames, known as Gpp-frames, was presented in \cite{ppp15}. Gpp-frames are used to define the concept of pseudo-compactness. An alternative and highly modified version of LPP-frames and Gpp-frames known as J-frame and pseudo-compactness J-frame (J-frames), was first proposed in \cite{ab18}. In this paper, it will be demonstrated that J-frames can be applied across a broader range of classes compared to LPP-frames and Gpp-frames. Additionally, the method of creating J-frames is based on existing universal structures which can be automated and rendered solvable through the implementation of a search algorithm. An implementation of this search algorithm was also made possible using the DLR+ program.

The optimal detection of entanglement in binary bosonic channels is being analyzed, involving direct and indirect detection methods that use optical systems for illustration. It's demonstrated that the direct approach, characterized by sending a universal probe and measuring all output fields, yields the greatest accuracy in entanglement detection. Furthermore, it's shown that for large-scale systems, this direct method can be simplified by focusing on a single, universally prepared field, outshining both classical-quantum and quantum-classical assessments. Notably, it's found that the requirement for multiple measurements in entanglement detection does not necessarily imply the necessity of multiple measurements for assessing quantum correlations between different system components.

The authors present an in-depth examination of the palm tree modes (PTM) observed in the JET tokamak, focusing primarily on their emergence, core characteristics, and influence on the plasma-edge stochastic magnetic field configuration. Extensive data analysis revealed that PTMs predominantly appear during plasma current iodine discharges when the magnetic axis is biased. The results indicate that PTMs occupy multiple plasma magnetically-ideal states. To further understand PTMs, the authors employed a ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) bi-parabolic axis symmetry model and showed that this symmetry is a hallmark of PTMs. The rapid, low-frequency fluctuations in the magnetic field correspond to sharp, high-frequency changes in the magnetic flux density, confirming that these two phenomena are interlinked. The rapid fluctuations arise from within the core plasma, originating from MHD activity, whereas the decay of these fluctuations at the boundary is attributed to stochasticity. The ideal nature of PTMs implies that they possess high-pressure, quasi-equilibrium characteristics reminiscent of quasi-axisymmetric alfv\'en modes. The rapid fluctuations resulted in partial stochasticization of the magnetic field surrounding the core plasma. The pressure associated with PTMs significantly exceeds the thermal pressure, suggesting that these modes may be pivotal in facilitating turbulent transport in the plasma edge through magnetic bifurcation.

To fully exploit the capabilities of pretrained models, it is crucial to grasp the underlying data patterns driving their exceptional performance. To this end, this paper delves into the application of the largest-pretained-language-model to real-world domain adaptation tasks, such as adapting a language model to a new domain without access to labeled data or a parallel corpus. Domain adaptation is a specialized topic within the broader field of transfer learning, which has gained significant attention in recent years. Nonetheless, existing research remains limited by the following key shortcomings: (a) most studies rely on artificially constructed datasets; (b) there is a lack of consensus on evaluation metrics; and (c) methods are often proposed as "one-size-fits-all" solutions without accounting for the inherent complexities of domain adaptation tasks. To address these shortcomings, this research establishes a comprehensive benchmark that incorporates publicly accessible, complex domain adaptation tasks across diverse domains, accompanied by detailed analysis reports, and encourages the research community to participate in evaluating the efficacy of language models in tackling domain adaptation challenges. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of interpreting the results of pretrained models through both their quantitative outcomes and the underlying data patterns that emerge during training. In doing so, this research demonstrates the capacity of pretrained models to capture inherent structural characteristics within data, thus facilitating the successful adaptation to novel domains.

This research introduces the HaveYouSeenThisExpression challenge, a benchmark for identifying hate speech in social media posts that incorporate emojis. To address this challenge, we investigated how emojis used in hate speech promote their own propagation. Our findings reveal that 11 specific emojis are commonly associated with hate speech across three languages (English, Italian, and Arabic). To mitigate the risk of overfitting, we developed a dataset of hate speech indicators without explicit labels through expert annotation. Moreover, we created an explanation rule set that translates the model's decision processes into plain text, demonstrating that the identified hate speech emojis act as a linguistic signal. To promote further research, we release the challenge's resources, including the dataset, benchmark solutions, and evaluation tools.

Synaptic connections between neurons are fundamental to various brain functions, including thought, memory, and regulation of sleep and wakefulness. The study of complex neural systems requires comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of their synaptic connections. While the locations of synaptic connections are crucial for neural development and spatial learning, the effects of varying connection extents have not been extensively explored. To investigate this, a mathematical model of a large population of type-I neurons with random synaptodendritic connections, known as a Erdös-Rényi network, is analyzed. By considering multiple synapse strengths, the research reveals that even weakly connected neurons can exhibit complex dynamics, including phase transitions and bistability, when triggered by sufficiently strong external stimulation. These findings have significant implications for understanding the role of random synaptic connections in simple neural systems, such as those found in the lamina in bee vision, and the effects of disease on neural function, including chronic neurodegenerative diseases and sleep disorders.

The effectiveness of fixing software bugs through program transformation heavily relies on applying the correct patch to the issue at hand. Unfortunately, existing methods of applying patching techniques are often limited in their scope and rely heavily on being close-ended. These limitations previous approaches sought to address by suggesting a list of potential fixes but overlooked a crucial aspect - the quality of the suggested fixes. In order to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of software fixing, we propose a new approach that involves the development of a contrasting transformation set to create opposing transformations. This method is proven to be successful by showcasing its use in repairing Z-notifying-related bugs in a J# code sample, demonstrating a remarkable 80% repair success rate.

This paper introduces a concept called data spectrum, defined as the distribution of data frequencies within a specified range. The capability region of a generalized inverse distribution function with an inverse catalyst is investigated in relation to different data spectrum patterns. Both theoretical results and numerical computations demonstrate that the optimal GIFC capability region corresponds to the data spectrum pattern characterized by the highest frequencies. The study also identifies the most frequent data spectrum pattern in conjunction with Gaussian distribution functions, and provides a step-by-step approach for constructing such patterns in conjunction with various distribution functions, including the Laplace, exponential, arcsine, and uniform distributions.

The flow of heavy ions on a target is followed by an explosion of debris particles that have varying velocities based on impact angle and energy. This complex motion contains information about how particles interact with each other during collision. Researchers have found that certain properties of this interaction can be determined from energy reactions, but not enough about how particles interact at different angles of impact are known. An instrument that measures three-dimensional flow has been proposed, called the Three-dimensional Flow Examinator, to investigate how particles interact under varying conditions for different collision energies and angles. Using this device, researchers can simulate real-world conditions and determine how particles interact under specific circumstances. An simulation using the Three-dimensional Flow Examinator was conducted to determine its capabilities, and it was found that this device can provide significant insight into how particles interact under specific conditions, such as at different angles of impact and energy levels.

The pandemic globally presents a double threat: the disease itself is deadly, and the efforts to contain it come with a significant cost to personal privacy.  By making early predictions with precision, we can potentially minimize the harm caused by lockdowns.  Notably, contact tracing is a key component of most COVID-19 containment strategies but raises substantial privacy concerns.  To address this, we employed adversarial training as a gold standard for creating robust models capable of withstanding data manipulation without sacrificing the model's predictive accuracy.  Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach on a diverse dataset of COVID-19 patient images by comparing it to other established defense techniques and revealing its superiority in withstanding sophisticated adversarial attacks.  Importantly, using only images of patient eyes, we were able to achieve a high degree of accuracy in diagnosing COVID-19, which could facilitate early detection and containment of local outbreaks.

In software-defined transmission systems, advanced modulation and coding methods can be implemented using sophisticated equalizers, yet these schemes require substantial computational power and complex controller designs. To address this, a new graph neural network-based approach called Decentralized Graph Neural Network equalizer (DGNN-EQ), is proposed for Channel Impairment Decoding Equalization (CIDE). This equalization process incorporates the nature of interference systematically, and can be applied to various types of distortions. Furthermore, a novel beta schedule is introduced to balance exploration and exploitation, leading to better convergence and improved performance. This method's efficiency is comparable to conventional methods such as Maximum-Likelihood (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) equalization, and offers promising scalability for decentralized systems.

The increased murder rate in Brazil, particularly in the state of Goias, has raised public concern, and understanding the regional variations is essential for developing effective interventions.  A clustering approach revealed significant areas of elevated murder rates relative to the national average, and not all hotspots have seen a rise in rates over time.  Moreover, areas that experienced an increase in murder rates were more likely to be considered high-risk regions.  This has implications for targeted interventions, as those in elevated murder rates may benefit from more intensive programs, while those in both elevated and increasing murder rates require immediate attention.

Stochastic gradient ascent is an algorithm widely used for optimizing complex, nonconvex, and high-dimensional functions that appear in numerous fields such as statistics, machine learning, and signal processing. The algorithm's efficiency can be significantly impacted by noisy gradient estimates, and its current forms lack the ability to respond to variations in noise levels and the local smoothness properties of the function, which may result in slow convergence or even false solutions. Our aim is to modify the algorithm in such a way that it is sensitive to noise levels, adapts to varying noise conditions, and achieves the best possible complexity bounds for which there are guarantees. Building on an existing method, we have developed a new, biased stochastic gradient ascent that is sensitive to noise, adjusts its step size in real-time, and provides improved performance bounds for certain optimization criteria. Furthermore, we have introduced a technique called "local variance estimation," which allows the algorithm to estimate its convergence rate and adjust its step size efficiently even when the variance of gradient estimates is unknown. The effectiveness of our approach has been demonstrated through numerical experiments which demonstrate reduced computational cost and faster convergence. Our method is complementary to existing acceleration techniques such as extrapolation, and we have modified these schemes to enhance their performance, particularly in noisy environments. Our modified methods outperformed their counterparts as confirmed through numerical tests.

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, introducing a new mass source for quarks and gluons while addressing strong CP issues. Various theories suggest axions interact either weakly or with electrons, making them plausible explanations for the dark matter phenomenon. Regarding their potential interaction with electrons, light sterile neutrinos, specifically neu- trinoless double beta decays, provide valuable constraints on their behavior. Regarding their potential interaction with photons, experimental bounds are most stringent, with further investigations necessary to validate the axion's role as a standard model's dark matter candidate. Specifically, the Pico axisymmetric solenoid astrophysics program aims to achieve a sensitivity of $10^{18}$ $\mu e^2$ for axions interacting with electrons, thus informing the axion's role in neu- trino masses and dark matter phenomena. This program can be achieved through the analysis of the 18.8 $\mu$G auto-correlation signal in the Jupiter plane, generated by the Sun. This signal's amplitude corresponds to the vector meson dominance model's predictions and can be described by the Hammerpeck function within a $10^6$ day time frame. This function would be used to determine the Sun's horizontal average magnetic field, providing insights into its differential rotation, thus constraining its subsurface turbulence level and structure, while offering a reference for the anticipated IAXO device's $10^{19}$ $\mu e^2$

We propose a novel bimodal model, capable of generating robust complex power grids that naturally inhibit blackouts and maintain a sustained dynamics with a wide operational range. The model can be applied to systems beyond power grids, such as biological and communication systems. In contrast to traditional systems, this bimodal model exhibits stable self-oscillating behavior when actively controlled, whereas conventional systems typically fail and become unstable under similar conditions.

Developing robots that can autonomously manipulate objects requires a substantial amount of data. Currently, there is a severe shortage of real-world robotic grasp data, with most existing datasets generated through costly and time-consuming robotic experiments. A novel approach presented in this paper enables the creation of a large robotic grasp dataset by leveraging computer simulations with a reduced number of simulated experiments. The proposed method is used to generate DexGraspNet, a 2.7 million robotic grasp dataset containing a diverse set of objects and grasps. The dataset is named DexGraspNet due to its association with the Dex-Net project, which employs monocular 2D grasp poses to program robotic grasping through a simulation-assisted framework. The dataset is named DexGraspNet and is made available to the research community. The methodology employed to generate this dataset is evaluated through a cross-dataset experiment and a real-world robotic experiment. The real-world robotic experiment demonstrates the significance of augmenting the dataset with diverse object orientations, which is found to reduce the grasping failure rate by 25% when cross-validated with a established grasp dataset called Cornell dataset. The research contributes a novel simulation-based method for generating a large robotic grasp dataset and contributes DexGraspNet to the research community, which is designed to complement existing real-world robotic grasp datasets to enhance robotic manipulation performance.

A novel approach is proposed to create four-dimensional (4D) T2-weighted turbo spin echo MRI data that incorporates motion corrections and accounts for respiratory variations in MRI sequences. This technique is essential in assessing various organs using T2-weighted imaging, as breathing significantly affects image clarity. To produce clear 3D images, MRI machines need to be adjusted accordingly, a task made challenging by constant respiratory changes. A study involving 50 volunteers used advanced modeling and data analysis to create a method for accurately measuring and accounting for breathing cycles in MRI scans, resulting in higher-quality 3D images with minimal need for image enhancement techniques. To our knowledge, this technique provides the most comprehensive study of in-vivo respiratory variations to date, offering new insights into the effects of breathing on human anatomy and opening doors for further research and medical applications.

Model efficiency has become a top concern in machine learning, and method development has accelerated in response. Specifically, knowledge distillation has emerged as a leading approach to model efficiency, but its effectiveness is largely determined by the choice of task and algorithm. We observed that the distillation process often conflicts with the inherent structure of the data, resulting in suboptimal performance and a lack of clear guidelines. We developed InDistill, a framework for preserving data flow in knowledge distillation, which can adapt to any task and algorithm. By integrating topology preservation, InDistill achieved superior performance with fewer parameters compared to prior methods.

Two different classes of smooth functions on the plane are defined, each consisting of functions that maintain a non-degenerate smooth attachment to linear functions across all but a finite number of points, with a specified constant smoothness level. We demonstrate that two such functions, each belonging to a unique class, are topologically equivalent when they exhibit similar behavior under a non-degenerate smooth transformation on their entire domain, but this property fails to hold if they only share a similar behavior on an increasingly large portion of their domain alone. Furthermore, this result has far-reaching implications as it proves that two linear-like functions on the plane that exhibit a non-degenerate smooth attachment to each other both inherently possess a smooth foliation that is topologically equivalent to that of a linear function across most of their domain. Conversely, this smooth foliation characteristic fails to exist for linear-like functions on the plane that exhibit a non-degenerate smooth attachment to each other across all but a finite number of points.

This research investigates the effects of non-local foraging on the development of plants in arid environments through a mathematical model that combines plant and herbivore populations. The model accounts for the plants' capacity for chemo-attraction, drawing in herbivores and stimulating seed production, as well as the herbivores' mobility influenced by plant chemicals. It shows that the plant population undergoes a bifurcation, transitioning from extinction to coexistence with the herbivores within a certain range of parameters. The model also exhibits instability in the herbivore population, leading to oscillations that can improve the chances of the plants' survival by periodically increasing seed production. These dynamics are similar to those observed in the model proposed by Kotila et al. in 2012, and it is demonstrated that the herbivores' mobility has a significant positive impact on the coexistence of the two populations.

A key probabilistic sketching technique called CountSketch efficiently calculates frequency vectors of large datasets by applying randomized operations and can recover a signal's support, but it has a significant flaw that can be exploited by clever inputs that take advantage of its randomness to hinder its performance. Researchers have found that there's an input class that can fool CountSketch and can do so repeatedly. Despite this limitation, the method remains widely used and useful, and there are variations that can withstand clever inputs to some extent. Our work provides the first hard evidence that limits its vulnerability to adapted inputs. Despite this, we explored hardwired variants of CountSketch that are immune to this limitation and provide near-optimal frequency vector recovery guarantees, and we propose a new variant that offers a trade-off between resistance to clever inputs and frequency vector accuracy. Researchers also developed an alternative sketching technique called HyperLogLog that offers efficient estimation of set cardinalities, but like CountSketch, it can be exploited by clever inputs. Our work provides the first hard evidence that limits its vulnerability to adapted inputs and provides the first trade-off between estimation accuracy and resistance to clever inputs.

Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) is an established method for computing the ground state of many-particle systems, offering a first-principles approach that's comparable in dimensionality to the density functional theory (DFT) method. Although QMC is less commonly used than it was in the past, it has recently seen a resurgence with the advent of more efficient algorithms and hardware, like graphics processing units (GPUs). However, QMC software is often tailored to in-house research and may lack versatility, featuring complex, low-level coding that's inaccessible to new researchers. To address these issues, a revised version of the ipie QMC code has been developed, incorporating features such as modular, language-agnostic interfaces and high-performance computing support for CPUs, GPUs, and hybrid systems. This updated ipie code has been demonstrated to effectively compute the ground state of small to large molecules containing up to 40 atoms on various accelerators. It has also been used in a study exploring the performance of different algorithms on a set of precise chemical benchmarks. Beyond its own capabilities, ipie serves as a prototype for a future unified quantum simulation framework, aiming to integrate multiple post-Hartree-Fock QMC methods into a single, shared code base.

Researchers have discovered that quantum computers can solve complex computational challenges faster and more efficiently than traditional computers, which could potentially transform fields such as cryptography and numerical simulations. Besides these applications, quantum computers may also revolutionize high-performance fields like numerical simulations, algorithm design, and complex problem-solving, leading some to believe that the future of computing will involve a hybrid model that combines classical and quantum capabilities, potentially altering industry landscapes. The potential impact of quantum computing on financial markets remains unclear, with some predicting that the first practical applications will appear on the "quantum cloud," a centralized network where secure, standardized quantum services can be accessed. To fully harness the potential of quantum computing, there is a pressing need for standardized, high-performance quantum cloud services that can enable a seamless and secure experience for users. The advent of quantum computing also raises crucial questions about data protection that need to be addressed in a timely manner, given that the transmission of data between classical and quantum systems, known as quantum-inspired technology, presents significant security risks due to potential leaks of sensitive information. The integration of quantum computing and blockchain technologies could potentially enable more secure and robust networks in the future, paving the way for advancements in fields such as data protection, network security, and distributed consensus. Our research involves implementing a quantum prisoner's dilemma experiment, which shows that entities will prioritize mutual benefit over self-interest when rewarded with positive outcomes, which could lead to the development of trustworthy relationships, eventually resulting in a collaborative environment where mutual benefit is the priority over self

To reduce energy consumption in electrical devices and lower associated costs,
a refundable energy rebate program has been suggested. This approach involves
offering customers a rebate for eliminating device usage or shifting it to off-
peak hours. Another proposal involves setting price peaks during times of high
electricity demand. These schemes aim to reduce energy consumption and raise
revenue for the power grid without violating refundability rules. This can be
translated into maximizing a profit function that considers the benefits from
reducing energy expenditure and maximizing income through rebate sales.
Optimizing this profit is an intricate problem due to constraints such as device
usage limitations, time constraints, and the requirement that total income and
rebate sales remain non-negative. This issue is resolved by dividing it into two
separate problems. Firstly, a minimum revenue target is achieved by determining
the optimal strategy for maximizing device usage across all times and days.
Subsequently, to optimize total profit, the optimal strategy for shifting device
usage to off-peak hours is found. Both problems can be solved using an adaptive
Newton algorithm. This algorithm reformulates non-linear problem constraints and
unlimited variables. Results indicate significant improvements in profit with the
proprietary price schedule, achieving 277.4% better than base profit and 44.7%
better than rebate sales. Meanwhile, the proprietary rebate scheme achieves 4.3%
better than price schedule and 12.6% better than rebate alone. Analytical

Generating a summary based on a document is a common task where a model interprets the meaning of sentences and combines key points to present the main idea. However, current methods struggle to extract crucial information, mainly because sentence comprehension is an intricate process requiring sophisticated models. Instead of relying on complex models, we suggest using a planner to direct a smaller language model into extracting significant details through thoughtfully designed prompts. Furthermore, we encourage the generation of higher-quality summaries by incorporating planning into the process and utilizing few-shot prompts that can be executed quickly. Experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses conventional methods in reconstructive summarization.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria. Additionally, the study offers alternative proofs for previously established theories and creates new mathematical theories related to the differentiability of functions with higher dimensions.

Human vocal expressions naturally synchronize with the contours of our spoken language due to their interconnected nature. To date, research on vocal synchronization in conversations has mainly focused on monologues, yet conversational interactions essentially consist of dyadic exchanges. This paper proposes a novel approach to detect vocal synchronization in dialogical contexts that takes into account the inherent structure and dynamics unique to dyadic conversations. Our computational method combines acoustic features with contextual factors, running across multiple time-scales from turn-to-turn to the overall conversation. It achieves a high accuracy of 85.4% when evaluated on a dataset comprising 1,672 conversational turns. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm not only identifies vocal synchronization but also reveals its relationship with the meaningful units of communication, the semantic units. This relationship affirms that vocal synchronization significantly contributes to the richness and emotional depth of conversational exchanges.

A fundamental challenge in physical systems corresponds to regulating their behavior, which involves implementing operations that preserve the quantum state.  Due to the restrictive nature of conservation laws, this task proves particularly difficult in physical laboratories.  However, the issue can be resolved by exploring the categorical equivalent of conservation laws, which provides an alternative perspective on the problem.  By integrating the principles of a strict sector ${\mathcal C}^{\bullet}$ of graded sets and a commutative diagram of functors $\Delta$, we can establish a meaningful connection between states, operations, and interactions on the unitary sphere ${\mathcal U}_1$, which represents the intersection of states with unit tensor norm and positive Hilbert-Schmidt norm.  A crucial regulator $\lambda$-S1 corresponds to a sub-bicategory of ${\mathcal C}^{\bullet}$ for any choice of real number $\lambda$, which allows us to define categorical versions of trace-preserving positive maps.  By analyzing the bicategory of regulators, we can establish an equivalence relation between equivalent elements, which provides a universal setting for describing interactions and their regulatory equivalents with no trace preservation.  A notable aspect of this approach is the linear nature of the functor $\Delta_1$ for any choice of real number $\lambda$, which facilitates certain inequalities for operator norms and arises from the geometry of the unitary sphere naturally.

Analytical, highly precise calculations of two types of quasiparticle disturbances' interactions in fractional quantum halls are performed, providing exact values for their interaction distances for specific distances and exact approximations for all distances. These precise analytical calculations validate recent exact numerical results, establishing a new benchmark for accuracy. They also set a benchmark for numerical research, revealing a broad range where analytical and numerical methods produce comparable results. Furthermore, exact calculations of two quasiparticle disturbance interaction within a fractional quantum hall's corrugated landscape are carried out, yielding exact distances for their interaction at any distance. A new technique for exact analytical corrections to this interaction is developed, enabling precise analytical calculations for the interaction at any distance.

In modelising the evolution of a ice sheet, scientists use a Stokes equation with a coercive part representing ice flow and a semicoercive part accounting for bed topography. However, the underlying mathematical problem associated with this model presents specific challenges, such as the presence of semi-coercive operators and elliptic inequalities with lower-order terms. These obstacles necessitate innovative numerical approaches that have yet to be developed. This work focuses on the finite element method for variational inequalities of Stokes type, with the objective of proposing and assessing a simple, limited-degree approximation for modeling ice flow with a fixed mesh structure, thereby avoiding the non-linear semi-smooth Newton method.

Galactic outflows are thought to be regulated by starburst-driven mechanisms that have a stabilizing effect on nearby interstellar medium, thus limiting the amount of material available for future star formation events.  To investigate this relationship in a controlled environment, we conducted a study of a distant starburst galaxy using observations from ALMA, MUSE, and MIR, which revealed outflows stemming from the galaxy's disk.  Using spatially resolved observations of [Si II] emission, a signature of the ISE, we mapped the outflows and discovered they extended beyond the galaxy's visible boundaries.  Nevertheless, the far-side of the outflows show elevated star formation activity, indicating the conclusion of a nearby starburst event.  Using a hydrodynamic model, we simulated the galaxy's behavior and found that the outflows result in the incorporation of material from the ISE into the central black hole's surrounding disk.  Consequently, the incorporated material appears to have triggered the black hole to emit high-energy radiation, thus facilitating the formation of stars in the galaxy's disk through a feedback loop.

We investigated triangular flow in 0.6 to 2A GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model. We discovered a distinct pattern where the ratio of triangular flow to elliptical flow is positively correlated with centrality, but only for collisions involving gold and a lab frame $p_T$ range of 1 to 5 GeV. This positive correlation is consistent with collective behavior during the initial 2-3 fm phase of these collisions. We noted that parton thermalization and a rapid equilibration of the medium are key factors contributing to this correlation. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that in copper collisions, $v_3/$\uzzz is negatively correlated with $p_T$, whereas in gold collisions, it is positively correlated in the 1 to 5 GeV $p_T$ range. This inverse relationship is influenced by an equal and opposite $v_3$ and $\uzzz$ response in triangular and elliptical flows.

A critical concern in robotics is the maintenance of stability and pose by (1) calculating the ideal system configuration through analytical methods, and (2) regulating the system dynamics to achieve and sustain a stable equilibrium. Deep learning has recently been applied to robotics, primarily for offline data analysis, whereas real-time, online predictions are typically based on conventional methods. However, the standard approach of combining separate pose estimation and control algorithms can result in slower processing and decreased overall efficiency. Furthermore, the conventional method employs individual features and can be prone to errors in pose estimation due to potential distractions or cluttered environments. We propose a novel algorithm that simultaneously processes visual and other data, and based on this, calculates and adjusts the system dynamics to maintain stability and optimize the results. Our experiments using a hexapod robot demonstrate that this new algorithm yields more effective outcomes compared to existing solutions.

We investigate whether depth prediction, a depth estimation task, serves as an effective means of pre-training convolutional neural networks for semantic segmentation, and thereby accelerate development of segmentation models. Traditional approaches rely on color images for depth estimation, making them suitable for pre-training convolutional neural networks. Since depth and color datasets often correlate, this allows for the transfer of knowledge from a large-scale color dataset to a much smaller dataset with labeled depths. This knowledge can then be leveraged for a variety of tasks, specifically semantic segmentation. Under the premise that networks initially recognize general scene characteristics, we analyze whether depth prediction, a task involving scene understanding with depth, can inform a more efficient identification of informative features for segmentation than classification, which primarily relies on low-frequency color information. Nonetheless, the link between depth and color images makes it difficult to accurately assess whether networks have learned meaningful features, as these may also correspond to the background's low-frequency texture rather than object boundaries. Our work addresses this issue by employing occlusion masking to distinguish between foreground objects and background, and uses the variation in shape rather than color and texture to define the informative features. We demonstrate that networks initially learned during depth prediction training are resilient to these variations. Our study is the first to thoroughly investigate the connection between depth and color information, and showcase that networks trained on depth can outperform those trained on classification by up to 2.3% mean intersection over union on the Cityscapes dataset.

For the class of log-harmonic functions, which is a subset of analytic functions, we derive the radius of the Bohr inequality within the unit disk. The logarithmic derivative of such functions leads to the definition of log-harmonic functions. The log-harmonic function has the property that its derivative within the unit disk is positive. The log-harmonic function can be parameterized using the definition, which results in its local univalence. The proof of our findings is achieved through the use of Potter's theorem and a convexity property. The numerical outcome obtained is considered to be an optimal solution. The method of our solution is considered to be distinctive. The class of log-harmonic functions is relatively novel within the literature of univalent functions. The method of our solution is considered to be distinct. The solution to the problem provides an understanding of certain parameters that define the class of log-harmonic functions. The solution to the problem is considered to be simple yet effective. The solution to the problem is further explored through its generalization, which is obtained by the limiting behavior of a function sequence. The solution to the problem is considered to be fruitful.

In statistical models employing Kendall's tau as its alternative hypothesis, the process of testing typically involves performing a hypothesis test by comparing the estimated parameter's value to a specific threshold. However, taking into account the parameter's statistical variability, which is reflected in its standard error, leads to the development of effective intervals where the alternative hypothesis would not be rejected. This study aims to explore the relationship between statistical models incorporating Kendall's tau by comparing their respective model effective intervals.

In automotive networks, edge cognition relies on collecting data from sensors along with edge processing units to expedite reaction times. The central hub, often present in modern vehicles, collects extensive sensor information. Although this setup simplifies system design, it poses security risks due to centralization and potential data exposure. This paper focuses on creating a distributed cognitive system that safeguards privacy by applying homomorphic encryption and a related technique called secure multi-party computation, utilizing an existing edge network architecture. A new protocol is proposed that integrates these methods, allowing two nearby vehicles to collaborate in cognitive tasks without disclosing their individual sensor data. This approach not only protects privacy by isolating sensitive information but also reduces communication demands. Preliminary evaluation demonstrates that the proposed protocol offers a balanced performance and security solution for edge cognition in automotive networks and confirms its potential scalability.

Data visualization benefits from dimension reduction techniques that allow for 
visual understanding of high-dimensional data. This becomes particularly 
important in the context of feature importance across various models. No 
research has been conducted on creating visualizations that convey importance 
across multiple features. This study introduces Euler Significance Surfaces, a 
novel dimension reduction method that facilitates the visual exploration of 
feature importance across multiple features. Euler Significance Surfaces are 
capable of maintaining intricate data characteristics and are computationally 
feasible for model interpretation. Experimental results demonstrate the 
accuracy of our method and its capacity to detect data structure patterns, 
revealing new insights in the field of text classification and latent variable 
selection.

Bigell and Allen's predator-prey model, developed from Holling-Tanner and Holling-Tanner-Ryder frameworks, introduces a predator behavior model. This model incorporates complex life stages of predators, satiation, response variables, predator responses to prey, predator mortality, predator birth rates, predator responses delayed due to low prey densities, and a significant effect of low prey populations on birth rates and predator responses. The model's requirements for stability have been identified and specific conditions have been established for stability within certain parameter ranges. Additionally, we examined how delays affect dynamic behavior in three distinct scenarios: small, moderate, and large delay, and confirmed previous findings for small delays while revealing new information for moderate and large delays. We observed that dynamic patterns for moderate delays resemble those for large delays and identified unique features of each. Lastly, we applied our model to specific ecological contexts: an arctic tundra ecosystem with migratory predators and a mountain ecosystem with climbing predators.

This second part of a study expands upon the initial concept of Aspect Pivot Simplex algorithm by integrating the second-order critical set into the methodology. The algorithm's enhanced version attains a linear iteration convergence rate under certain conditions, surpassing the previous non-linear rate. The new approach, termed APS2, establishes a connection with Cholesky factorization algorithm and QP simplex algorithm, and demonstrates that these three algorithms share a common iteration structure.

This research investigates the structure of the NK1 multilinear collective group, built from a graded ring, with particular emphasis on a specific type of graded ring that satisfies a certain condition. It finds that if a particular component of the graded ring fails to meet this condition, the NK1 group will not demonstrate key characteristics and may not even be generated by a single element. Additionally, this research clarifies the relationship between the NK1 group and another related collective group, while exploring the connections between the Nakayama monoid, the reversible element factorization class, and certain types of group monoids.

The top quark plays a pivotal role in many significant processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Specifically, the top quark's observability is critical in extracting its mass from events involving top quark pairs, which are further influenced by additional jet radiation. Accurate predictions of the top quark's behavior require a thorough understanding of all particle shell states. Notably, the current theoretical framework used in top quark research, known as Fixed-Order Perturbation Theory, does not yet fully take into account off-shell shell contributions. To bridge this gap, a phenomenological correction has been developed, which effectively captures the influence of these off-shell contributions and aligns with results from a more comprehensive theoretical method known as Parton Shower Perturbation Theory. This phenomenological correction is then applied to events involving top quark pairs in conjunction with a hadronic jet, which involve complex interactions such as additional jet radiation, leading to a significant correction of approximately 30% of the underlying Born process. This highlights the top quark's intricate behavior even in what initially appears to be simple events.

The proliferation of accessible deep learning resources online poses a significant threat to privacy, as images can be easily queried to extract personal data. To determine the efficiency of vision transformers for extracting facial features, a zero-shot facial countermeasure framework is applied to existing datasets. Experiments were conducted on three public facial anti-spoofing datasets, comparing the performance of vision transformer models with various hidden dimensions. Results demonstrate the superiority of vision transformer models over conventional architectures, with a 25% accuracy improvement on the COLON dataset. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's stability across diverse datasets indicates that vision transformers consistently outperform their baseline counterparts, serving as a robust and efficient solution for zero-shot facial countermeasure tasks.

Autonomous vehicles pose a significant challenge to researchers and engineers, 
who must develop techniques that ensure the vehicle behaves as human drivers would 
by considering vision, distance judgments, and other factors. Deep neural networks 
have shown great potential in replicating human-like decision-making for self-driving 
vehicles. This paper presents a profound reinforcement learning system for autonomous 
vehicles that combines high-level decision-making with low-level control. Our approach 
integrates a deep neural network that integrates visual data with sensor readings, 
positioning, and other vital data. This module enables the vehicle to navigate by 
assigning importance weights to sensors and adjusting its position accordingly. 
Additionally, a deep neural network is employed to regulate the vehicle's speed and 
steering. To teach this module how to drive, we have developed a custom dataset and 
training method that analyze vehicle behavior and learn from these parameters. 
Results demonstrate that our system achieves reliable and efficient decision-making, 
despite facing uncertainties during training. Furthermore, our approach outperforms 
other methods in real-life driving situations.

A newly proposed parent selection scheme is presented to mitigate the effects of evaluation time bias, a phenomenon that occurs in parallel evolutionary techniques. The cause of this bias arises from the prioritization of solutions with lower fitness values that have spent more time evaluating their fitness. The proposed NCF parent selection scheme determines parent populations based on the frequency of solution evaluation instead of fitness. It ensures that solutions which have been evaluated for a longer time have a relatively higher chance of being selected. Experimental results across six widely used benchmark suites demonstrate that NCF is capable of decreasing the impact of evaluation time bias to near zero, resulting in a distribution of inverse generation ranks that is consistent and comparable to that of bias-prone Parallel Genetic Algorithm. Furthermore, when compared to parent selection schemes that account for the uneven cost of solution evaluation, it has been shown that NCF is capable of producing superior quality solutions. The source code of NCF and the MOEA using NCF parent selection scheme is publicly available at https://github.com/fortrude/ncf-parallel-moea.

The gravitational lensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth asteroid that had the potential to being one of the most massive objects to have been discovered through this method, with a mass that could reach up to 0.99 masses similar to that of Earth. Initially identified as having a moderate angular gravitational force, with peak strength close to 4.3 units, the event was identified for two years due to weak Gravitational Michaelson-Morley wave interference. Located at a distance close to the galaxy's disk plane, with angular gravitational force multiplicity of 7.7, the event used isothermal ellipsoidal models that took into consideration the planet's effects on electron mobility across the source star. Isophotometric data from the source star also validated the planet's mass and the effects of lensing effects, with a significant impact being identified only for the central region of the star due to its high density, with the outer layers having minimal effects due to their low mass. Furthermore, the data used to identify the planet also ruled out the possibility of a rogue planet, with the effects of the environment being identified only when the planet's mass was taken into consideration, with the surrounding area remaining unchanged. With the primeval gas disk having an exterior density that could be similar to 10% of the Earth's mass, the model used to identify the planet also showed that it could well explain ISM properties. We define a class of operators called pseudo-differential operators with complex inner support. We derive an approximation method for these operators by leveraging their expansion in terms of hyperbolic Fourier modes, effectively reducing the approximation error to a certain measure of the operator's smoothness. This approximation method is particularly useful for high-speed iterativley converging algorithms in the context of the iterated perturbation approach, commonly applied in the analysis of open quantum systems.

Using zone plate-focused neutron beams, we investigated ferromagnetism in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{x}$ using long-wavelength neutron diffraction and dipolaron resonance neutron spectroscopy. Our findings from the first method focused on wave vectors near (220) and revealed the onset of ferromagnetism below 20 K for 0.05<x<0.15, where T$_{CF}$=19 K for this range increased linearly with x, implying magnetization. For 0.17<x<0.32, this research yielded higher-order magnetic satellite structures, providing ordered moment values, and showing immune spins from the dipolaron spin glass for 0.23<x<0.32. Utilizing polarized neutron reflectometry, we determined the dipolaron spin glass transition at roughly 15 K for nearly all compositions studied. Our analysis reveals neusron depolarization from the dipolaron spin glass contributes little to the primary magnetic mode detected, but likely affects higher-order modes, as seen within the range 0.17<x<0.32.

Research into the emission spectrum of hydrogen at narrow frequencies is crucial for understanding the complex physical conditions within dense interstellar clouds. A study of the star-forming region, G176.51+00.20, focused on HI narrow-line emissions, revealing conditions similar to those found in other massive star-forming clouds. Further analysis into the emission spectrum of hydrogen at high frequencies observed an asymmetrical frequency distribution, supporting the model of cloud pressure gradient. By incorporating radiation pressure in models of cloud formation, results suggested the presence of dense, cloud-generating molecular shells. A generated map of cloud column density, based on hydrogen emission data, showed patterns aligning with outflowing jets, observed through other spectral emissions. Findings indicated that cloud pressure, rather than density, drove the movement of cloud material, supporting the model of cloud material drawn towards a central protostar by gravitational force. Observed frequencies of hydrogen also suggested protostar mass estimates and identified a region of low cloud pressure at a specific distance from the central protostar. A calculated ratio of cloud pressure to total pressure within this region compared well to pressures measured in surrounding interstellar clouds. Estimated flow rates of material leaving the cloud through outflows compared well to those observed in other massive star-forming clouds.

A theoretical framework is introduced to investigate intermediate beta decays, a type of transition that occurs when a nucleus undergoes beta decay as a result of complex interactions driven by the transfer of neutrons, protons, or alpha particles. This theory posits that these intermediate states can be formed distantly prior to the final decay and, in some cases, not in the initial stages of the decay process, with the initial and final states typically having distinct orbital angular momentum values. Furthermore, the transfer of particles plays a crucial role in determining the beta decay rate, with this rate being influenced by the energy released during the transfer and the associated distance between the initial and final states, effectively forming a type of third-order process. This third-order process competes with the first-order process, causing its signature to manifest in various phenomena: (i) in beta-doubleton systems, it may result in a shift or splitting of the decay rate, depending on the relative strengths of the involved particle transfer and the beta decay processes; (ii) in systems undergoing beta decay as part of a particle transfer reaction, it can give rise to a spectrum consisting of a group of closely spaced, weakly emitted particles followed by a strong beta decay; (iii) in systems undergoing beta decay as part of a particle transfer reaction with the final state having a gap in its neighboring energy levels, it can result in a spectrum consisting of a group of closely spaced, weakly emitted particles followed by a strong beta decay after a long delay

The study provides an initial assessment of the CP-violating phase, φs, in certain decay processes, specifically Bs->J/π+π- with both pi mesons having intermediate states. Each intermediate state was analyzed to ensure it doesn't belong to a specific system's wave function and to detect any possible CP violation within the resonant particles. After applying this analysis to all available data from LHCb experiments, it has determined a φs value that is consistent across various measurements, thereby yielding a combined result of -0.08 ± 0.12 ± 0.03 radians, indicating that it deviates from the Standard Model's predicted value by 0.4 standard deviations. Furthermore, the study demonstrates an average deviation in φs from the Standard Model's predicted value as the s-wave component grows, indicating that it's in line with predicted squaring behavior from the amplitudes model.

Deep learning models, being significantly large in number, necessitate careful selection before deployment across varied contexts, yet training them for a specific task without expecting similar results for another is impractical, given the influence of the dataset and design on their performance. Research suggests that similar models, when trained on different datasets, exhibit distinct performance characteristics, prompting the need for methods to adapt or modify existing models for new tasks without requiring them to be retrained from scratch. Our study focuses on the comparison of open-source domain migration methods in the context of image classification, where we evaluate several deep learning models, trained on different datasets, against a range of migration techniques. Our analysis indicates that the performance of images can vary based on the domain, domain shift affecting the performance of models regardless of their complexity or architecture. Our comparison of migration methods reveals initial successes with ADAMLAR, DOAM, and DMLAR methods but calls for further investigations due to issues like overfitting with large datasets for image classification tasks.

In the fields of combinatorics and algebra, a growing area of study has been
establishing precise calculations for diverse objects that can be considered
projective configurations over finite fields. The study of arcs and extended
arc collections in these environments has been a significant area of focus. A
specific sub-set of these arcs, known as sectars and influence arcs, hold crucial
importance for both linear and nonlinear covering problems in finite fields.
Following established methods by Dembowski and later Baker and Norin, we
determine the exact counts of curves in 2D finite fields that meet a minimum
separation requirement from point pairs. The result generalizes prior findings
concerning crossing numbers in graphs and provides implications for a specific
case involving a petal arrangement in a 3D sphere.

A visual demonstration of a geometric relationship involving triangles in a grid showcases that in a triangle, the sum of the interior angles equals 180 degrees. This relationship is further validated through a parallel angle theorem.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant attention in recent years due to their capabilities in handling graph-based data, outperforming other models. GNNs are being utilized in multiple applications such as drug representation, protein analysis, and chemical property prediction. In contrast to existing approaches, our proposal takes a different direction by proposing GraphNN, a parameterized interpreter that explains and analyzes the internal workings of GNNs. Instead of generating an explanation per sample, which can be lengthy and unfeasible for large datasets, our model produces explanations per sample with negligible computational overhead. Additionally, explanations generated by GraphNN are transparent, comprehensible, and modifiable. We validated the efficacy of our model through extensive experiments conducted on multiple publicly available datasets. The source code and explanations are accessible at https://github.com/pcpc3/GraphNN.

We examined the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 using the NOEMA interferometer, analyzing its galaxy distribution and the thermal gas within the cluster. At a redshift of 0.28, this galaxy cluster offers a rare opportunity to investigate the dynamics of a galaxy cluster at a distant distance through a far-infrared frequency range. Our observations revealed a situation where the thermal gas within the cluster was experiencing adverse conditions that could indicate either adiabatic compression or adiabatic expansion within the 400-600 kiloparsec radius zone. As a result, we saw a substructure in this galaxy cluster that forced us to reevaluate our assumptions about the dynamics within the cluster. Our observations revealed the presence of individual stars and protostellar objects within the 10-100 kiloparsec radius zone of four galaxies. We were able to identify 14 protostellar entities located at a significant distance from their host galaxies, indicating they were formed early on. Two of these early formations were associated with galaxies that have only recently started to lose their mass. These associations show signs of being young star clusters rather than mere clouds. Our analysis also revealed signs of recently interrupted star formation in several galaxy elliptical entities within the cluster.

The recently introduced Legendre Memory Module, incorporating a forgetfulness mechanism into LSTMs and GRUs, significantly improves convergence and performance by mitigating vanishing gradients. Yet, its sophisticated component, the Bank of Sigmoid Capacitors, poses challenges for parallel training. This paper presents two optimized LMMS implementations with parallelization strategies tailored to low- and high-resource hardware. The resource-efficient approach, leveraging a shared memory layer, allows for efficient training on CPUs. In contrast, the distributed LMMS variant replicates memory components on separate GPUs and combines its output before inputting it into the recursive network. The proposed parallelization strategies were evaluated across a range of tasks and demonstrate reduced training and evaluation times of up to 20.96x and 10.29x respectively.

Recent experiments using sensitive technologies have shown promising results in identifying elusive particles like dark photons and new, rare forces, offering a rare opportunity to amplify the Standard Model's parameter space and potentially reveal clues for future particle physics studies at large facilities.

In studies of the origins of language, 'labeling games' and 'evolutionary games' have been employed to model human language usage and understand its development. Previous research has primarily focused on the effects of gradual population replacement on linguistic patterns. Conversely, this study investigates what happens when groups of individuals with established language patterns interact through participation exchange. A theoretical model devised for this purpose reveals that, unlike previous findings, the standard labeling language may not be the ultimate equilibrium, and instead, non-standard languages can coexist and resist extinction. Additionally, the model's results depend on the rates at which players engage in labeling tasks and maintain consistency, and it is observed that a symmetrical equilibrium is the most likely outcome.

Momentum-based methods in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) significantly reduce the impact of spectral bias by incorporating a connection mechanism that effectively redistributes residual errors towards features with larger absolute values in the residual space. This results in better PINN performance and reduced spectral bias, and notably, improves the network's ability to handle problems involving small residual errors by shifting its focus to features with larger absolute values. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between residual errors and network weights, and propose that momentum mainly reduces the spectral bias of the data rather than addressing the issue of underfitting or overfitting.

In this study, we examine the behavior of solutions to a modified Kelvin-Helmholtz equation, which accounts for the interactions of two wave equations within adjacent regions with distinct viscoelastic properties. We specifically investigate the presence of exponential stability in the absence of damping within the interior domain and the behavior of energy in the exterior domain. Using a combination of the extension principle for elliptic problems and the separation of variables, we establish rigorous proofs of our findings, which contribute to a deeper understanding of hyperbolic equations with non-uniform viscoelastic properties.

In the increasingly complex AI landscape, a pressing issue is gaining insight into AI systems that frequently fail to meet this demand. As such, we introduce an innovative reinforcement learning algorithm that enhances transparency. This algorithm, developed for control tasks, utilizes Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) to analyze the reward function and train the agent. ILP's ability to provide insight into AI system's decision-making enables the creation of crystal-clear reward functions and facilitates the extraction of high-level rules governing agent behavior. This approach is highly effective in complex, high-dimension environments where traditional reinforcement learning may face difficulty. Our proposed method empowers users to extract transparent high-level decisions from reinforcement learning agents even in resource-constrained environments with limited observable state information.

We explore an idea that varies the orientation of an optical beam's polarization state as it moves along its path, born out by numerical simulations that show how the phase and amplitude of left and right circularly polarized states change in relation to each other during propagation in a parabolic mirror cavity. This polarization state variation arises from the quantum compression of optical beams entering the cavity, resulting in their asymmetrical behavior. If a perfectly symmetric input is applied to the cavity, the cavity will produce optical radiation exhibiting asymmetrical polarization, explicitly demonstrating the non-classical characteristics of the beams entering the cavity due to their intrinsic asymmetrical polarization property.

This paper investigates two Fenton-type minimax problems related to the total of certain translated functions. We establish a theorem providing a criterion for the existence of solutions, as well as a statement governing the number of solutions. Our findings are achieved through the use of variational methods, particularly the direct variation method and Morse theory, in the setting of the Banach algebra of total transfinite functions.

The $^6$Li detector technique is utilized to explore novel approaches for identifying dark matter interactions that are sensitive to spin. Research indicates that such interactions can be effectively detected using Li-based detectors due to their naturally occurring mix of isospin states. The $I=1$ scattering state of the $^6$Li isotopes is particularly notable for this, as it exhibits unique characteristics not found in other dark matter targets. Notably, Li-targets are capable of distinguishing between spin-dependent and spin-independent interactions simultaneously, providing separate clues about dark matter interactions at a detailed level. This distinctive property presents an opportunity to identify Li-based targets as a unique asset within the portfolio of dark matter detection experiments.

This research introduces the Kernel Mixture Model, an unsupervised learning approach comprised of a mixture of Gaussian kernels. It is then applied to the field of blind image restoration, where the kernel parameters and weight are concurrently optimized. The kernel mixture is formed by sampling from a neighborhood of each image pixel's gradient. The model's coefficients and gradient parameters are optimized using the alternating maximization algorithm. The optimization of the coefficient vector enables the identification of the most prominent kernel, while the gradient parameter matrix is filled with diverse kernel positions. The identification of the most prominent kernel suffices to perform a limited detail transformation on the image, the reconstruction of the image's neighborhood based on multiple kernels ensures details preservation, and storing diverse kernel positions enables the retrieval of adjacent kernels, thereby safeguarding image information during the restoration process. The effectiveness of the proposed KM Model is demonstrated through various experiments on well-known image denoising and deblurring datasets, where the results are obtained at approximately the same training time as the state-of-the-art FastNLOF algorithm.

This paper introduces a new concept called uniform and nonuniform multiparameter associative Yang-Baxter equations, and establishes connections with bihom and algebroidal cross products, as well as non-unital extended algebroidal cross products. We derive methods for constructing weak Hopf algebras, semigroups and quasitriangular bihom Hopf algebras from solutions to these equations, and prove that the uniform and nonuniform versions have equivalent properties.

Formal verification through Hoare logic is highly effective at ensuring correct program performance, yet its primary limitation lies in the program's annotation requirement. In this study, we propose a novel approach called Natural Hoare Reasoning, an advanced technology that integrates natural language program annotations with Hoare logic, allowing for the formal proof of program correctness based solely on Hoare logic and the semantic translation of these annotations into logical expressions. Furthermore, we establish a method for automatically interpreting the semantic meaning of these annotations through linguistic analysis. This methodology breaks down an algorithm expressed in a programming language and expresses it in a more high-level, logical manifestation that facilitates in-depth reasoning and verification. To achieve this goal, we utilize compositional semantic techniques and a library of predefined program fragments along with their corresponding Hoare logic specifications to assist in the proof process. This approach is successfully demonstrated in a range of examples, revealing its potential for expanding the scope of formally verifiable programs and enabling the formal proof of program correctness from naturally expressed descriptions.

Distributed consensus faces two significant challenges: ensuring consistency in the presence of failures and protecting against rogue nodes. The two problems have distinct solutions, particularly for state machines, which require specific input data to maintain accuracy. In contrast, object-level consensus can provide flexibility in handling failures, while resisting rogue nodes requires the implementation of a virtual vote system. The existing consensus protocols often involve a balance of performance, reliability, and security, with different algorithms prioritizing these aspects differently. The current consensus protocols span multiple categories, with many not meeting the criteria for at least one of these dimensions. Among the reliable protocols, many fail to meet the criteria for performance, and those performing well tend to fail the reliability criterion. A new protocol, RCanopus, is introduced, which is designed for high-performance operation under various failure scenarios while remaining resilient to rogue nodes. The protocol is built upon a novel data structure, called an ordered bidirectional self-adjusting list, to improve efficiency and is tested in a distributed environment for its performance characteristics.

We have used molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how a specific type of phospholipid interacts with cholesterol in an aqueous environment. Cholesterol is known to interact with lipids in a specific arrangement, leading to variations in membrane structure depending on the concentration of cholesterol. To further understand this interaction, we utilized different types of lipids containing specific chemical groups and assessed how these groups affect the membrane in the presence of cholesterol. Our simulations reveal that as the membrane adapts to the presence of cholesterol, certain lipids with specific chemical groups exhibit more efficient mixing than others, particularly when containing hydroxyl hydrophobic groups. To provide a more comprehensive explanation, we used theoretical models to analyze the geometric structure of the lipids and relate it to their behavior in the presence of cholesterol. Our results show a significant correlation between this geometric structure and the efficiency of mixing of the lipids. However, these geometric variations also lead to significant inaccuracies in estimating the membrane's bending rigidity, particularly when considering the presence of cholesterol. Therefore, we developed an alternative method for estimating this parameter, and our results demonstrate a much higher accuracy. Our simulations provide approximately a 10-fold reduction in the precision error. Our results can offer insights into the biological mechanisms that govern the interaction between lipids and cholesterol in membranes.

Traditional approaches to integrating quantum gravity and cosmology, such as the Hamiltonian formulation and LQC, rely on the asymmetrical dilation of time, making it a well-studied topic in the past. Recent findings indicate that incorporating asymmetrical dilation into the Hamiltonian leads to significantly differing results compared to the conventional loop quantum cosmology model. This being the case, it is essential to explore models derived directly from the ADM Hamiltonian, using a scaled metric tensor, to see if they align with the established LQC model. This article seeks to address that question. Following a thorough discussion of the underlying methodology, this paper constructs cosmological models from the ADM Hamiltonian for both scalar metrics, the paddle-like and De Witt, incorporating quantum corrections while keeping key aspects of the theory intact. Subsequently, this model is compared to conventional LQC models. Notably, our results indicate that these new models exhibit quantum effects at a higher scale in comparison to the conventional LQC models. This is an essential consideration for any new cosmological models emerging from the integration of quantum and gravitational theories.

This register showcases the universe's most energetic particles captured by the Pierre Auger Observatory between 2003 and 2008, which serve as validation examples for the experiment's fiducial volume's sensitivity to ultra-high energy particles.

In deep object detectors, overspecification and failure cases can lead to falsely predicted bounding boxes. The uncertainty associated with these cases is crucial for real-world decision-making, such as in autonomous driving, but is often lacking in current deep learning-based approaches. To address this gap, we propose BayesOD, a novel framework for assessing uncertainty in object detectors through a multi-stage object detection process. By assuming object existence, BayesOD relies on a classification uncertainty to filter out valid detections and utilizes correlation to suppress overlapping bounding boxes. Our approach also incorporates a uncertainty-aware non-maximum suppression to further refine the output. Our results indicate that BayesOD outperforms existing uncertainty-related methods and provides significant performance improvements, particularly in high-density scenes.

Recent interest in traffic forecasting has been sparked by the potential for smart
city planning. Many existing methods are limited to predicting large sections of
roadway, ignoring the complexities at an intersection micro-level. They primarily
utilize historical flow data, neglecting the significance of time-of-day and day-of-
the-week factors. Furthermore, these methods focus solely on predicting total
traffic density, rather than the intricate movements of individual vehicles. In
response, we developed a new approach involving convolutional neural networks
and attention mechanics. Our approach leverages current traffic patterns along with
the time of day and day of the week to forecast future traffic with enhanced
spatial resolution. We demonstrated the efficacy of this novel method by achieving
lower average speeds on bus routes in New York City.

In logic and proof theory, a well-known concept known as Gentzen's Intuitionistic Natural Deduction is employed to derive coherence theorems for various kinds of categories. Building upon this foundation, researchers have developed an extension called Natural Gray, which incorporates revisions and "gray" rules into Intuitionistic Natural Deduction. However, the original method had a limitation in its ability to apply to categories that are not gray, causing researchers to explore alternative approaches. One such innovation is the creation of a new method called gray structure, which serves as an implementation of Natural Gray. This allows researchers to work within a specific class of gray categories that can be treated as if they are instances of the original category, known as the 2-indexed gray structure. However, this approach comes with a limitation as it is only applicable to certain categories. To address this issue, researchers have developed a more general method called a gray category, which can be used to derive coherence theorems. This approach is based on a 3-indexed gray structure, which can be used to simulate a gray category in a way that is analogous to the method employed by researchers to treat categories as if they are equal to 2-categories. Building upon this, researchers have derived a method to apply revisions in gray categories, which enables the creation of a coherence theorem that can be applied universally. Additionally, researchers have applied this method to derive results in S4 modal logic.

Convolutional neural networks have been heavily utilized in medical imaging and related research, particularly when analyzing hippocampamal images in relation to seizures and Alzheimer's disease. Previous studies involving 1D CNNs were found effective in determining hippocampal boundary locations in the anterior to posterior direction. However, when trying to analyze the boundary in the x and z dimensions, accuracy suffered due to the presence of lesions and the complexity of x and z directional data.
