A recently created TTS model called FastPitch was designed for speed, using 1 second wave Nets and Sinsewerse for timbre control.  However, FastPitch's frame-level structure makes it poorly suited for longer-than-1-second speech generations and difficult to manage its pitch at longer durations.  Our solution involves separating the speech into sub-timbres at 10 cent intervals and using these to control pitch.  Our model is called TimbrePitch FastPitch.  In comparison to FastPitch, our modified model provides more accurate speech even at 5 second durations, as well as better pitch management across speech durations.  Our results also indicate that TimbrePitch FastPitch generates more natural sounding sentences with higher mean COS scores.  Our code can be found at a GitHub repository.

Video body media retrieval and video-to-video translation are highly complex
tasks, involving video frames' temporal evolution and spatial distribution.
Current approaches often focus on straightforward predictions or straightforward
supervisions, but this narrow focus hinder's performance on challenging video
data.  We introduce a novel video understanding model, called Hopper, which
explores multi-hop reasoning within videos' temporal and spatial domains.
Hopper generates a sequence of semantic frames by incrementally refining its
temporal representation of video content. It then extracts a comprehensive
video sequence by combining these frames. We evaluate Hopper on important
video tasks such as video copy detection, video retrieval, person re-identification,
and video-to-video translation. Hopper achieves significant improvements
on four challenging video tasks while being efficient due to its relatively
low parameter count (around 104M) and fast inference speed (around 20fps).

To minimize systematic uncertainties in semileptonic final states, we examine the production of same- and opposite-charge W bosons along with two hadronic b-quarks, specifically in the context of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at a 13 TeV LHC energy. These experiments have previously constrained the W boson mass, and to further understand neutral current double differential distributions, we investigate a new template technique involving lepton pair creation in association with two b-quarks. We explore potential gains in statistical accuracy and identify scenarios where additional statistical benefits can be obtained, as well as instances where analysis bias is introduced due to template overlap issues. Moreover, we assess the feasibility of separating single-top and W boson contributions using this analysis approach.

Telepresence robot (TPR) remote access allows users to explore virtual environments via mobile robots that map real-world settings onto remote computer interfaces. To improve the TPR experience, a quality of experience (QoE) metric was developed to quantify the impact of network disturbances on remote viewing by measuring user satisfaction. This feedback was positive for smooth interactions but severely negative for degraded performances such as freeze, loss, delay, and tramlining. An online experiment with over 210 participants confirmed that network disruptions severely affected user experience, with mild impacts from increased latency. This study's findings provide TPV service providers with quality of experience guidelines to navigate network disturbances and enhance the remote viewing experience.

Time series forecasting models, such as ARIMA and Exponential Smoothing, offer efficient solutions for small and medium-sized datasets but become impractical for large sets of datasets (datasets of 50-500 time series over a significant time frame). In such cases, more advanced time series forecasts with deeper neural networks are preferred but become challenging to manage and impractical to iterate over for analysts and researchers when tuning hyperparameters and interpretations. The integration of a Bayesian framework into these models helps to overcome these challenges by providing a straightforward way to specify prior distributions and obtain accurate posterior distributions of the parameters. The model becomes even more efficient by applying hierarchical modeling techniques that allow for different parameters to be modeled at various levels, resulting in the Bayesian Hierarchical Linear Forecasting model. The model can be easily modified and improved upon by incorporating theoretical time series components and other scientist's knowledge of time series characteristics and can also be used to accurately determine uncertainty levels and forecast errors, thus making it a reliable tool for analysts. The model has the potential to become a more widely used and influential tool in the field of time series analysis and forecasting.

The numerical model we're proposing mimics the gameplay of the popular Mafia game, including features like player roles, voting, and deadly nocturnal activities. We've developed an open-source code using Python, enabling users to simulate the game by generating random role assignments, playing through multiple rounds, and saving data for further analysis. This code also includes a data visualization tool. Both the model code and this description are intended to inspire an investigation into the game's underlying statistical properties.

This study investigates how gas accumulation in a developing planetary system impacts the characteristics of the planets and their surrounding disk. Using a advanced simulation tool, we modeled a dual planet system forming within a disk that experiences an external pressure gradient, with one planet developing up to double the mass of Jupiter while the other reaches Jupiter's mass. Throughout the simulation, we examined gas accumulation, planet movement, and how gas accumulation affects the transfer of material from the outer to the inner disk. Our results show that external pressure gradient effects minor distortion to the disk's configuration but establishes a distinct gas accumulation pattern in which the less massive planet attracts gas, while the more massive planet experiences reduced gas accumulation due to its internal pressure. This phenomenon determines the final mass of the planets, and their movement is primarily influenced by a gravitational interaction that results in the less massive planet orbiting within the outer massive planet's Roche limit. Ultimately, our simulation concludes with a massive dual planet system comprising one planet with 1.2 times the mass of ten Jupiter masses and the other with 0.6 times the mass of ten Jupiter masses, and their movement continues to be mutually regulated despite gas accumulation.

Theorists suggest that mode-specific electrical conductivity mediated by phonons could exist in carbon nanotubes' low-diameter ranges.  However, this concept has yet to be supported by experimental data.  In this context, single-wall carbon nanotubes with a uniform alignment were grown on a silicon substrate and had their resistivity measured over a broad temperature range.  An unusual, temperature-dependent transition was observed at around 40 K, along with two distinct resistivity components that could be interpreted as resulting from a combination of two different conductivity mechanisms.  One explanation points to phonon-assisted electrical conductivity between nanotubes, while a second hypothesis suggests that the observed behavior could be caused by a change in nanotube dimer lines due to interatomic distance changes.  These findings offer the first empirical confirmation of a phonon-assisted electrical conductivity in a collective nanomaterials system, and they shed new light on the role of phonons in low-temperature conductivity of individual nanotubes.

In high-dimensional data sets, information characteristics often present redundancies and dimensions often hinder clustering algorithms. To combat this issue, our approach utilizes the fuzzy entropy concept to determine the local redundancy of each dimension and optimally selects features, making us susceptible to sub-optimal solutions. Unlike static feature selection that only identifies primary features and discards others, our approach continuously adjusts feature weights dynamically throughout the clustering process. Since human assessment of class labels is generally subjective, our entropy-based method automatically identifies optimal feature weights without relying on user input. Once the feature weights have been established, they are merged with fuzzy cluster properties to support a more comprehensive understanding of each cluster. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the entropy-driven approach leads to better clustering accuracy and more in-depth understanding compared to conventional methods.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Although traditional algorithms like Follow-the-Leader (FTL) are widely employed, their convergence rates are often too slow in modern models. This results in a network that may not reach sufficient accuracy within a vast number of training iterations. To address this challenge, we developed a new algorithm, Follow-the-Gradient (FTG), which enables faster convergence and reduces the number of iterations needed. Our algorithm works by calculating gradients based on the current ensemble parameters and mixing them according to a soft assignment that adapts to the stage of training. This approach allows FTG to achieve greater accuracy with significantly fewer iterations compared to FTL. We also introduced an algorithm called Follow-the-Gradient-Assigned (FTG-A) that incorporates the expert assignment as part of the gradient calculation. However, we discovered that FTG-A converges too quickly in the early stages of training but struggles in the later stages. In contrast, FTG maintains its performance consistently throughout the training process. We provided mathematical justification for FTG by analyzing its dynamic model and proving its stability under certain conditions. Our experimental results show that FTG outperforms FTG-A and the standard FTL algorithm across various configurations.

This research explores an enhanced framework of the token-firing game concept initially applied to the study of birational self-coverings of curves. We derive a method to compute the Jacobian of a curve, its Jacobian covering, and the corresponding Galois representation when the base field has characteristic zero. Moreover, we will describe the prymian cover of a curve if it possesses a trivial Jacobian. This method extends the typical classification into hyperelliptic, genus 2, and high-genus curves.

Modifying Einstein's gravitational force by introducing a scalar mediator beyond spin-2 yields a theory with global symmetry involving scalar and vector components. However, if this global symmetry is broken, the scalar component can become unstable, which would have significant implications for quantum properties and lead to a acceleration of charged particles. Since constant electric fields lead to the Schwinger process creating particle-antiparticle pairs from the vacuum, the probability of this process is proportional to the Maxwell stress tensor's squared fluctuations. These fluctuations decrease with distance from the source but are limited by the cosmic birefringence observed due to gravitational fields' impact on photon polarization, which shows that the symmetry breaking must occur at a very low energy scale, below MeV, to avoid contradicting current measurements.

Photometric observations of certain globular clusters like NGC 4147, rich in ultraviolet light, offer valuable insights into their overall evolution. Using data from the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope on board AstroSat, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of these stars. Our findings indicate the presence of multiple blue horizontal branch stars and B-type main sequence stars within the cluster. A distinct subgiant branch was also detected, characterized by brighter and redder stars that could be warm horizontal branch candidates or blue loop stars. Further distinguishing these stars based on temperatures, surface gravities, and helium abundances led to identifying five blue loop stars. Characterizing these stars enables us to understand the level of horizontal branch second parameter effects present in NGC 4147, as well as the extent to which blue loops influence the position of the horizontal branch. The cluster's subgiant branch, consisting of fewer and cooler stars with characteristics similar to blue loops, could represent an additional phenomenon or simply the initial stage of the blue valley sequence. The presence of certain stars with surface temperatures greater than 70000K was also observed, which may potentially belong to a new class of stars. The second parameter effects responsible for their existence and characteristics require further investigation.

A significant research area known as the b-principle revolves around the idea that complicated functions with bounded derivatives can be broken down into simpler components with similar properties. Recently, researchers made a breakthrough by proving that if the sum of the second symmetric power of a variety's lisse sheaf admits a Mumford transformation, then the original lisse sheaf must have a geometrically integral conjugacy class, which in turn implies the base field has a specific property known as being separably closed. Building upon this concept, we provide a more general form of the main theorem, involving the study of symmetric powers of lisse sheaves and their relation to the Mumford hypothesis.

Deep neural network generalization has remained an elusive concept, with many prior studies struggling to pinpoint the underlying mechanisms driving generalization. A widely accepted theory posits that neural networks' generalization is linked to their agreement on specific class-level representations, but the specifics of this agreement remain unclear. In our study, we revisit the notion of generalization by investigating the two implicit agreements implied by the transferability property. We found that these agreements are related to (1) the agreement of feature spaces, which refers to the overlap between features shared by different classes, and (2) the agreement of decision boundaries, which refers to the consistency of boundaries encountered by different classes. Our findings reveal that these agreements facilitate transferability, with the overlap of feature spaces and the consensus of decision boundaries affecting generalization performance, while also demonstrating that an over-emphasis on decision boundary agreement can impede transferability when using complex models.

The spread of information within a network relies on its complex structural elements, specifically the connections and properties of the links that transfer information. By analyzing the principles of link symmetry and neighborhood overlap in various real-world networks, we observe how these characteristics influence the speed of information dissemination. Numerical simulations confirm that both factors impact the speed of the process, but its rate and characteristics remain consistent regardless of the starting node position and strength of the active links. Moreover, we found that the speed of the process tends to grow as the degree of the neighborhood increases, which correlates with the speed of the process in typical networks characterized by community structure.

A unique geometric characteristic called distinctiveness was first described by Yau in a general context and later specifically investigated in the context of special Lagrangian submanifolds within Calabi-Yau manifolds. Building upon his earlier definition, Thomas-Yau distinctiveness was formulated to account for the more quantitative form of this concept. This paper seeks to explore some of the implications arising from a theorem initially proposed by Behrndt and Gabbert and specifically to derive consequences in terms of the invariance of the geometric properties it implies, including the Reeb vector, the contact type and the symplectic homology, all for the conformal concircular metrics involved.

The time-domain standard perturbation model (SPM) describes signal distortion when a signal is transmitted through a cable and an interface that alter its impedance. This usually occurs in data acquisition systems, converting analog signals to digital form. An analog filter is often used at the sending or receiving end to mitigate effects but introduces impedance mismatch, causing signal degradation. An ideal analog filter cannot be implemented, so a discrete-time digital filter is utilized instead, but its digital characteristics lead to additional distortion not present in the analog version. A fundamental issue lies in how these digital filters are treated within the SPM, which assumes an ideal, analog transmission path. This work adresses this problem by developing a discrete-time precision model (DPM) incorporating digital filter behavior, allowing a direct comparison between SPM and DPM to evaluate transmission errors. The ultimate goal is digital transparency - the ability of a digital path to mimic its analog counterpart. The research findings indicate that, as expected, SPM can't achieve perfect agreement with DPM due to fundamental differences between analog and digital signals. However, by enabling a direct comparison between SPM and DPM, both theories can converge when the transmission period is extremely short, effectively making DPM a more refined version of SPM. This ensures consistency in measuring and describing signal degradation effects under rapidly changing impedance conditions for both unamplified and amplified signal transmissions.

The modern Android operating system's open nature and widespread availability on a vast array of devices have transformed it into a preferred choice for both personal and professional use. Due to its versatility and adaptability, it is encountered in scenarios ranging from basic consumer use to complex industrial and enterprise settings. The adaptability of mobile apps has made them indispensable in numerous life situations and professional environments, with many being utilized either as standalone products or integrated components of larger systems. The data they collect enables businesses to develop in-depth customer insights and the ability to offer tailored services, while also allowing governments to stay informed about their citizens' activities. Unfortunately, malicious users frequently exploit the open nature of Android to disrupt users' privacy and security, with resulting harms ranging from financial loss to national security threats. In response, researchers and security experts have developed various countermeasures to mitigate evasion attacks, which we will discuss in this study. Our research involves conducting an in-depth analysis of evasion attacks on the Android operating system to identify common characteristics and challenges. This research sets out to investigate a distinct form of attack that shares characteristics with evasion assaults and seeks to bypass detection systems, which makes it an area of interest within the security community.

Our solution enhances the complexity of processing in Deep Learning (DL) models by introducing an innovative, unified system. This system enables the virtualization and customization of computational resources allocated to each DL task. The value of task-specific processing is increased due to the subdivision of large datasets into smaller sections. This approach accelerates training and inference times, allowing for a high level of resource management through our tool, Ozy. This vessel offers dynamic resource distribution among tasks and provides adjustable computation and memory allocation. Ozy's virtualization capabilities improve task resilience, dynamic resource management enhances performance, and task prioritization is supported. The method of slicing and allocating data is implemented in Ozy to expedite computation. The system offers adaptive task prioritization and incorporates a profiler for task monitoring.

Research focused on the detailed electronic properties of the five-fold degenerate quantum Hall state at 5/2 filling is scarce. In this study, we employed a novel sample design featuring a step-like potential profile to deliberately induce moderate Landau-level mixing, thereby distinguishing it from earlier observations made on smooth quantum Hall samples. We discovered an unconventional reentrant sequence of partial and full polarization transitions within this highly degenerate state, occurring at high magnetic field strengths. The observed reentrance behavior suggests that the original ground state at high fields changes to an excited state as the density increases or the magnetic field decreases. The overall density-pressure phase diagram exhibits multiple phases, including full polarization, partial polarization, and a previously unreported highly degenerate phase, all of which transition back to a fully polarized state at higher densities. The density-scale at which this reentrant behavior emerges matches the previously observed thermal activation gap in the same highly degenerate state. Utilizing a combination of these experimental findings and results from variational wave function calculations, we propose that this highly degenerate state corresponds to a cluster of three electrons that varies in size throughout the observed phases, accounting for both the original ground state at high fields and all subsequent changes that occur upon increasing the density or decreasing the magnetic field.

Our research demonstrates that the Thakurta metric, originally designed to model mature primary black holes with dim outer layers, bears resemblance to the Schwarzschild metric for areas with large dimension. Consequently, the observational constraints imposed by the LIGO-Virgo experiment remain effective in dismissing the existence of primordial black holes as potential contributors to the dark matter ensemble, given their potential dimming towards the outer regions of their event horizons.

Creating a giant planet through pebble accumulation can be modeled using a simplified equation that combines local and external pebble accretion, yet current models neglect how density fluctuations affect this process. We found that these fluctuations are crucially tied to two key factors: the amplitude of density variations and the timescale of these variations. If the amplitude of these fluctuations is too extreme ($\sim 10$), density variations hinder pebble accumulation and planet creation. We also found that external factors, such as the thermal evolution of the disk, can produce predictable patterns of density variations with a timescale of a few million years. Under these conditions, the thermal evolution could potentially stifle the creation of giant planets through pebble accumulation.

We examine how the interaction between computational constraints and data fitfulness influence the risk and stability of linear regression models with various levels of overparameterization. Unlike previous studies, this research takes into account a wider range of computational possibilities. Two distinct data models are explored, one with a limited number of dimensions and data that varies fitfully, and another with an infinite number of dimensions and data that is more informative. Our findings indicate that under the first data scenario, overparameterization leads to enhanced risk reduction and increased stability. Conversely, under the second data scenario, overparameterization results in reduced risk reduction but increased stability. This analysis also reveals that the algorithm's convergence rate can provide a computational equivalent of the well-known bias-variance tradeoff in cases where risk minimization does not account for computational limitations.

Building on previous work, we establish the existence of exceptional Bohr structures within the object boH(G) for each countably infinite, discrete abelian group G that is not torsionable, but also show that these structures have no significance in boH(G) for groups that are torsionable or finite. Additionally, the obtained Bohr structures in boH(G) exhibit unique and isolated patterns specifically attributed to the unique characteristics of G.

The dial-a-ride problem, specifically metropolitan, aims to minimize total costs,
including both service and congestion fees. As a result, solution proposals are
evaluated based on not only a balance between the service time and waiting time
but also the number of trips. Despite its demand-sensitive nature, traffic
congestion is not considered in traditional dial-a-ride models. However, in
metropolitan settings, it is acknowledged that a fixed service cost per customer
along with an operating cost per passenger and per trip occur. To address this
issue, this research introduces a new model with varying costs and the possibility
of traffic congestion. To solve it, a novel method, referred to as BB-DRP, using a
branch-and-bound approach, coupled with a commercial solver, is applied to solve
small-scale problems while showing promising results for larger-scale instances.

The foundation of e-commerce search engines lies in combining text data with visual elements, supporting product categorization and facilitating relevant item retrieval for customers. Current methods focus on integrating text and image data but neglect the insight that users gain from product ratings and descriptions. Therefore, a new approach known as Insight-aware Image-text Pretraining (IIPT) has been developed, allowing the model to leverage product insights as additional modalities during the pretraining process. By participating in a product insight recognition task and analyzing accessible insight labels, the proposed IIPT achieves remarkable performance improvements of 9.0-11.6% and 3.0-6.5% in terms of recall and accuracy compared to the best non-informed baseline, respectively. Furthermore, empirical evidence reveals that product insights share common semantic attributes, further highlighting their valuable contribution to search task functionality.

A key feature of many machine learning algorithms is the ability to incorporate diverse data types into model development. As a result, DL algorithms have become preferred choices for various medical applications. Despite their success, these algorithms often rely on straightforward optimization techniques, which may limit their effectiveness. Methods like Deep InfoMax (DIM) have shown promising encoding capabilities in unsupervised image processing. This paper investigates the application of DIM to create feature extractors for CT images and multi-modal clinical data. We introduce an enhanced version of DIM, referred to as JSDM, aimed at improving feature extraction. This method generates shared features from multiple data sources and demonstrates better performance than alternative optimization techniques. Our experiments using CT modality data alone and a combination of modality datasets show that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline features and several medical classification benchmarks, including the well-known MCI Alzheimer's disease classification challenge.

The core task of Natural Language Understanding (NLU) involves grasping the meaning of input sentences without referencing external information. To facilitate this, the proposed language semantics comprehension model utilizes a structured dictionary with common words, their associations, and the relationships between them. The introduced method uses a specialized neural network component to analyze the dictionary and determine how the various concepts relate to each other. Given a sentence, this network dynamically selects and prioritizes the underlying semantic elements based on their relevance. The input information is then integrated with these concepts to produce a coherent and understandable meaning of the sentence. The approach is presented through a simplified example and demonstrated to be effective in understanding multiple sentence patterns.

Recent breakthroughs in electrical manipulation of spin and charge in semiconductor devices and the discovery of topological spin textures in novel materials have generated significant interest. By incorporating heavy elements like Bi, the spin-orbit interaction in semiconductors can be enhanced, and heavy elements also introduce disorder, which may impede device performance. In this study, using advanced numerical techniques, the spin-orbit interaction is investigated in a correlated alloy model featuring heavy elements and it is found that this interaction is only impaired by disorder at high concentration of heavy elements. Alternatively, the use of thin films made of heavy elements could offer a way to achieve this interaction without compromising device performance through the regulation of heavy element concentration within the two-dimensional material.

A new type of shadow matter, referred to as Metastable Conformal Shadow Matter, is introduced. This matter type can remain in a metastable state, analogous to superconductors and superfluids, and remains invisible to electromagnetic radiation. A theoretical model of a scalar field has been developed to describe shadow matter, and its potential self-interactions have been explored. Depending on parameters, this field can either organize matter into compact units or remain disordered at the critical point. Unique properties of shadow matter arise from a non-minimal coupling of the scalar field to the Ricci curvature tensor. For instance, a conformal transformation can be applied to transform the Lagrangian of a single particle into the Lagrange multipliers of the ZK equation. Due to its non-minimal coupling, a particle can decay into a dark matter particle, resulting in a decay rate proportional to $v^4$. Furthermore, a symmetric potential can be achieved through a global $Z_2$ symmetry breaking, giving rise to a stable domain wall separating $Z_2$-invariant regions, and also leading to a zero-mode associated with the scalar field. This zero-mode enables a particle to decay into dark matter particles by the non-minimal coupling, resulting in equal probabilities for particle and antiparticle decay. Additionally, a dilaton-like behavior can be observed in the Compton scattering of shadow matter, and either a second-order phase transition can occur, bringing Metastable Conformal Shadow

To measure the performance of AI healthcare instruments such as medical imaging devices and laboratory test equipment, we need to assess their predictions or classifications against established health benchmarks. Since the distribution of future, unseen health data may differ from that of past data due to various factors like changes in patient demographics and medical conditions over time, we've developed a conformal prediction-based approach. This approach allows us to predict how future, shifted distribution-based predictions or classifications will perform relative to their past or training distribution counterparts. We've tailored this method to suit the unique requirements of reliability growth studies, particularly exam-reliability designs which involve repeatedly administering the same exam to establish consistent standards. Furthermore, we've adapted our approach to accommodate multiple exams by utilizing a multi-task conformal predictor, all while maintaining scalability thanks to implementation in Python with TensorFlow and the FForestry open-source framework.

Large-scale simulations of DNA fragments regularly yield non-intuitive results, yet these outcomes are often plagued by inaccuracies stemming from the employed force field. To overcome these shortcomings, our approach involves integrating a rigid foundation that influences local base pairing and thus improves the overall structure and mobility of the DNA molecule. By utilizing the NPT-NNCT approach, our goal is to mimic the natural DNA conformation that would be achieved through enzymatic refinement. This robust and efficient technique is compatible with existing protocols, and our case studies reveal that it offers improved structure and mobility results, and most importantly, does not impede the investigation of specific biochemical reactions. Additionally, our research indicates that representations of rigid foundation variability may be needed to accurately represent the DNA structure. This methodology holds great promise for future studies of DNA and RNA as well as viral and retroviral genomes because it allows for the improvement of de novo sequencing and design procedures.

In the field of operations research, thermodynamic optimization has emerged as a novel approach, leveraging principles from non-equilibrium thermodynamics to create a comprehensive framework for decision-making. A crucial concept within this field involves the analysis of information forms and their dynamic characteristics. This paper delves into two critical aspects: the systematic representation and numerical quantification of information structures. A primary focus of this study lies on understanding and analyzing the inherent information content of thermal fluctuations in nonequilibrium systems, specifically the renewal process exhibited by the Arrhenius law, which governs nonequilibrium Arrhenius neurons. By employing Arrhenius neurons, we can model and represent complex thermal fluctuations in a more comprehensive manner, exceeding the limitations of conventional binary systems. Furthermore, we've developed an information compression protocol, the Shannon-Arrhenius protocol, which combines principles from Shannon information theory and the Arrhenius law. Through this protocol, we can reduce random noise based on thermal fluctuations while maintaining essential system parameters, thereby contributing to the development of thermodynamic optimization methods and mechanisms for real-world applications. The effectiveness of the Shannon-Arrhenius protocol has been numerically evaluated and proven, with its outcomes and methods potentially influencing the development of future thermal engineering technologies.

To enhance the safety of structures built with cement, it's crucial to understand how cement and pore fluid interact, affecting the dielectric properties of materials. This study investigates the dielectric behavior of pore fluids in cement through various concentrations and temperatures, and experiments reveal their response to different conditions. This knowledge will aid in validating numerical models and informing the development of predictive tools that can assess cement-based material properties over time.

Note on Regge Trajectory:  The well-known connection between the trajectories of regge poles and the moments of parton distribution functions has significant implications, particularly in high-energy scattering. While the ground state regge pole has well-established characteristics, with a trajectory that begins at zero and inherits quantum numbers from the hadronic matrix elements, the nature of massive-massive hadronic compounds is less understood. These exotic objects are associated with massive-massive regge poles with complex structures, influenced by both physical and unphysical moments. To better grasp their properties, we must consider the impact of the light-cone wave function's normalization and the large-$Q^2$ expansion's theoretical limitations. Given this context, our discussion will focus on a comprehensive review of massive-massive regge poles relevant to high-energy hadronic compound structures.

Research into the technological trajectory of military swarm drones reveals the
significant role played by natural language processing, which has driven military
research in this area since the late 1990s. The study examines the military
research community's shifts in research focus as captured in published texts,
revealing a change from basic research to applied topics like swarm drones,
participatory politics, and related ethical issues. The research employs
quantitative methods, analysis of scientific papers, and interviews with experts
to identify the underlying drivers of these shifts, which are found to be linked to
particular strategic and political requirements. The findings emphasize the
importance of considering the broader implications of new technologies on future
social, political, and strategic landscapes, not just their technical feasibility.

The primary goal of this research is to make an informed guess regarding the universe's current expansion speed by drawing inferences solely from the characteristics of observed Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions and without relying on simulations or assumptions concerning the universe's properties. By examining various $b$ value minima and identifying their range, which corresponds to a narrow interval of $0.3509$ to $0.3617$, this research achieves its objective. Notably, this range is dominated by a single, slow-moving dark matter model and largely disregards the influence of Lyman-$\alpha$ data's inherent uncertainties, primarily due to its nonlinear nature. By applying a straightforward calculation, this research places an upper limit on $b$ at $0.3617$, which in turn yields a $2\sigma$ lower limit of $0.3509$. Assuming that dark matter behaves as described on a Gross-de Gennes plane with parameters $\phi_0=1.1$, $\omega=0.0256$ and $\nu=0$, these bounds correspond to a $2\sigma$ interval of $6.480\times 10^{-3}$ to $6.552\times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, this research suggests that its observed Lyman-$\alpha$ data patterns are consistent with $b\approx 0.360$, which in turn indicates an effective dark matter model parameter on a Gross-de Gennes plane of $\phi=1.10

A novel beam dynamics phenomenon has been successfully captured through an experiment at Fermilab, specifically the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances during a beam training process at a weak-focusing arc. The study revealed that a beam with reduced emittances can be produced using this method, suitable for accelerated particles and sensitive particle physics experiments. The experiment also confirmed that the phenomenon is influenced by the arc's magnetic field adjustment speed and the beam intensity. The observed beam dynamics has potential applications in various particle accelerator applications, including particle colliders, radioisotope production facilities, and advanced particle physics experiments, particularly the Long-Range Neutrino Detector.

Current research on autonomous driving trajectory forecasting usually involves predicting future paths on a static map representation, but this approach has drawbacks, as it doesn't account for a map's dynamic elements that can influence movement patterns. To tackle this limitation, static map features are sometimes integrated with other data sources, like sensor data and goal objectives, but these methods can be cumbersome and unresponsive to changing conditions. In our research, we propose the Sliding Sequential Convolutional Variational Autoencoder (SS-CVAE) to tackle the challenges of forecasting trajectories on dynamic, socially-aware paths. SS-CVAE uses a novel variant of CVAE to predict future trajectories based on a single-scene, single-timeframe observation, featuring a novel type of convolutional operation that evaluates the likelihood of goal achievement in relation to map features. We also use an innovative variant of CVAE to generate latent variables, where the potential trajectories of a given agent are calculated by taking into account varying timeframes. We evaluated SS-CVAE using Sumo simulation data and found it outperformed other methods, even when the training data didn't match the conditions in real-life testing.

Using large-scale simulations, this study examines the correlations between different information-theoretic metrics and their potential to gauge the organizational complexity of systems. We generate numerous stochastic processes on finite, undirected graphs with various parameters and observe the evolutions of these processes as they converge. Our analyses of thermodynamic quantities, such as the relative entropy and entropy production, along with information metrics like transfer entropy and mutual information, reveal distinct behaviors and suggest new approaches for quantifying system complexity. We further demonstrate the usefulness of these metrics as indicators of organizational complexity through applications in a model ecosystem.

This trial application aims to facilitate communication between humans and a swarm of drones through an innovative hand gesture recognition technology using a single, strategically positioned camera. A cascade of algorithms generates recognized 10-digit hand gestures in 3D space, and the implementation involves two distinct models: a first-tier model aimed at small-scale entities, and a second-tier model designed for larger entities. Although the proposed system is demonstrated using a virtual environment, the potential for real-world implementation is also discussed. Future research will focus on optimizing the hand gesture models, integrating them with a drone navigation system, and assessing their performance in real-world settings. This study offers insights into a novel drone navigation method and the potential applications of hand gesture recognition in drone control.

The blood analysis task involves categorizing cells into seven classes: Basophil, Eosinophil, Lymphocyte, Monocyte, Lymphoblast, Metamyleocyte, and Neutrophil. To enhance the accuracy and robustness of our blood analysis model, we've developed a major contribution by integrating multiple neural networks. Specifically, we've combined different classifiers trained on different datasets. Our approach is unique because it's applicable to a broad range of problems, not just the blood task. We've also analyzed the performance of these combinations, exploring potential generalizations to other classification issues. Our findings reveal that ensembling neural networks can significantly improve accuracy and robustness. While the blood task holds value for its medical applications, its limitations necessitate further research to clarify the model's strong performance.

In quantum simulation, it's beneficial to have a reliable method for preparing the ground state of a model, especially one that's as crucial as the Hubbard model is to understanding complex systems of interacting electrons. A method known to efficiently change quantum states with minimum excitation is the counterdiabatic driving technique, and in our work, we apply it variationally to prepare the ground state of the Hubbard model. The CD technique combined with variational optimization has several advantageous features, including a direct connection to ground-state preparation, the ability to reach exact ground states with infinite time, and a negative derivative of the action, leading to a simpler algorithm with less necessary time steps. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in finite-time simulations of the Hubbard model by applying it to small clusters of up to 16 sites and varying coupling strengths, and we argue that this approach can handle more complex systems and larger clusters with the help of machine learning.

A novel approach incorporating hue temperature into high-velocity decoloration has been developed and tested.  The high-velocity decolation technique, powered by gasdynamic medium, is capable of applying color gradients to solid objects.  The technique may find use in security, defense, and entertainment industries.  Existing experiments utilizing red and green pigments on non-heat-resistant surfaces revealed mutually exclusive velocity ranges, leading to the conclusion that different velocity regimes are essential for optimal color combination processes.  A successful implementation of this decolation technique could pave the road for a more advanced color management system in the future.

One-dimensional functions can be approximated via Taylor series using Lagrange reminders, producing an explicit polynomial expression with explicit error terms for any given radius. When attempting to capture the behavior of an exponential function within a specified radius, an infinite series of its Taylor expansion may not converge, prompting a re-evaluation of the representation of exponential functions through Taylor series. This paper demonstrates the feasibility of representing exponential functions with explicit polynomial expressions and error terms for any given radius, mirroring the validity of certain theorems like the Fej\'er-Leja theorem, which deals with the convergence of rational zeta functions.

A key concept in this research is harmonic branched maps, a category of branched maps that incorporate elements of harmonic function theory. This paper demotes a specific harmonic branched map relevant to surface topology, establishing a crucial connection between certain types of surface maps and a widespread approach to simplifying complex geometric shapes. Additionally, our methods yield direct proofs of two longstanding theories: Ahlfors' Big Regularity Theory and the Nirenberg-Torchizer's Uniformization Theorem.

We've introduced a conceptual framework for creating, controlling, and utilizing
extremely short pulsed x-ray and MeV photon sources at an unprecedented rate.
These sources are produced through the interaction of high-intensity laser light
and plasma, combining the benefits of both high brightness and high flux.
We demonstrate the feasibility of generating a massive number of pulses within
a 10 nanosecond time frame, facilitated by a laser wavelength of 1.05 micrometers
and an energy release of approximately 100 kiloelectronvolts per pulse.
X-rays within this range can bridge the gap between hard and soft sources,
enabling novel applications, such as coherent absorption and nonlinear science,
coherent control and imaging, as well as the creation of x-ray spectra through 
resonance, resonance-enhanced, or nonresonant electron collision processes.

In a context of two Higgs doublet models with a conservative approach to electroweak physics, we conduct a numerical analysis to assess the sensitivity of future experiments in measuring the soft breaking parameter $m_{12}$, which determines the mass mixing between two Higgs fields. By incorporating experimental results from particle collider experiments, LHC and future facilities like the 100 TeV HL-LHC and HL-SPP, as well as low-energy studies in particle decays with updated constraints from Bao-Xiang Ni, we arrive at conclusions indicating that HL-LHC and HL-SPP may identify $m_{12}$ to two significant digits in almost the entire accessible region. Nevertheless, our findings also reveal limitations to these experiments in determining $m_{12}$ within specific ranges, particularly where the mass mixing is predominantly influenced by weak or flavour-changing interactions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that precision low-energy studies alone can set the most stringent constraints on $m_{12}$, particularly when the mass mixing is dominated by flavour-changing processes.

This research focuses on converting relational databases to RDF datasets, allowing data to be shared across organizations and enabling data integration to be handled at the database level rather than during query execution. By incorporating RDF data and query compaction into relational databases, it becomes possible to boost the performance of applications that utilize RDF data by leveraging the optimized processing capabilities of relational databases and overcoming limitations present in existing approaches. To achieve this, it builds on an existing concept known as Shape Expression Framework, expanding it to incorporate RDF data and query definitions that facilitate efficient compensation. Additionally, it offers two new translation algorithms for relational databases to RDF datasets that conserve space and ensure compaction, termed Rel2RDF Compact and Rel2RDF Cons compact. A comprehensive evaluation of these methods is conducted, comparing them to existing solutions in terms of storage requirements, overlap between stored data, and query execution performance.

A new field of study, known as frontier assessment, utilizes convex regression to create boundaries that separate efficient data points from those that are ineffective. To support this area of research, a new library called pyStoNED has been developed with the goal of expanding the scope of convex regression applications. This library offers flexible tools for managing datasets and performing computations as needed. Additionally, pyStoNED integrates with other existing tools for data analysis, including Pandas and Scikit-learn, to create a unified computational environment. Furthermore, it includes essential functions for validating the accuracy of computation and offers various tools for assessing and visualizing data efficiency. To demonstrate its capabilities, a case study involving the evaluation of new, non-convex, and non-monotonic frontier functions is presented. This study demonstrates how pyStoNED enables the implementation of custom frontier functions to create more effective and meaningful boundaries in frontier assessment.

To better understand the LHC's findings for the top quark's mass, researchers are developing new, precise methods to measure the LHC's Higgs boson production coupled with top quarks. The focus is on creating more accurate measurements of the LHC's $\phi$-averaged Higgs boson production cross-section. The new method is named "asym", named after one of its key characteristics, and it has been compared with another well-established technique, the "sideband-subtracted" method. The study finds that the asym approach offers advantages over existing methods for determining the LHC's $\phi$-averaged Higgs boson production cross-section. The researchers also developed a new strategy for detecting the LHC's Higgs boson's branching ratios. The approach is based on combining asym and sideband-subtracted methods to make highly-precise measurements of Higgs branching ratios. The LHC's predicted $\sin^2 \phi_{t \bar t}$ values are also presented in addition to known parameters. Finally, the researchers outlined a strategy for further enhancing the LHC's $\sin^2 \phi_{t \bar t}$ measurement accuracy by 5% using these methods.

Pretrained language models have exhibited impressive performance on various NLP tasks. Unlike traditional models, they can process input sequences directly without requiring explicit task definition. However, due to their inherent versatility, they tend to struggle on specific tasks without extensive supervision. In cases with minimal labeled data, task-specific fine-tuning often leads to overemphasis on noise, ultimately hindering model performance. In response to these challenges, we introduce the idea of leveraging model outputs as auxiliary guidance for model training. By incorporating monolingual knowledge during the training process, we enable the model to detect task-specific markers and thus boost the model's accuracy on data with limited annotations. Furthermore, we propose a parallel training approach that fine-tunes the model on multiple tasks simultaneously, effectively mimicking an "assistant" that assists models in learning "new languages". Our experiments, conducted on datasets for Question Classification, Named Entity Recognition, and Sentiment Analysis, demonstrate the effectiveness of this paradigm in enhancing model performance with limited supervision.

Automated speech recognition technology, commonly known as ASR, is highly developed
for English; however, it is still lacking for many other languages. In this study,
we focus on German, taking advantage of two approaches - a novel, unsupervised
method based on a large English-trained neural network, and a supervised approach
utilizing approximately 6 hours of manually transcribed German speech data. Our
results reveal that our models can efficiently transmit knowledge from an English
model to a German implementation, achieving a significant reduction in training time.
Furthermore, our research indicates that our models can compete with a traditional
ASR system, even without being specifically optimized for German. Additionally, we
made our German speech dataset transmissible for other researchers, enabling
removable ASR solutions and improved linguistic diversity.

The appearance of Be-type stars is attributed to a disk of debris surrounding a compact, central object, which distinguishes them from other stars with emitting emissions. A study employing high-resolution optical spectra of Be stars within the 30 Doradus galaxy, observed with FUEGUELA, has analyzed spatial relationships between stars and their surrounding environments. The analysis revealed Be stars exist within both younger OB associations (such as NGC 2060 and NGC 2070) and an older system (Sk -69 262). These research findings suggest a prevalence of compact, inner disks among Be stars. Furthermore, a correlation between the characteristics of Be-type stars in 30 Doradus and local interstellar environments has been detected. Notably, systems surrounded by stronger H I clouds contain fewer Be stars. The possibility that these Be stars may transform into RSGs through mass loss while interacting with these H I clouds has also been explored.

The goal of inverse text standardization is to take a collection of writings with varying styles, norms, and languages and convert them into a uniform set of writing standards. This process was previously accomplished using machine learning models that accepted a mixture of written data and outputted a normalized version. However, the challenge lies in creating a large, diverse dataset of written texts to train these models. To overcome this, we've developed a method that allows for a small dataset of one writing standard to be used in normalizing texts from another standard, by first enhancing the dataset using image processing techniques to simulate data from the other standard. This is then combined with existing data in a new joint dataset. We've shown that this method allows for successful normalization between two highly distinct writing standards - Farsi and English.

This paper demonstrates a Robin constant version of the Faber-Krahn inequality for the Hermite operator, which has equivalent applications in theory and physics for studying eigenvalues in limits of the limiting case for the first order perturbation of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Furthermore, it shows a related inequality related to the Lichnerowicz inequality for the Dirichlet case.

Continual learning models are necessary to address the problem of improving
performance on growing sets of data. One such model called the Tangent Classifier
has shown potential in this area by effectively training on data that builds upon
previous information. However, traditional methods that deal with non-exchangeable
data structures (such as calendars) that exhibit varying relationships between
successive data points are limited. This research proposes a new approach called
Tangent Cores, which allows for multiple continuous updates without data restriction
by creating several continuous updates from different set points. These updates
are distinct and independent and can be combined using a combination or averaging
method. The approach has been successfully tested on a widely used non-exchangeable
calendar dataset and also used in another setting for learning a video sequence.

Studies on interacting systems hold great importance in fundamental theory and practical applications of non-Hermitian topological matter. A notable aspect is that, under certain conditions, dispersion relationships in one-dimensional systems can transition from a bulk-gap structure to an entirely bulk one when interactions come into play. This phenomenon occurs due to the possibility of overlapping energy bands resulting from interactions. Conversely, if non-Hermitian bulk energy bands do not intersect with gap energy bands, the bulk energy bands may remain resilient against the impact of interactions, thereby preserving the system's non-Hermitian bulk characteristics. Nonetheless, if non-Hertmitian bulk energy bands do converge with gap energy bands, the system's bulk energy characteristics will be erased by interactions, giving rise to a gapless state. This state can, according to a recently developed method, exhibit topological attributes. A distinguishing attribute of gapless states is that they can potentially display indications of non-Hermitian topological characteristics, characterized by a finite, non-Hermitian energy-related flux around the periodic system's unit of measurement. This may give rise to quantized distinct features in the system's non-interacting, but perturbed, energy spectrum. An example involving an \(sp^3\) semionic topological phase displays this property, with the example involving an \(sp^3\) semionic topological phase displaying this property.
