For various control applications, it's beneficial to design policies that are versatile and adaptable to different tasks with minimal reliance on exhaustive initial data. Our approach, called One-Shot Policies (OPOPO), involves utilizing augmented interaction data along with instructional objectives and operational constraints to create flexible policies. These policies are trained and validated within a single interactive session. OPOPO incorporates five key components: one-shot learning for robotic arm tasks using a mixture of four simulated objectives; deriving trajectories for underactuated legs using a push-and-pull method; applying a novel perturbation-based method for hovering aerial systems. Using the DroneLab dataset, our approach allows the creation of policies for aerial robots in one attempt, even when supplementary data and performance metrics are not available. Additionally, our method achieves a significant reduction in data requirements for various robotic arm applications when compared to model-free reinforcement learning approaches.

The Toda conformal quantum field theory for $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ is used to derive a comprehensive set of equations for calculating the self-energy of three particles and one particle, which relates to the self-interaction of three bosons. These equations are formulated in terms of the upper trace W n; they are a set of hierarchical equations, connected by a first-order derivative, with the lowest order being related to the three-point function. Furthermore, the relationship between the equations and the Toda Q-function is exploited using integrability, which leads to a complete solution for the self-energy of three particles and one particle, expressed in terms of the $\tau$ function. This solution is valid at all levels of the loop algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ without the need for perturbation theory. Ward identities derived from the Toda T-operator are also found to be valid even when the spectral parameter is eliminated, which is allowed since we are studying a conformal field theory.

Generative Adversarial Networks, an highly regarded yet challenging task for deep learning, is generating realistic images for a target domain, with numerous applications across different fields and industries. Despite significant advancements in the field, achieving a satisfactory balance between performance and quality proves to be problematic for most existing methods, particularly when the goal is to produce high-quality images for a specific distribution using a network trained on unrelated data. This research addresses this challenge by introducing an innovative architecture, the relation GAN with triplet loss (RelGAN), designed to leverage the expertise of multiple fine-tuned image translation networks. By establishing a connection between these networks and their corresponding latent spaces, the proposed method ensures that the generated results are of high quality and realistic by minimizing the distance between two specific types of information. Experimental results confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, with evidence and examples available on an online repository.

We have introduced a new method of quantum communication, known as twin-field QKE, which enables secure key exchange without the need for previous synchronization of phase. By utilizing an entangled photon source, which produces entangled pairs in a specific plane, and detecting them using a time-divided approach, we achieve scalable long-distance key exchange. Unlike conventional QKE methods, which require synchronization of optical phases, our approach eliminates this constraint and facilitates key exchange between multiple nodes without the need for prior agreement. Experiments confirm our concept and highlight its practical applications in reducing complexity for large-scale quantum networks.

Let $\Dom$ denote either the Fock space or or the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$ for $n \geq 2$.  The author has shown that any Toeplitz algebra with respect to a subinner function on the Fock space or the unit ball leads to a linear limit of the Wiener algebra.  This result is achieved through the construction of certain continuous functions that can be identified as the Szegö kernels for specific reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.  Furthermore, for the Fock space, this function can be expressed as a product of two functions, one of which has a Taylor series that equals the classical Wiener p-uclidean function, while for the unit ball, this function can be expressed as a product of two functions, one of which has a polar development of the Bergman kernel, along with an additional geometrically defined factor.  As an immediate consequence, any Toeplitz algebra with respect to a subinner function on the Fock space or the unit ball is limitely linear.  This generalises the corresponding observation for multipliers of analytic functions, as well as the findings of B lowy-Komornicki-Szefelkowicz-Wysocki.

In NLP and vision fields, research on object detection has achieved significant progress through the use of large-scale datasets. Nevertheless, collecting precise bounding-box annotations for every object instance is a labor-intensive and costly task, limiting the expansion of annotation datasets. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method for identifying objects without relying on expensive box labels. This method uses pseudo box annotations derived from lexical databases that map word meanings to geometric descriptions, allowing us to segment sentences into individual objects. We evaluate our approach on two datasets, lexical-aided object detection and the Wikipedia Dataset. Our results indicate that, despite a lack of box labels during training, our method achieves performance comparable to or exceeding that of existing object detection models on the test set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique can enhance domain adaptation by facilitating cross-domain object detection with minimal human labor.

The Rho Ophiuchus cloud complex shares boundaries with the Rho Ophiuchus-48 Libras cloud system, and its southern source S1, located near the boundary, initiates the cloud complex's western expansion. To gain insights into the source S1's influence, researchers used VLA radio observations to study the cloud complex's ionized gas, and observed that it forms an arc shape around the source, with a 1 to 3 parsec radius. These findings indicate that S1 has triggered the cloud complex's western expansion, and its influence extends up to 3 parsec radius. Furthermore, researchers used SOAR/CLUAS optical and near-infrared observations to verify that the source S1's influence extends up to 5 parsec radius, and observed that it forms an elongated shape around the source. These findings suggest that S1 has triggered star formation in the cloud complex, and its surrounding molecular gas forms an elongated shape, and potentially extends up to 5 parsec radius, and potentially influenced the surrounding molecular cloud.

The Transformer model's introduction has significantly impact on the advancements in the natural language processing field. Various adaptations and modifications of the Transformer have been proposed, leading to advancements in the areas of translation, question-answering, text-classification, and other tasks. The primary objectives of this paper are to examine the underlying architecture of the Transformer, its potential limitations, and to compare different variants of the Transformer model. Furthermore, this paper discusses its applications in different natural language processing tasks and leverages elastic consistency regularization to enhance its performance. A thorough assessment of the Transformer model's vast array of related models is provided, along with an analysis of its prospects and shortcomings.

The purpose of our investigation is to evaluate and compare the performance of econometric techniques in addressing the challenge of predicting mortality rates, building on the findings that factor models are capable of accurately capturing the complex fluctuations in time-series data associated with macroeconomic risk factors. By applying factor models to historical data on stock prices and life insurance policies across various countries, our research reveals that factor models can effectively capture the links between financial market volatility and mortality risk. What distinguishes our study is the distinction between the loadings and factors components of a factor model as time-constant characteristics inherent to individual companies and time-varying fluctuations influenced by events such as financial crises. Through our analysis, our refined factor model loaded on specific factors, notably the Merton model's financial institution factors, revealed predictive information on the performance of individual companies, an insight that may have practical implications for updating company risk assessments and adjusting premium rates with greater precision.

When training neural architectures from scratch, random initialization inevitably results in performance deterioration during early iterations. This widespread issue is often misunderstood, with researchers attributing it to adverse effects from previous epochs. In reality, the cause lies in the architecture's inherent properties. A novel framework is proposed to quantify disruption levels across different neural architectures. Experimental findings indicate that increase in model complexity leads to higher disruption levels. This phenomenon is explored in conjunction with continuum learning, where existing knowledge should ideally build upon previous achievements. However, the existing approach training CNNs from scratch leads to neglecting previous gains. A new method is presented that leverages previous model knowledge to train more effective CNNs, showcasing improved results on various benchmarks, including ImageNet, CIFAR and VTAB datasets.

Time series data analysis has numerous applications and implications across various domains. A new package, theft, has been developed to facilitate the implementation of several state-of-the-art algorithms for attribute-based inference on time series. These algorithms, such as ARIMA and LSTMs, are already available in existing R packages, but the theft package integrates them with a cohesive set of functions and automatically handles the selection of hyperparameters. Additionally, the theft package includes support for both univariate and multivariate time series data, as well as functions to split datasets and evaluate models. A pre-built R package is also provided to demonstrate its usability.

Given a group, G, which admits a proper, minimally weakly symmetric action on a valued category at zero, we demonstrate that it also has a minimal, weakly symmetric action on a complete, geodesic space with the same property.

Translators are evaluated in terms of their efficiency and reliability. Although several metrics exist for measuring efficiency, specifically translation speed and productivity, establishing a quantitative metric for dependability is more challenging. This study aims to outline a Bayesian approach to assessing translators based on feedback from commissioning clients, focusing on aspects such as timely project completion, meeting expectations, and adhering to instructions. The proposed method involves creating a Bayesian reliability model, which can be used to provide initial information about a translator's dependability and improve understanding of their behavior.

We derive three key principles regarding energy absorption in systems that rely on scattering, such as quantum or unguided systems. These principles establish that energy absorption is consistent and predictable, given the channel configurations and the target strength. Additionally, we define a concept called "energy absorption eigenchannels" - specific channel configurations where all incoming energy is fully absorbed by the target - and develop associated eigenvalues, which are directly linked to the target strength. Notably, these eigenvalues remain unchanged by the number of channels, making these scattering systems uniquely versatile.

We've found that removing the final stages of a convolutional neural network (CNN) and switching to a fully connected version often results in better generalization performance and reduced complexity, as measured by the NNP-decomposable property. This phenomenon suggests that the last stages of a CNN may not be crucial for its performance and can be safely trimmed back, much like how selective attention can be applied to filter out unnecessary information. Interestingly, our findings show that using trimmed CNNs, we can achieve comparable results to traditional designs, all while maintaining a significantly lower number of parameters (approximately 5.91 times fewer). This discovery presents a straightforward strategy for simplifying complex CNN models into more efficient, high-performing variants.

The concept of LSTMs has been widely adopted in natural language processing, with various experiments being performed on this topic. Despite numerous attempts to understand the composition of large, training-friendly models known as "lottery tickets," this study takes a different approach, exploring the financial potential of these models as investments. By treating the computation capabilities of these models as a portfoliio, this research proposes a new algorithm aimed at maximizing their return. This algorithm, known as TICKET, prioritizes models that yield the highest returns when tested, throughout the investment period, allowing for continuous model switching in order to amplify gains. In addition, TICKET analyzes a range of factors before selecting an model, including its capacity, complexity, performance on unseen data, as well as the computational resources required for its implementation. This investment strategy is applied to various models, including LSTMs, making it easier to understand their structure and potential returns, and even enabling the creation of better models through a process of iterative testing and improvement.

This work builds on our previous research where we used Six-Operator Product Expansion in the large-$N$ $O(N)$ symmetric quantum field theory setting to show that the unusual dimension of the $\phi^Q$ operator is zero at one-loop. We found this result to be consistent with a pre-existing two-loop calculation. Although a one-loop zero implies no UV irreducible six-point interaction, our six-loop calculations confirm that the six-point function is zero. Notably, our six-loop results also reveal that the usual and unusual dimensions of the $\phi^Q$ operator are in agreement, which is in line with our previously calculated two-loop values and also supports the Conformal Bootstrap program. We also use renormalization group equations to show that both dimensions match as $Q/Q_*$ approaches zero, where $Q_*$ is the critical exponent.

To modeling the behavior of electrons in a 2D material, we developed a computational framework that accounts for interband processes influenced by both acoustic and optical phonons. Our findings show that acoustic phonons play a pivotal role in electron transitions between valleys, a role that's often underestimated in existing models focused on optical phonons. This is because acoustic phonons introduce a constant energy shift between valley states, effectively inducing a finite valley Hall conductivity even in the absence of external voltage stimuli. Furthermore, we discovered that acoustic phonons accelerate electron scattering while acoustic phonons accelerate electron scattering when acoustic phonons are absent. This is because acoustic phonons introduce a constant energy shift between valley states, effectively inducing a finite valley Hall conductivity even in the absence of external stimuli. Furthermore, we discovered that acoustic phonons accelerate electron scattering within a given valley. When acoustic phonons are absent, interband transitions driven by optical phonons dominate, suppressing intra-valley scattering. However, at a certain optical phonon frequency, acoustic phonons facilitate intra-valley scattering through a resonance that's matched to the carrier temperature. This condition triggers a thermodynamic feedback that increases the overall electron mobility.

The Visual Domain Adjustment Contest that took place at NeurIPS 2022 showcased cutting-edge, real-world applications of learning under domain shifts. A dataset composed of the Oxford-IIIT-Pet Dataset and the Car datasets was provided to test methods tackling object category recognition and verification tasks. Our winning entry on the LDAA track, which involved adapting to unknown domain labels for both tasks, is a basic yet efficient multi-learner system, consisting of two task-agnostic predictors: (i) a deep learning model simplifying domain shift adjustment, and (ii) a statistical model resolving uncertainty where confidence levels originate from one-dimensional features of each learner's predictions. Our approach took only a few hours to develop and achieved first place in both verification and classification tasks.

We introduce the Variational von Mises-Fisher distribution (VMF-SNE), a probabilistic model for clustering spherical data that we integrate with t-SNE for visualizing and dimension reduction. Building on the conventional Gaussian-based t-SNE, which is suited for Euclidean data, our approach preserves key properties and improves representation of spherical information. In comparison to alternative spherical distributions, VMF-SNE offers more efficient computation and accurate probabilistic outcomes. Through simulated and real-world datasets, including astronomical and fetal ultrasound observations, we demonstrate VMF-SNE's ability to perform equivalent or superior surgical procedures compared to traditional t-SNE, while achieving faster computation times than alternative spherical distributions.

Our research utilizes the innovative tooling developed for diagrammatic Monte Carlo in dual dimensions to thoroughly examine the properties of Fermi polarons in two-dimensional lattices with weakly interacting particles. We explore how diagrammatic methods perform compared to quantum Monte Carlo simulations, specifically in terms of polaron energies, the effects of interactions, and how these characteristics evolve as the lattice reaches its superconducting critical point. To further our understanding, all results have been physically justified based on analytical calculations employing the variational Monte Carlo method, thereby validating the outcomes of diagrammatic Monte Carlo. This research reveals that in the context of polarons, dual dimensions serve as an extremely accurate approximation of continuum models.

Recent advancements in quantum error correction and quantum computing coverage provide promising opportunities to simulate intricate many-body fermionic systems that are challenging to model using classical approaches. Nevertheless, accurately representing fermions with qubits while replicating fermionic interactions poses a significant problem due to the breakdown of fermionic anti-commutation relations caused by a non-zero probability error. Our proposed hybrid digital-analog approach can potentially simulate fermionic properties such as Fermi surfaces, energy gaps, and more, using fewer qubits than the exact method, can be employed with current quantum computers, and offers a feasible path towards simulating larger systems with the help of a rapidly advancing quantum hardware roadmap.

Graph polynomials and their related series generate a broad array of mathematical concepts that allows for differentiating various types of graphs, or even topological cellular structures in general. The given text discusses specific types of graph polynomials known as $L(f,s)$ and $G(f,s)$, along with the corresponding formal power series. It also explores an established connection between these polynomials and formal series, as well as a related duality principle. Additionally, further research finds that the formal series can be characterized through a respective generating function, while also analyzing under what conditions the formal series yields a formal Laurent series. We further derive explicit formulas for the formal series in specific instances and establish relationships between the formal series and other known graph series. The text also investigates the respective duality principles for the formal series in various graph series, including the cubic chromatic polynomial series. The study concludes with several open research questions.

We establish a connection between the moduli space of one-dimensional abelian varieties and a specific component of the Veech curve in the Teichmüller space of a genus-two surface. This connection leads to an expression for the associated "Veech arc" based on the x-coordinates of points on the corresponding algebraic curves, which is derived from the x-coordinates of points on a Veech curve for a genus-two curve. We find and validate an integral equation that governs the moduli space of one-dimensional abelian varieties, which is analogous to the Hitchin connection, and in the process, we determine the values of Chern-Simons in the moduli space, which provide a type of partition function due to its integrality. We verify that the Veech curve corresponds to a Lagrangian submanifold of the cotangent bundle, which is separately determined, and observe that the complex structure is determined by the Chern-Simons, resulting in the moduli space being a symplectic base.

This research takes a comprehensive approach to examining how remote working affects the achievement of Scrum projects. An initial survey with 44 measures in three areas - team performance, quality of work, and achievement of goals - was administered to Scrum masters and project managers, who then provided concrete examples of how remote working affected their projects. Follow-up interviews with selected respondents allowed for in-depth exploration of particularly noteworthy stories, while a quantitative analysis was also conducted to provide additional insights from the survey data. Our findings from the various studies show that the effectiveness of remote working as a means to achieve Scrum projects depends significantly on factors such as working culture, project management practices, and the role of key individuals, such as Scrum masters and in-house consultants, and highlight opportunities for improvements in the implementation of remote working in Scrum projects.

The study determines the Gau-Wu value for a specific type of matrix known as the arrowhead matrix of degree r with dimensions 4x4. Additionally, it calculates the Gau-Wu value for matrices of degree r chosen from (1-rw11-rw22), where rwij are factors of a perfect square. In contrast to earlier research which only considered these factors to be relatively prime, this study calculates the Gau-Wu value for matrices of degree r chosen from (1-rw11-rw22) where rwij are any factors of a perfect square.

Electron trajectories resulting from the decay of open-beauty hadrons exhibit complex movement within the ALICE detector due to various factors, such as the influence of a magnetic field and the reconstruction methods of the Si-tracker. These factors cause the electron momentum to vary significantly in the longitudinal direction, even before accounting for effects caused by the transformation of beauty hadrons into electrons. Although the magnetic field has a uniform intensity, the electron momentum appears to be displaced due to this phenomenon, resulting in an imbalance between the left and right movement of the electron population, which can be described using an asymmetry parameter. These characteristics are similar to those of other particles that undergo significant spatial and momentum distortions, such as muons captured by nucleons or particles detected in the presence of a distortion field, and their distortion patterns can be predicted using simulation methods like GEANT4. In simulations of Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, the movement of electrons is found to extend beyond the detector's region of uniform field, with their distortion patterns following a lognormal distribution, which may offer valuable information about the detector's magnetic field. These findings could have far-reaching implications for future experiments, particularly those involving detector cells with varying intensity fields, which would complicate the identification and analysis of particles by introducing a bias that must be corrected for or addressed through alternative methods.

We investigate the application of homology to capture the underlying structure of point clouds across various spatial dimensions. Unlike previous work focusing on black and white noise, our approach extends this concept to colorful data by utilizing weighted alpha-complexes from a geometric point of view. By utilizing the geometric properties of these complexes, we are able to derive explicit formulas for computing persistent homology for point clouds in one and two dimensions. Additionally, we have developed an algorithm using Delaunay triangulations and progressive sampling that allows for efficient computation of persistent homology in higher dimensions.

This work utilizes the notions of Generalized DoF (GDoF) and binary power settings to analyze the effects of control and communication strategies in multi-user interference networks. It notes that optimal and binary power control have similar GDoF performance for small numbers of users, which increases as the number of users grows, increasing the potential for optimal control to outperform binary settings. Noting this disparity, it investigates the GDoF performance gap between these methods, which is found to rise at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of users, independent of channel characteristics, thus quantifying the benefits of more sophisticated power control for large user populations. It achieves these findings using a new GDoF performance metric and a linearly increasing power control approach.

Auditing is a crucial aspect of financial verification that needs to be adapted to different scenarios in order to ensure effectiveness, specifically when it comes to the classification of transaction behaviors. One method that can be used for classification is the Dempster-Shafer theory, however it presents certain difficulties during the learning process. To overcome these challenges, a novel approach called adaptable classification is proposed, built upon the principles of formal concept analysis. This method allows for the learning model to be adapted and used across various applications, resulting in a more generalized approach. To showcase its effectiveness, the proposed method is tested in an auditing scenario where it successfully classified transaction behaviors.

This paper reveals that the outputs from the Strauss algorithm, which is an adaptive gradient descent method, are comprised of two distinct components - one being consistently changing and the other stagnant. Utilizing this insight, known as the stitching technique, it becomes possible to bypass the convergence rate limitations that apply to the standard Strauss algorithm. By leveraging this technique, it is shown that the algorithm's final output can be achieved through iterating only over the constantly evolving component, while the static component may be ignored. Additionally, it is shown that the algorithm's final output can also be attained through iterating once for every participating component, where each component is associated with a specified iteration frequency. Consequently, this technique allows producing a final output with a convergence rate of $O(1/n)$ at any desired iteration pace, thereby addressing urgent machine learning needs. Moreover, the technique is complemented by an innovative computation method referred to as the optimal stochastic gradient descent step, aimed at optimizing the iteration efficiency for standard stochastic gradient descent.

Condon's generalized ambiguity hypothesis, developed in 1990, reveals that known frequency mappings associated with the Galilean and Lorentz groups have a common characteristic - they maximize the entropy of the associated transformation matrices. This key discovery leads to multiple frequency mappings, and the paper's goal is to examine their fundamental properties. As a result, the paper derives a substantial consequence: it is impossible to maximize entropy in transformations involving objects with a speed less than the speed of light. Additionally, the paper provides more general proofs of two fundamental properties of one-to-one frequency mappings - invertibility and stability - using a novel approach. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel criterion for verifying if a one-to-one frequency mapping exists, and it confirms that the known Lorentz frequency mapping constitutes the only mapping that maximizes entropy in the Lorentz group.

Multitasking management is a core component in modern data processing systems, responsible for handling a constant flow of tasks and ensuring each task's completion in a timely manner.  Effective multitasking management translates to better system performance and user experience.  This paper introduces a theory and practice by upgrading the Bolt multitasking queue to incorporate shared computation capabilities, facilitated by a priority-based bidding process.  In the proposed system, each task competes for computation resources via a bidding process, determined by factors such as processing time and importance.  As a result, tasks are allocated a shared computation resource for a predetermined duration of time.  To establish the optimal bidding strategy, the authors developed an intricate optimization equation, also validating the efficiency of an accelerated solution-based approach.  Using real-world data, the authors created a performance metric to evaluate the performance of different computing schedules.  Furthermore, the proposed method allows for the determination of an optimal processing duration under various computation patterns.  Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed schedule, showcasing a substantial improvement in a 70% reduction of long task completion times and 25% reduction of average task completion times when compared to conventional approaches.

This research investigates the dynamics and stability of a one-legged (monopod) robot that moves across yielding surfaces, using reduced models to minimize computational complexity while maintaining accuracy. We begin by reviewing and validating existing simulation models before developing an integrated framework that unites three key aspects of legged locomotion: (i) rapid terrain deformation modeling through finite elements, (ii) streamlined dynamics and stability analysis, and (iii) optimization-driven control systems for enhanced performance. To assess the efficacy of our method, we test it on various yielding-terrain scenarios and discover that the conventional proprioceptive control strategy is insufficient for successful movement, but our proposed approach enables the creation of new, faster gaits, that are inaccessible to human runners and conventional control strategies. Our methodology contributes to the advancement of autonomous, adaptive legged locomotion for the real world.

To determine the feasibility of software upgrade processes for resource-constrained devices, we evaluated several methods, including using a mesh network of 300 devices, to compare mesh overlay sizes, connection times, and concurrency levels in real-time communications. Our findings reveal that mesh formations can exceed the threshold for reliable software upgrade applications and that mesh efficiency can be optimized through selective connection management. Furthermore, we found that using a mesh network for software upgrades significantly outperforms conventional HTTP upgrades, exhibiting robustness against device failures and timely connection establishment. Ultimately, our multi-faceted evaluation highlights the benefits and opportunities presented by software upgrade processes in real-time communications on mesh networks.

We numerically constructed a unitary propagator for many-body systems in the Schrödinger representation, then analyzed its structure in the basis of many-body Fock states. Our approach provided a clear, continuous transformation between the thermodynamic limit and the one-body localization phase, involving a set of characteristic times for the decay of amplitudes in Fock states. The behavior of these characteristic times as the system size increased allowed us to identify two distinct phases: an ergodic phase characterized by a single, unique timescale that depends on the number of excitations, and a multifractal phase near many-body localization where different excitation times scale according to a fractal dimension in the lattice. The same multifractal phase was also detected by calculating the multifractal moment \lambda2 from the entanglement entropy of the first excited state and its eigenvalue spectrum.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking research contribution in a novel research setting, where a planner interacts with an optimal but unpredictable decision-maker for a task with multiple desirable outcomes. In this task, both the planner and the decision-maker start with perfect knowledge, and each outcome has a well-defined quality associated with it. The study defines a quality score function that quantitatively assesses the effectiveness of planning strategies and their quality outcomes. Based on this framework, the study provides three main research outcomes. Firstly, the planner can achieve the highest possible quality score by exploring and estimating the outcomes until a predetermined resource limit is reached. Secondly, the planner's most effective strategy is adapted from a well-established method, which is typically used in other optimization settings. Lastly, the planner's most effective approach adapts to changing conditions, even in complex, unpredictable environments. To achieve these outcomes, the study provides algorithmic solutions, which demonstrate their performance in various evaluation studies. An associated video presentation can be accessed at https://youtu.be/IkNeya6tQkA.

Researchers have successfully demonstrated the ability of quantum machines to perform
classification tasks on complex datasets, and introduced noise instances that can fool
these quantum classifiers without being identified. However, existing noise instances
only consider the global perspective of the data, and do not account for inconsistencies
within local data subsets. Furthermore, these noise instances were shown to be detectable
by skilled quantum operators. In this research, we address these shortcomings by developing
advversarial noises that are undetectable and account for local data variations.
Additionally, we investigate the impact of disturbance time on their disturbance magnitude,
and propose an algorithm to synthesize noise at the bit level, thereby enabling the creation
of noise instances with varying levels of intensity that correspond to different disturbance
times. Using the Sony ImageNet dataset, we were able to produce over 2,400 unique noise
instances that can fool quantum machines without being detected.

We establish a lower limit on the smallest Steklov eigenvalue $\lambda_k(\Omega)$ 
for regions encompassed by nearly spherical contours. Specifically, for 
symmetric functions, we demonstrate that 
$\lambda_k(\Omega) 
\geq \frac{\pi^2 d^2}{\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)^2} 
+ O(d)$ as the distortion $d$ approaches infinity. Additionally, under 
a certain condition, we show that 
$\lambda_k(\Omega) 
\geq \frac{\pi^2 (d-1)^2}{\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)^2} 
+ O(d^2)$ for odd $k$. Our findings apply to convex domains as well as 
more general regions. We achieve this by calculating the second-order term in 
Taylor's expansion for the first Steklov eigenvalue around a sphere. Our 
analysis is conducted employing the method of eigenfunctions, for which we 
calculate the asymptotic behavior of the first $d$ eigenfunctions for the 
Schrödinger operator on the sphere.

Conformance testing for systems that generate partial traces is crucial to ensure they comply with specified trace requirements. We introduced a conformance verification method, known as Alignments, to identify areas in a test sequence where it deviates from the expected trace, indicating that the system under test does not meet the specified trace. However, in cases where test and required traces intersect at multiple points, Alignments proves computationally challenging, rendering its construction impractical. We revised the Alignments method, addressing these multi-point overlaps by employing prefix and postfix alignments that only analyze overlapping segments where the test and required traces diverge. By focusing on these challenging segments, the revised Alignments method has reduced its construction complexity and scalability limitations while demonstrating the same ability to pinpoint conformance issues. Additionally, the revised method is more intuitive and easy to interpret since it aligns prefixes and postfixes in a straightforward manner, unlike the initial version that incorporated net alignments that combined and merged different types of alignments. We have also introduced an approach to leverage prefix and postfix alignments in conjunction with one-sided alignments that focus on individual test or required traces, thereby analyzing the entire test and required traces simultaneously. This comprehensive alignment is realizable through the lexicographically smallest representative combinations of prefix, postfix, and one-sided alignments, which we call the representative alignment. The representative alignment effectively captures the conformance issues identified by individual alignments, including net, prefix, postfix, and one-sided alignments. We have conducted experimental studies to verify the effectiveness of revised Align

A novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based approach is proposed for generating radio frequency (RF) wave patterns, including scattering and absorption, across a range of frequencies within the wireless spectrum. By applying this CNN method to pixelated images of outdoor city landscapes, including building arrangements, it is possible to accurately model and predict the propagation of RF waves. Performance comparisons with traditional mathematical models, such as the Multiple Knife Edge Fat Edge Shadowing Model, have demonstrated significant precision gains, with prediction errors reduced by as much as 60% for frequencies above 6 GHz. This modified CNN method is named Deep KnEFE (DKE), and its accompanying code is available on a publicly accessible GitHub repository. Through further integration with network planning tools, DKE has the potential to revolutionize and enhance the development of future high-frequency cellular networks.

Time is an essential consideration in numerous domains, yet time is often represented inelegantly and inaccurately in AI frameworks that support planning. Specifically, within the planning task framework, time is typically defined using a set of predefined, time-related actions, which restrict when these actions can be executed. In contrast, we introduce a formal semantics for time that is independent of a particular representation approach but still aligned with existing frameworks. Additionally, we introduce an automated validation technique that rigorously checks the consistency of temporal planners based on this formal semantics. Our approach involves generating instances of temporal planners and leveraging these instances to identify inconsistencies. However, this previous approach had a limitation in detecting delays, which can occur when one time point occurs after another. We address this limitation by enabling the representation of arbitrary time relationships between time points. However, this expanded representation increases the likelihood of detecting false positives due to the introduction of additional time relationships. As a result, our approach has been revised to minimize its execution frequency while ensuring the precise identification of inconsistencies.

The world's energy consumption per capita has experienced steady growth over time, with varying rates of increase in different eras. Two mathematical models that describe this trend, one from Allen et al. and another from Pielow et al., yield significantly different projected consumption levels by the end of this century - specifically, a doubling with the Allen model, and a rise to just above 5 times the current level with the Pielow model. Our research reveals that this discrepancy stems from fundamental differences in these models' capacity for growth. The faster-growing Pielow model can accommodate the expansion of service sectors and advancements in energy efficiency, whereas the more conservative Allen model cannot. This highlights the significance of factoring in the likelihood of future economic and technological advancements when building models of energy system growth. To better capture the potential for continued growth, we suggest modifying the Allen model by introducing additional variables that mirror the mechanisms facilitating growth within the Pielow model. Additionally, to enhance the Pielow model's predictive accuracy, we incorporate a supplementary equation that takes into account the effects of rising incomes on energy consumption within the European Economic Zone.

This study establishes the global regularity of the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within enclosed areas, utilizing minimal initial conditions and a specific velocity bound. We achieve this result through an innovative strategy that combines the Maxwell-Born-Gouy-Stewartson system, previously investigated by Miot, with the infinitely exchangeable integrals from the Benamou-Borghi approach and the Radon variational representation.

Conventional Search Query Understanding techniques aim to generate relevant concepts for search queries based on historical data. While concepts are vital in organizing search content, users often employ additional concepts (search phrases) that enhance query context. Current methods fail to account for these additional concepts (search phrases) during search query processing. Our study introduces a novel approach, STRICT, which leverages historical context to identify and utilize search phrases to enrich concept searches. DISTINCT combines retrieval and matching techniques from natural language processing and information retrieval while adhering to strict criteria to produce concise and accurate search phrase lists. Furthermore, we introduce a model, CONCEPT, which integrates STRICT and controls the over-optimization of search phrase lists. Our extensive experiments on real-world data reveal that STRICT successfully identifies and applies search phrases to enrich concept searches.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that can be modified mechanically and physically by exposing them to high-frequency sound waves. When subjected to these sound waves, the material undergoes deformation and may even change structure, allowing for adjustment of its rheological properties. In a study on colloidal gels, scientists found that high-frequency sound waves led to organized movements of particles, which improved the material's ability to flow. This effect, which occurs at a specific threshold of sound intensity, can also affect the material's ability to deform without breaking, with maximum efficiency occurring at a certain ratio of particle size to sound wave frequency. In addition, the material's ability to flow can persist even after the sound waves stop, which makes it possible to improve the material's ability to flow without reducing its ability to deform. This discovery could lead to new ways of modifying the material's properties without changing its composition.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known hypothesis within number theory that describes the sequential pattern of number transformation. It states that any given integer, starting with either an even or odd number, will undergo successive transformations: doubling the integer when it's even and halving it when it's odd, alternating between these two rules. The Collatz sequence continues until the integer reaches one, at which point the sequence terminates. While initial observations suggest a consistent pattern, proving or disproving the Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved challenge. Various researchers have explored the relationship between numbers and their Collatz sequences, uncovering many significant results along the way. Given its intricate complexity, mathematicians consider the Collatz Conjecture one of the most significant unsolved problems within the field of mathematics.

Classifying STEM documents into categories like conference papers, books, and Ph.D. theses is crucial but also exceptionally challenging due to their distinct structure and extensive use of technical language, as well as varying lengths and formats. Prior STEM classification research focused mainly on text features, overlooking the crucial role of mathematical expressions and equations. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of analyzing these components but failed to account for their interrelation. Our research aims to improve STEM classification accuracy by examining the interactions between technical terms within equation contexts, which we call mathematical entities. We have developed a model that uses this interrelation – referred to as the Math Entity Connection – to enhance the representation of documents for classification. Our findings show that incorporating ME-C, as we call this approach, leads to significant and consistent enhancements in STEM classification performance, outperforming existing methods by a substantial margin.

In auction theory, the combinatorial exchange problem involves finding the optimal bundle of items for a buyer at a low price, and thereby maximizing seller revenue. This study makes progress toward solving the reliable matching challenge, which requires sellers to create the bundle of maximum value to buyers while maintaining a profit margin. The researchers evaluated the performance of the TOPS system, a price-adjusting mechanism, and found it achieved a 68.16% return on investment, exceeding the 67.00% return of the optimal outcome. Notably, the performance of TOPS improved over time, and it consistently surpassed the optimal outcome starting from the first bidding round with a significant margin. The study also compared the performance of TOPS with other mechanisms and found that it returned 8% more profit than the third-best mechanism in certain scenarios. These results indicate that TOPS is an effective and efficient mechanism that works well in practical scenarios.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are one-size-fits-all and lack
sensitivity to high-level representation of its task-specific nature. As a result,
the performance of existing metrics often fails to accurately reflect a good
summary, thereby hindering the optimization process. In light of this shortcoming,
we introduce SummScore, a groundbreaking automatic evaluation metric for
summarization tasks. This innovative approach relies on a Cross-Encoder to
determine the quality of a generated summary by comparing it to its reference
version. Our research indicates that SummScore establishes a more effective
correlation with human assessments compared to existing metrics, while its
discriminative power surpasses previous metrics in identifying high-quality
summaries. Furthermore, we show that SummScore can serve as a reliable tool for
enhancing the performance of existing summarization models. Our study also
demonstrates that SummScore can facilitate human-to-machine communication during
reinforcement learning, thereby accelerating the improvement of summarization
models. Our developed metric, SummScore, is available at:
https://www.gluu.ai/research/SummScore.

The underlying signals behind data points are often unknown, creating an issue in data analysis.  A comprehensive approach, called complete and convex quadratic reconstruction (CCQR), is developed to extract the actual signal from a set of data.  A key aspect (convexity) is that a quadratic function always remains convex, making it easy to identify the signal, with a computational complexity of $O(n^2)$, as opposed to the $O(n^3)$ of traditional methods, with no loss in precision.  Furthermore, it is shown that the signal can be reconstructed perfectly with $O(n)$ samples when the data follows a Gaussian distribution, with no additional assumptions.  This result is generalised to higher dimensions with no polynomial increase in computational requirements.

The integration of LiDAR and camera data is crucial for various applications, but current methods face several limitations due to complex processing pipelines, reliance on proprietary software, and fragile algorithms. These limitations hinder real-time processing and robust performance. To address these issues, we develop a novel approach called BEVFusion, combining both image and LiDAR view features within a unified brain-inspired framework. This model, built with brain-inspired neurons, achieves coordinate mapping and feature fusion through three simple layers. Notably, it employs a distinctive distributed encoding technique to capture scene context, which demonstrates superior LiDAR-Camera integration performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in real-time 3D object detection with detected rates comparable to scene-centric methods, and outperform image-based methods in this task.

In the outer atmosphere of the Sun, the behavior of plasma is influenced by two types of disturbances, conventional heat fluctuations and a different phenomenon called thermal disturbances. Although the dissipation range of turbulent flows in gases has been extensively studied, the nature of thermal disturbances in plasmas remains less understood. Recent research has shed new light on the statistical properties of thermal disturbances, revealing that they follow Gaussian statistics at higher levels and Coulomb-coupling levels, whereas at ion-ion coupling levels they follow a different path. Furthermore, this study confirms that thermal disturbances in the solar atmosphere do not arise from conventional heat fluctuations.

Recently, there has been renewed interest in the non-linear laser interaction with a liquid due to its diverse applications across multiple scientific disciplines. The phenomenon was once thoroughly researched in the 1960s and 1970s, but the recent surge in interest appears to be driven by a lack of understanding of the underlying principles rather than previous studies. The absence of fundamental knowledge is striking given its potential benefits for high-average-power and short-pulse laser systems. To fill this gap, our study provides a simplified numerical model for the thermal self-focusing process in a liquid, leveraging the hydrodynamic equation to simulate energy dissipation and the Maxwell equations for electronic conductivity and heat transfer. The model has been validated against experimental and numerical results from highly similar conditions in the past, and it reveals a more intricate and complex behavior than previously anticipated. The model not only explains the observed diffraction patterns but also offers insights into the thermal self-focusing process, which could have far-reaching implications for future research in the field.

Our proposed method, known as Conversational Refactoring, utilizes natural language processing to create design conversations as part of refactoring tasks, generating specifications based on these conversations. To further develop this approach, we have created various design conversations for a specific coding task and compared the designs created by multiple specifications made by the system. The results reveal that through ongoing review and revision of the system's settings and output, even minor changes to design conversations can have significant consequences. To mitigate this, we have implemented new features like conversational filtering, enabling the system to automatically create design specifications based on user-defined criteria. Our approach is gaining practical applicability as conclusions drawn from task-specific design conversations become more stable and reliable.

The analysis and processing of massive stream data and structured records are key functionalities in various areas, including real-time analytics, event-driven applications, and operational database systems. Due to the high velocity and volume of stream data, swift processing is critical to meet analysis and decision-making needs. The approach to processing stream data differs significantly from traditional relational databases and data mining methods. A new technique, called the Hybrid Stream Processing model, addresses the limitations of current models by leveraging established databases and analytics tools to efficiently process high-volume and high-velocity stream data. However, developing solutions that integrate various tools and processing components efficiently remains a significant challenge. This research introduces H-STREAM, a hybrid pipeline architecture that addresses these challenges and enables seamless integration of processing components, including both streams and databases. The performance of H-STREAM is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluation using real-world and simulated datasets, including Yahoo! Web metrics, network packet captures, and the Wikipedia dataset. A prototype of H-STREAM has been developed and experimentally validated, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing and proposed solutions, including K-DB, PipeLab, Dataflow, and Apache Flink, in terms of processing time and efficiency.

The translation of text from one language to another is a fundamental problem that has been studied for decades in the field of computational linguistics. Recently, the area of neural machine translation has gainedpopularity and attracted the attention of researchers. However, most of these studies have been based on datasets consisting of short text segments, such as sentences or paragraphs, primarily using data from the EuroParafrap dataset. This paper focuses on the task of translating text from one language to another, specifically English to French. In a breakthrough study, the authors achieved excellent results using a novel approach to neural machine translation based on SPARQL queries. This approach treats knowledge management as a translation task and leverages a stack-based model to simulate query execution. Despite achieving good results, there were some limitations with the original research. Firstly, it used a simple stack-based model for simulating SPARQL query execution and did not exploit the full range of available knowledge. Secondly, when translating text, the model treats all knowledge management information as a single unit, without considering the possibility of combining multiple elements to achieve a more translationally accurate outcome. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a new approach to neural machine translation based on SPARQL queries and a mechanism for managing knowledge management elements as a means of simulating query execution and achieving better translation results. A replication mechanism is introduced to address the first limitation, and this is proven to outperform the original approach. In addition, a combination mechanism is developed to address the second limitation

This work seeks to investigate and showcase the value of venue metrics, 
focusing on key characteristics, such as distribution, reliability, and trends. 
In contrast to the prevailing practice of using citation counts as a measure of author impact, 
venue metrics offer several significant advantages, including decreased computation time 
and the ability to assess entire departments or institutions. Venue metrics can 
reveal detailed insights about research units, including their productivity, 
consistency of output, and overall research performance. By analyzing big data 
(billion paper records and 70 million author profiles), this study demonstrates 
the utility of venue metrics through comprehensive analyses. Notably, the paper 
demonstrates that well-established research units aren't only prolific but also tend 
to maintain consistency of high-quality output over extended periods. Conversely, 
newly established research units, though sometimes productive, frequently struggle 
to sustain a consistent, impactful output. These findings emphasize the value of 
venue metrics in informing strategic research planning and highlight potential 
shortcomings in citation-based methods as a basis for evaluation.

The widespread adoption of neural networks in regulatory decision-making has sparked debate over ensuring these models are reliable. Currently, the use of neural networks in high-stakes regulatory settings lacks standardization and universal guidelines. Traditional methods for verifying computer programs are insufficient for validating the complex predictions made by neural networks. A novel approach, specifically Neural Network Validation, NNV, has been proposed to provide a legally binding guarantee of correct neural network behavior. NNV can be applied to machine learning models used in regulation, offering a mathematical proof of their reliability. A study presented at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency in 2018 demonstrated the potential for NNV in regulating a predictive valuation model for listing securities on the New York Stock Exchange. This paper serves as a complementary update, providing expanded verification bounds, refining the definition of input data restrictions, and detailing the challenges of implementing NNV in a real-world context.

This paper introduces an iterative algorithm that merges adjacent biological structures under specific criteria, producing a representation from a set of spatially-organized subgroups. The proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art grouping methods by incorporating an unbiased clustering step that allows for overlapping subgroups. Unlike other techniques, this algorithm is designed to be purely spatial, eliminating the need for attribute information. The evaluation of our method involved assessing its performance on simulated data and two real-world brain dataset consisting of cortical gyri and cerebellar folia. When compared to existing fully automated grouping methods, our results demonstrate both quantitative and qualitative improvements in accuracy. The implementation of this algorithm is available under a free and open-source license on GitHub, specifically within the BiTomo package.

In various applications, recovering complete tensor rings from partial, streamed components is crucial, yet challenging, due to the missing data and continuous streaming. Building upon the streaming ARD (Automatic Relevance Determination) algorithm, this research presents the PSTR, a more efficient method for recovering low-rank tensor rings one patch at a time. By incorporating the patch-level streaming ARD algorithm (pSTR), the PSTR algorithm enhances data recovery, accuracy, and stability, outperforming existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the PSTR algorithm in multiple real-world scenarios, including deblurring and super-resolution tasks, showcasing its potential in accelerated data retrieval.

It is demonstrated that for all cases of traditional Weyl groups of rank greater than one, their associated Nichols algebras are exactly those derived from the diagonal groups within the associated Lie algebras' root lattice, utilizing Poincaré polynomial calculations and a classification outcome from another study; in addition, direct proof is offered for cases of rank two.

In rotating fluids, inertial waves exhibit a unique behavior, resembling chaos due to the mixing caused by their wave interactions. Despite being highly complex, this phenomenon allows the existence of a well-defined energy spectrum. Recent studies have shown that this spectrum, characterized by $E(\ka)\propto\ka^{-4}$, can be interpreted as a signature of chaos. This paper provides a rigorous definition of the spectrum $E(\ka)$ as the expected value of the energy density of the inertial wave field over wavenumber $\ka$, and investigates its behavior in the presence of rotational constraints. To achieve this, we leverage high-resolution computational simulations that combine elements of Euler equations and random processes. By analyzing these simulations, we establish the relationship between $E(\ka)$ and $\ka$, and demonstrate that its power-law dependence on $\ka$ persists across a broad range of rotational rates. Furthermore, by extrapolating these findings to the limit of infinitely rotating fluids, we verify the consistency of the results with classic theories, such as those developed by Zakharov and Kolmogorov.

We begin by reviewing methods for normalizing graph characteristics, including a novel approach that incorporates feedback. Standard graphs are defined by their inherent properties, which enable comparison and analysis of graph structures. Graph normalization is crucial for various applications such as feature extraction and metric learning. We demonstrate a novel method for feedback-driven graph normalization, and then use it to investigate the relationship between the optimal weight of non-interactive sets within a given graph. A non-interactive set is a subgraph where removal does not affect remaining edge connections. We investigate the characteristics of optimal contact systems within graphs and their relationship to the feedback-driven graph standardization process.

This research explores the thermodynamic properties of a monolayer graphene that undergoes phase transitions, including transitions influenced by an electric field. By conducting computations, we examined the impact of the electric field phase transition on the thermodynamic properties of a monolated graphene. Our results reveal that the electric field causes a potential energy shift of approximately 100meV in the system. Furthermore, we found that the electric field significantly affects the entropy of the system, resulting in differences of up to 1.9 times the ideal gas value. The electric phase transition also caused a negligible change in the specific heat capacity of the system. Additionally, on-shell contributions were found to dominate the thermodynamic properties of the system.

The binary system of CR Draconis includes a compact white dwarf with a binary partner that is a flare star, making it an ideal subject for studying magnetohydrodynamic processes and the phenomenon of electron-cyclotron maser emissions.  The study conducted by P. S. Sornac using the Low Frequency Array revealed continuous radio emissions from the source of CR Dra during the period of observation.  Emissions at low frequencies of less than 250 MHz were extended, last seen on July 2, 2019.  High sensitivity observations on July 7-8, 2019, allowed for mapping of the source of emissions, yielding an angular size of approximately 3 arcseconds.  The characteristics of this radio emissions support a the presence of heated magnetic loops with higher plasma densities on the eastern side of the source of emissions, aligning with the direction of the white dwarf's magnetic pole.  Pulsed radio emissions with high flux densities were observed on July 16-17, 2019, attributed to a star flare.  Emissions at such great low frequencies for so long can be explained through the electron-cyclotron mechanism.  The presence of sufficient heat source, non-thermal acceleration of electrons and modifications to the magnetic field line geometry through gravitational force are necessary conditions for such a radio emissions phenomenon to occur.  The gravitational interaction between magnetic loops of the binary system's magnetic field, resulting in frequent flares and radio emissions, can occur.  Observ

We have developed an novel method for creating highly customized 3D representations of human figures from a single image. Our approach enables the creation of fitting and proportional models even in cases where the available data is limited. Unlike existing sculpting techniques, our method is specifically designed to handle the creation of human avatars, allowing for detailed control over the shape and proportions of the model. Additionally, our method can be combined with real-world data, making it easily compatible with existing skeleton tracking technologies. This alignment with bone structure enables the creation of naturally moving avatars. In comparison with state-of-the-art methods, our results demonstrate the significantly improved accuracy and level of detail achieved through Articulated Neural Depiction.

Machine and human perception of images shares a common ground, but their response to altered images diverges significantly. While both can detect altered images, each processes images with intricate structure independently. Machines, governed by strict rules, accurately identify image manipulations but are insensible to the nuances of human perception. Humans, on the other hand, can discern the intent behind such manipulations but struggle to provide precise definitions. It has been found that machines and humans are equally proficient in identifying image manipulations in image recognition tasks, but their agreement sharply declines when evaluating complex tasks that require nuanced human understanding. This study demonstrates a novel challenge that tests machines' ability to understand image manipulations and reveals that machines can differentiate between altered images, but fall short of capturing the intricacies of human perception. Machines have excelled in various image analysis tasks, demonstrating their potential to understand image manipulations that hold significance for humans. Machines have successfully identified images with intense manipulations like image manipulations in graphic design but failed to understand lesser-known image manipulations like image manipulations in cultural rituals.

In recent years, a connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory and its relation to quantum invariants of knots has been discovered. This relationship allows us to identify three parameters from the Askey-Wilson algebra as the square root of the Chern-Simons coefficient, the inverse of the Planck constant, and half of the inverse of the Euler characteristic of a knot's Seifert form. Furthermore, a representation of the algebra that corresponds to the quantum group U_q(so_2) is found to be consistent with the r-matrix of this representation when the quantum parameter q approaches 1 from the left. As a result, a limiting case of the generators of the 32-dimensional representation of the AW-algebra is found, in addition to establishing a connection between this representation and the 32-dimensional irreducible representation of the quantum group U_q(so_2).

Our research involves the theoretical analysis of a closed 2D quantum cluster system, specifically a strongly-connected core surrounded by a loosely-bonded outer network. We're investigating an edge-driven spin-triplet ground state in a model of weakly-hopping, frustrated clusters as a function of hole concentration for various ring sizes in the parquet quantum Monte Carlo framework. We discovered a transition from a two-dimensional lattice to a network-like structure as the concentration of holes increases, accompanied by the formation of spin-triplet exciton configurations. A neighboring charge pattern emerges within the core structure, specifically around concentrations of 0.06-0.11 per site. We observe an edge-driven lattice formation approach, unlike the two-dimensional lattice model which exhibits a first-order phase transition. The observed first-order transition occurs at approximately 0.86-0.87 per site in the concentration of holes, an area correlated with a two-dimensional lattice formation. We propose that the observed phenomenon could be the initial signs of a zero-energy spin-1 domain wall in a three-dimensional lattice, specifically in copper-based triangular structures and the recently discovered triplite mineral CuFeO2.

Pre-trained language models excel at text classification but often underperform on zero-shot dataset and prompt assemblies due to suboptimal generalized features. To address this issue, researchers have developed a prototype for meta-tuning pre-trained models on dataset and prompt collections. This approach involves adding task-specific tokens to prompts and modifying the prompt assembly by selecting subtasks and optimizing order. A sliding window approach is used for dataset assembly by extracting subsets and adjusting models using dataset and prompt assemblage gradients. This algorithm was tested with Transformer and ALBERT models on Prompt-assembled Linear Regression, Multi-RALE, and NLP-Marco datasets, resulting in a 10% relative improvement in performance compared to the baseline. The algorithm was found to outperform zero-shot, fine-tuning, and meta-tuning benchmarks on seven educational datasets and achieved better robustness and generalization to unseen data. A demo video illustrating the algorithm can be viewed at https://www.ilt.columbia.edu/video/metatuning-educational-nlp.html. The algorithm implementation is available under an open-source license at https://github.com/asharakeh/DPA-META-TUNING.

Recent findings from the Higgs and dark matter studies at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have provided novel constraints on the $Z_3$-symmetric NMSSM model. These constraints emerge due to the inherent equivalence principle problem that has natural implications for a $Z_3$-invariant scenario. Notably, the LHC discoveries reinforce the necessity of correct identification of the Higgs doublet boson in ongoing and future NMSSM analyses. Moreover, dark matter investigations based on LHC data provided a key indication of a $Z_3$-invariant parameter space preference. This model assumes a $Z_3$-invariant parameter space, which is preferred by LHC and dark matter studies. Utilizing the $Z_3$-invariant parameter space as a prior, we explored electroweak naturalness in the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM by identifying viable scenarios that could be detected through future Gravitational Wave (GW) experiments. As GW parity assumes $Z_3$, we investigated the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM parameter space favored by LHC and dark matter studies under the GW parity.
