Photometric redshift predictions for objects emitting certain types of light are discussed. A newly developed approach, the High-z Sudoku algorithm, utilizes a prior-based probability distribution to calculate redshift probabilities for objects detected by spectrometers and infrared cameras. By employing a robust statistical model, High-z Sudoku generates reliable and consistent redshift estimates that align with spectroscopic data, even with uncertain or high signal-to-noise ratios. It effectively identifies contiguous z-distributions and prioritizes them, differentiates between robust and spurious redshift estimates, and identifies and excludes unreliable redshift estimates. High-z Sudoku's effectiveness in generating accurate and robust redshift estimates is demonstrated through its analysis of a mock line-integrated spectral dataset in the 1 mm wavelength, which yielded a 97% agreement with spectroscopic data. It has also been applied to a set of millimeter and submillimeter redshift estimates from the ALMA REDS program to obtain a median redshift of z = 2.55 and a 79% agreement with spectroscopic data. Overall, High-z Sudoku provides a reliable and independent redshift estimation approach that complements spectroscopic data, which is particularly useful in selecting robust redshift estimates for further follow-up with spectroscopy, even in datasets with small signal-to-noise ratios.

Investigating the $\CeTe$.$_{3}$ compound, researchers have uncovered the phase diagram of a $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice, exhibiting both solid and liquid states resulting from symmetry disruption. The symmetry-disrupted solid state displays a $q=0$ order via the calculation of nonmagnetic excitation properties and two-magnon excitation properties. Furthermore, researchers have identified the liquid states as highly anisotropic antiferromagnetic state and also spin-liquid state, however the latter needs further theoretical verification to fully understand its origin. The symmetry-disrupted liquid state, though not observed in $\CeTe$.$_{3}$, is highly comparable to the symmetry-disrupted solid state as both exhibit $q=0$ order. The findings from magnetic properties computation are consistent with experimental measurements, whereas computational methods identify two-magnon and one-magnon excitation within both solid and liquid states. The symmetry-disrupted and liquid states exhibit identical two-magnon excitation properties and nonmagnetic excitation properties. The study also establishes a clear correlation between one-magnon and two-magnon excitation, and further reveals that one-magnon excitation properties can be rectified by treating the long-range interactions using high-temperature expansions. The study concludes by highlighting the need for further research into the establishment of a phase diagram of low-dimensional and Dirac materials under the influence of randomness, pressure and

Deconfinement and continuous chiral symmetry are two phase transitions that occur simultaneously in the finite temperature and density phase diagram of theories with strong interactions, such as those described by $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across various density ranges. The relationship between them is explored through a variational approach utilizing $1/N-$expansion, which indicates that deconfinement arises from a complex phenomenon involving the interplay of many particles and anti-particles in the medium, resulting in a transition characterized by broken symmetry and large fluctuations. On the other hand, continuous chiral symmetry breaking is shown to occur as a result of density-driven screening between quark and anti-quark pairs, potentially leading to a further transition at low temperatures and densities, known as the crossover phase transition. Our findings support the existence of a specific region in the phase diagram where deconfinement and chiral symmetry breaking occur simultaneously, consistent with numerical data obtained from lattice simulations, which also demonstrates the occurrence of a particular transition scenario, known as the deactivation route to the deconfinement phase transition.

A new compound, Cr2Al, was investigated using a combined approach of neutron diffraction, neutron pair-distribution function analysis, and first-principles calculations. This study aimed at determining the internal magnetic arrangement and exchange interactions at temperatures up to 770 K. The results showed that Cr2Al exhibits an in-plane antiferromagnetic structure with exchange interactions along the a-axis and within the ab-plane, consisting of ferromagnetic and antiparallel spin interactions. The findings also revealed a unique property where the spin interactions stabilize the high-temperature magnetism. According to first-principles calculations, the magnetic stability is attributed to the unequal exchange interactions, characterized by the ferromagnetic coupling across the plane and the antiparallel spin interactions along the a-axis. This property distinguishes Cr2Al from other high-temperature antiferromagnets.

A new kinetic framework is proposed, incorporating a novel velocity-dependent collision frequency macro-model, to analyze rarefied gas flows. This kinetic model incorporates precise expressions for collision probability, derived from the Ornstein-Fenwick formula, which takes into account the higher order relationships between collision and viscosity coefficients. As a result, the kinetic framework proposed here can capture the influence of molecules' interaction potentials, a limitation in the conventional Boltzmann model based on the assumption of weak monomolecular interactions. Additionally, the kinetic framework proposed has the potential to be reduced to the standard Boltzmann model under certain conditions and is therefore compatible with a variety of numerical solution methods traditionally used for the standard model.

Building on the concept of Minimizing Misinformation, our approach educates a language model to accurately interpret the meaning behind specific words by incorporating additional knowledge from general knowledge sources, such as the internet. By assuming that words have a single clear interpretation, our approach aims to achieve results similar to what is achieved in established fields of study like linguistics, without needing vast amounts of data - we've achieved this with just a few examples. We've demonstrated this algorithm's effectiveness by assessing its ability to correctly understand the underlying meaning behind unfamiliar phrases solely based on its ability to understand individual words and their relationships. Furthermore, our findings illustrate that this algorithm not only provides accurate interpretations but also makes logical sense when given minimal training. We've also observed that this algorithm is capable of generating original, coherent, and informative responses to unfamiliar questions without any prior training.

For the electron-ion collider, a next-generation nuclear physics facility is being developed to sequence the groundbreaking discoveries of quantum chromodynamics across various nuclei. A detailed understanding of the EIC's future luminosity production infrastructure, comprising a high-field magnetic field and advanced radiation-resistant tracking sensors, is crucial for realizing this vision. Following breakthroughs in silicon technology and advanced design methodologies, the development of cutting-edge radiation-resistant silicon sensors is actively progressing for the future collider. Silicon sensors, utilized in precisely positioning charged particles, are set to play a pivotal role at the EIC through its compact rubber-insulated pipe structure and capacity to endure high-intensity beam radiation. Silicon sensor advancement is an ongoing process, with numerous researchers contributing innovative ideas and engineering solutions to the field. A current focus lies on the development of low-density, radiation-resistant sensors featuring an oxygen-rich design, requiring minimal detection signal, and equipped with sophisticated technological solutions to effectively operate in intense radiation environments. Through ongoing efforts and collaborative advancements, the achievement of these ambitious goals is within reach, paving the way for groundbreaking EIC research at the interface of quantum chromodynamics and nuclear physics.

A newly identified, low-intensity low-frequency flare was found in the low-powered radio galaxy 3C 186. This event's behavior diverges from expectations established with higher-powered outbursts. A model that assumes the phenomenon is the result of rapidly expanding radio waves, known as radio pulses, demonstrates a stronger fit when analyzing the observed patterns across multiple frequencies and times. Calculations indicate a typical size of the radio emission source, known as the core, to be around a few hundred to thousand astronomical units in radius. Alternatively, the observed pattern could be the result of multiple, separate expansions that may be powered by a star explosion, known as a supernova, in the host galaxy of the AGN. Research suggests that the AGN's behavior was fluctuating at a rate between 425-1075 years before the observed event occurred.

The study demonstrates, for the first time, the immediate change in the radial magnetic field that occurs when an external magnetic field is applied to a star. This phenomenon was observed during the spectropolarimetric observation of HD58260, which featured a modifiable external magnetic field with variable strength and direction and was conducted on March 19, 2015. Prior to the observation, the strength of the magnetic field around the star's surface was undetectable. Following the injection of the external magnetic field, a level of around 1.5 kilogauss was reached. This was the highest magnetic field that could be detected and it remained at this threshold for under five minutes before decreasing in strength over the course of the observation period, which lasted for a little over an hour and a half. This magnetic field's increase and decline can be fully accounted for through the geodesic adjustment theory.

A representation of the intertwining operator under Dunkl induction in one dimension is given using free bosons. This representation shows that the operator's action on functions that depend on $z$ can be equivalent to the operator's action on second-order polynomials that depend on $z^{-1}$.

Using ALMA's high-resolution imaging capabilities, we've observed the 119.2 GHz H30$\alpha$ line emitted by H$^{-}$ ions in the low-metallicity galaxy NGC 5253. Our findings are based on three frequency bands gathered in 2019, offering a detailed  in terms of linear size ($\sim$630$\times$275 parsecs at 119.2 GHz). Our analysis of NGC 5253's stellar genesis indicates an extremely restrictive low-metallicity environment. Our observations demonstrate the presence of external gas inflows in smaller and more massive star-forming complexes within and outside NGC 5253's disk, respectively. Furthermore, we provide an extensive comparison of  H30$\alpha$ emission between the spiral galaxy NGC 5194 and NGC 5253, highlighting distinct differences in star formation processes and environments at low and high metallicity. Finally, our study reveals the intricate structure of star-forming complexes in NGC 5253, offering new insights into massive star formation processes.

We demonstrate the presence of a characteristic property in the field of ergodic theory; this property maintains the similarity in transition dynamics between two dynamical systems, provided that their underlying mathematical structures remain unchanged and identical. Specifically, this characteristic leads to a uniform proportion in the number of measurable parts within maps that preserve measure, regardless of the specific measure in use. As a direct result, this property defines a distinct category of dynamical systems that are inherently equivalent, known as constant orbit equivalence stiffness. Our investigation centers on this equivalence category within the context of topological systems, where it is revealed that constant orbit equivalence stiffness is both highly adaptable and versatile. A key area of focus within our research involves the development of a framework of rigid bodies, where our definitions and identification of distinct categories remain consistent, thus yielding numerous consequences within the field of topological dynamics.

This study offers a comprehensive review of the theoretical underpinnings and practical implementations of a widely applied estimation technique for statistical models with non-uniform error distributions. Focusing on a specific type of nonparametric estimation for functional regression models with one categorical predictor and continuous response variables, the analysis establishes underpinning theoretical frameworks and probes its practical applications. Beyond establishing the necessary mathematical convergence for data reconstruction and pattern extraction, the paper explores novel algorithms and assesses their performance using simulated data for a three-level response variable.

This research centers on estimating epidemic disease parameters, specifically in prone-to-outbreak settings. An observer construct is developed to estimate the total number of infectious individuals, building upon previous work by Kirschner (2002) and Bl\"omker et al. (2020). Constructing an observer that can accurately estimate infectious individuals is only possible if all parameters are known, which is not the focus of this study. Instead, this work makes preliminary findings on developing observers to estimate total infected individuals and relevant parameters. Two specific scenarios are examined: predicting total infected individuals with known average infectious periods and estimating the average infectious period while predicting total infected individuals. For the first scenario, this study establishes observers that can accurately estimate total infected individuals. In contrast, for the second scenario, this research introduces a novel observer that can estimate the average infectious period as well as total infected individuals. Moreover, this research makes connections between the constructed observers and total infected observer constructs developed in (Bl\"omker et al. (2020)).

The growing interest in Knowledge Graph Construction has led to the development of several methods for enhancing graph details, particularly through text-based information extraction. Recent texts have focused on augmenting knowledge graphs with temporal relationships. Current approaches to predicting connections in temporal knowledge graphs often rely on model training on the graph's entire structure. However, these methods can be inefficient and require adjustments to the model for different graphs. In contrast, the structure of language remains relatively constant, which prompted us to explore using fixed models. Our proposal leverages the potential of fixed models, pre-trained on vast amounts of text, to predict connection candidates in temporal knowledge graphs. We evaluated various fixed models, incorporating a BERT component, and achieved notable success, ultimately achieving a 7% reduction in wrong suggestions and maintaining accuracy levels comparable to existing solutions.

The investigation of Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-energy and ultrafast oscillators relies heavily on analyzing the dynamics of their beam propagation parameter. This involves examining the interplay between nonlinear lensing, intracavity intensity, and transverse beam dynamics that shape the modeband for generating pulses of short duration. Specifically, this research highlights the structural features within the oscillator that predispose certain modes to be part of the modeband, and it uses the beam propagation parameter to calculate the expected performance of these modes. Notably, this approach contradicts a long-held assumption that the oscillator's output pulse duration is constant and independent of the pump power. Instead, this effect is shown to be influenced by nonlinear lensing, and a geometric, spatial approach provides insight into a potential technique for generating pulses of varying durations by adjusting the pump power. Overall, this research emphasizes the complex interplay among spatial, temporal, and angular aspects that contribute to the mode-locking process, and it challenges the conventional concept of mode-locking.

The trend of increasing model complexity to improve accuracy may need a readjustment due to the limitations in computational power, data accessibility, and energy efficiency. Nevertheless, recent advancements in distributed training have provided an opportunity to harness collective computing resources and unlock the full potential of more complex models. Nonetheless, distributed training also introduces challenges, such as unequal training times and model discrepancies, which could negatively impact the model's performance and stability. This paper presents an innovative, autonomous framework for distributed regression modeling that aims to balance training speed and precision while accommodating diverse resource capacities. Given the inherent unpredictability of asynchronous training, the proposed framework incorporates adaptable techniques to ensure data consistency and convergence. Moreover, it employs sophisticated strategies to synchronize model state and converge toward a unified solution despite model discrepancies. To achieve optimal results, the framework combines collective model aggregation with selective feature extrapolation to refine the collective model. This approach allows the framework to mitigate the effects of asynchronous training and maximize the benefits of diverse participants. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods.

To optimize the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells using a ground break technique, a 3D photonic band gap back reflector was investigated with various hole sizes in a silicon material. The addition of a layer made of silicon dioxide poured with nanoparticles was discovered to be effective in enhancing absorption when the hole size is 120 nm or smaller. The maximum absorption enhancement achieved was 3.4% at a minimum layer thickness of 260 nm. Simulations revealed that the effectiveness of this method primarily affects the material with thin layers but leads to reduced absorption in larger layers due to limited effectiveness against surface reflection.

We introduce an approach for evaluating multidimensional function asymptotics with the use of dominant pricipal terms. The asymptotic behavior of iterated exponential functions, specifically tetration, is thoroughly examined with this method. The same technique is further applied to solutions of autonomous partial differential equations, revealing the dominant features in their asymptotic profiles.

In high-dimensional data analysis, finding a suitable basis is crucial, but with the advent of machine learning and big data, the traditional methods no longer suffice. This paper introduces a new family of dimensionality reduction techniques, starts with a given basis, and repeatedly constructs new bases that capture subtle changes in the data. The proposed methods can handle large datasets and maintain theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of approximations, while demonstrating superior performance in practice by creating more adaptable and dynamic bases that capture important patterns. The experiments showcase the benefits of these methods over traditional approaches.

A comprehensive study of the magnetic properties and the phase transition in the recently discovered GdInO$_3$ single crystal, featuring a unique a $3$D-centered honeycomb structure, is presented with a focus on its antiferromagnetic arrangements at different temperatures. Evidence suggests that the magnetic properties can be described by two different types of magnetic modes, referred to as $1$A$_1$ and $3B$_2$ modes, which cause the proposed antiferromagnetic arrangements. Furthermore, the activation of the $3B$_2 mode at $9$K results in the breakdown of the proposed antiferromagnetic arrangements and the subsequent formation of a spin-frozen state. Magnetic heat capacity and magnetic susceptibility show a high temperature fluctuation due to the weakly interacting ionic nature and the presence of a ratio of $d$-wave component to $s$-wave component of $0.43$.

The social network's intricacies are influenced by individual behaviors, which can be understood by predicting the actions of unseen actors in the network. Current approaches utilize comprehensive social and attribute data but often fail when these inputs are scarce, whereas simple methods rely solely on network structure, which is suboptimal for predicting nuanced relationships. To address this issue, we present a social network model that incorporates a latent representation of actors similar to that of language processing. Specifically, our approach converts social data into a numerical format by learning node representations from available information and then utilizing these embeddings to predict connections. Surpassing existing standards, our model achieves this prediction based on limited data with enhanced accuracy and efficiency. Comprehensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our approach in diverse scenarios, which can be found on github.com/arguprakash/SSNE.

We introduce and characterize a new atomic vapor cell, integrating a 1.5 mm deep reactive ion etching- modified silicon chamber with an 800 micron silicon plate featuring 100 micron diameter apertures. The apertices serve as atomic vapor chambers for distribution to the three-dimensional volume of a heated substrate, facilitating the production and study of pairwise interactions between heated atoms. The internal chambers maintain ultra-high vacuum insulation from the external environment, encompassing the silicon structures in a vacuum chamber that is then sealed within a cryogenic bath of helium. The helium bath offers cryogenic stability while providing the required optical window thickness for the observation of interactions between atoms, facilitated by a silicon membrane with perforations that regulates vapor and He flow while maintaining 100:1 atomic density within the chamber to 800 micron thickness silicon depth. The chamber's low optical window thickness poses no obstacle to observation. The chamber was filled with rubidium and used to measure three-body interaction coherent $-1.5 \text{G/N}$, coherent loss, common-mode interference, and signal noise for isolated rubidium atoms within the chamber in relation to the surrounding helium bath.

We introduce an innovative model for calculating the nonlinear propagation disturbance within the context of dual-polarization systems employing M-Q amplitude shift keying and rotational symbol mapping. These formats are capable of providing polarization diversity, thereby offering a superior means of mitigating the effects of nonlinear distortion in systems that incorporate multiple polarizations. Building upon the second-order nonlinear Schrödinger equation model originally developed by Hermann-Hildebrand, we adapted and refined it to accurately account for RSM's inherent polarization properties. We compared the performance of our model against both the Hermann-Hildebrand model and a non-linear cubic-quantum model in terms of bite regulation, revealing that our model more effectively estimates the impact of nonlinear distortion. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of varying PMI and PAM factors on single-polarization and dual-polarization systems, uncovering that efficient PMI and PAM factors not only minimize nonlinear distortion but also maintain a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio.

Large wildfires have been devastating global ecosystems, therefore precision wild fire management is essential. Current approaches rely on detecting wildfires through satellite technology, yet this technique has its limitations during daylight visibility. Satellites are only capable of sensing fire intensity not providing visual evidence. To overcome this limitation, we suggest fusing near-infrared and visible spectrum images with the aim of revealing wildfire visuals. Several AI-based methods exist but are prone to similar limitations and interpretative difficulties as satellite technology. To address this challenge, we have developed a innovative approach called Fire Generative Adversarial Networks (FIRe-GAN) that uses deep learning to merge near-infrared and visible spectrum images, generating synthetic normally interpreted images. FIRe-GAN employs a innovative system of 3D spatial and channel attention mechanisms that allows it to focus on key features within the images. FIRe-GAN represents a substantial improvement over current approaches by producing high quality wildfire visuals in low image quality conditions, outperforming other techniques by 84.11% in quality assessment. FIRe-GAN also boasts a level of interpretability 94.23% higher than other methods and has been open-sourced for community use.

Early detection of mental health issues, specifically indications of depression, on social media platforms can play a crucial role in providing timely support to those in need. However, identifying accurate signals from vast amounts of user-generated content poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, researchers need to overcome two primary obstacles: first, developing a dataset that combines diverse content from social media platforms with annotated labels; second, refining data analysis processes to accurately capture online behavior and update machine learning models without disrupting performance.

To address these challenges, we conducted two key activities. Firstly, we gathered a large dataset from Twitter and annotated it for indication of depression using machine learning techniques. Secondly, we employed various statistical methods to examine depression signals on social media and evaluated the accuracy of machine learning models using our annotated dataset. This comprehensive approach involves data collection, empirical analysis, model training, and testing. The resulting findings provide valuable insights for future research on mental health on social media, and we make our dataset available to the research community to to allow for the identification of depression signals on social media. 

This work is a culmination of our past investigations, in which we collected raw data from Twitter and conducted an initial analysis. For this study, we refined our approach by correcting the data bias, updating our dataset, and conducting a more in-depth analysis to assess the performance of mental health detection models.

We've developed a novel stochastic model for COVID-19 that leverages randomly assigned latent classes and randomly assigned infectious classes. Unlike existing models, this framework avoids the assumption that latent periods inevitably lead to infectiousness. Instead, we've isolated two latent categories: one that progresses to infectivity and another that directly becomes infectious. Additionally, our model incorporates a previously unconsidered compartment that temporarily postpones infection. Focusing on the stochastic dynamics of the model, we analyzed the COVID-19 data from Connecticut, USA, and found notable discrepancies between our results and those of existing studies. Our findings suggest a significantly higher natural death rate than previously estimated, and a death rate linked to infections that occur outside of hospitals. Moreover, our research indicates a more severe impact on African Americans in Connecticut, with a higher infection rate and a substantial increase in natural death rate compared to their Caucasian counterparts.

The isoscalar giant monopole resonance (GMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was studied through inelastic scattering experiments. Measurements of GMR strength distributions were combined with theoretical calculations using the $ab-initio$ APR and N3K and N3D cubic-Yukawa global models. Unlike previous research, which considered a residual neutron-proton interaction separate from the phosphate coupling, the databases used here include phosphate coupling. Unlike the findings of Weidenmuller et al., these results indicate that, when taking into account phosphate coupling, the GMR strength in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si is not reduced when compared to the $ab-initio$ APR result and also reveal a significant discrepancy in the broad GMR components between the N3K and N3D models. These results highlight the complexity of isoscalar resonances and the need for further investigations of photonuclear science.

Biological and mechanical systems rely heavily on actuation mechanisms that feature stick-slip motion, which involves a combination of sticking and slipping. Research into these mechanisms is highly active, driven by the importance of understanding systems that are subject to friction. While there has been extensive research focused on the theoretical basis of stick-slip motion, particularly in systems that rely on constant friction coefficients, less is known about systems that feature Coulomb friction. In this study, we explored the theoretical foundation of stick-slip motion in systems that are governed by Coulomb friction and utilize a force feedback mechanism. We modeled the system as an equilibrium problem with a non-smooth resolution, which enabled us to demonstrate that the phase space of the system can be divided into distinct regions separated by stable manifolds that facilitate stable sticking and slipping behaviors. Additionally, we identified conditions that enable stable slipping behaviors and highlighted the key differences between systems that rely on constant and Coulomb friction.

Reinforcement learning algorithms can be vulnerable to errors brought on by noisy data, a problem that is systematically addressed by our approach, ProBM.  By combining a novel distance metric with the Bellman equation, ProBM enables reliable state-action pairs to be filtered and places a constraint on the Q-function, thereby guaranteeing improved generalization.  Our results demonstrate that ProBM offers significant advantages over existing methods, providing a reliable guarantee on its performance with minimal additional computation.  The efficiency of ProBM is also showcased through its successful application in deep reinforcement learning scenarios, including both max and min games.

Incompleteness and ambiguity plague user intent identification, which is crucial for personalization but often goes undetected by state-of-the-art recommender systems. Current approaches fail to incorporate explicit user intent detection, ignoring the potential for hidden user intent that might lead to poor recommendation quality. To address this gap, a novel framework leverages user interactions with recommendations to derive intent from implicit signals, modeling the complex relationships between intent, items, and users. The proposed framework enables efficient user intent modeling and optimization, which can be integrated into existing recommender systems to improve effectiveness. Evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed framework's ability to identify intent and demonstrate superior performance over baseline methods.

The focal point of the present findings is a particular form of the Heun equation, which exhibits the double confluent feature and has a convergent series solution under all three Fokas-Leble twists. The solution is straightforward to obtain to any order, as confirmed by a novel approach utilizing the modified Bessel polynomial solution of the fourth-order Fokas-Leble equation. The derived solution is initially expressed as a series of the modified Bessel polynomial (MBP) solution of the unfolding equation. Next, an iterative combination of the MBP solution and Heun equation parameters is applied to express the result in a convergent, twisted series form pertaining to the original problem. The application of the Fokas-Leble transformation to the original problem allows the derivation of an explicit, twisted series solution for the original problem, the form of which is identical to the original Bessel J0(z) solution of the Bessel equation, but with the variable z replaced by a twist-dependent combination of the Heun equation parameters and the Fokas-Leble parameter. Due to the solvable nature of the unfolding equation, the solution of the original problem can be expressed in terms of four distinct "unfolding parameters," which are determined by the Heun equation parameters and the Fokas-Leble parameter in a manner that is readily identifiable via the solution of the Bessel equation. Matrix valuation techniques, such as min-max norms, are frequently used in mathematical and computational sciences. These norms have a fundamental constraint that ensures their unitarity when transforming matrices with identical group-based structures. The constraint also applies to projections and rank-one matrices with specific subgroup-based structures. Additionally, it limits the eigenvalue magnitudes for matrices with uniform structure. Our research demonstrates that this constraint is tied to the matrix element determinants, specifically its largest and smallest values. We provide technical proofs for three specific matrix valuation norms, such as the Frobenius, Frobenius-Hopf, and Schur norms, and show how their properties apply to matrices with uniform or subgroup-based structures. Our findings have implications for matrix valuation methods, and we utilize an illustrative example involving a family of tensors to demonstrate its applicability to multidimensional arrays.

The underlying essence of topology is best exemplified through the concept of symmetry breaking, which is fundamentally a topological phenomenon. Despite its significant role in modern physics, symmetry itself plays no part in topological theory, and physicists must rely on physicists' intuition to grasp topological concepts. To address this, a new representation of topology is introduced, utilizing symmetry only as a visual aid tool. This paper demonstrates how to utilize symmetry to clarify four fundamental topological transformations: the crossing degeneration reflection, the Heegaard splitting, and the sphere and torus connections. Additionally, the paper illustrates how to apply these concepts to solve a real-world problem.

We introduce semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Equivalence (LFE) as a novel constraint on the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition, specifically examining the semi-inclusive $\ell^+\ell^-$ mode within $B\to X_s$ decays. This LFE constraint is directly proportional to $2R_D^2+2R_S^2$, where $R_{D,D^*}$ are ratios of Wilson coefficients over the $b\to c\ell^+\ell^-$ transition, and $R_{S,S^*}$ relate to the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ transition. Our analysis reveals that, at present, semi-inclusive LFE poses the most severe constraint on $R_D$ compared to inclusive $\ell^+\ell^-$ LHCb data and forward-backward asymmetry $\mathcal{A}_\xi^{l l}$, with both tests to follow. Should the future Belle II experiment non-reconstruct the $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{B}\to X_s)$ branching fraction with precision, semi-inclusive LFE will become the most sensitive probe of $R_D$ until the end of its run in 2025. Furthermore, semi-inclusive tests of LFE will be crucial in detecting lepton flavor violation, with potential new physics contributions corresponding to electron and muon flavor equivalences of $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-9

This research explores the potential issues associated with communication dependencies in decentralized estimators used for large-scale linear systems. It is found that conventional estimators may not be effective when some agents communicate with each other. To address this limitation, a new decentralized approach is introduced, along with an innovative distributed regulation strategy for multi-channel networks. The proposed solution enables plug-and-play functionality with ease, allowing for the seamless integration of new agents without recalculating existing parameters, and also offers enhanced flexibility in network communication. Furthermore, it is shown that our estimator and regulator designs work in harmony, leading to optimal performance and meet the requirements for innovation in the error state-space, and we have also provided stability guarantees for the closed-loop system. Numerical simulations have been conducted to verify the performance of our approach.

The global pandemic, COVID-19, has led to the development of numerous
classification systems for categorizing patients. To balance efficiency with
accuracy, a simple three-category system was initially adopted, consisting of
Suspected, Confirmed, and Recovered. However, a more precise approach is now
required to track the outbreak effectively, so digital artists designed an
attribute-based system with additional categories like High-Risk, Unknown, and
Transmitted. Inspired by the potential of BERT, a transformer-based model,
in natural language processing, this paper proposes an innovative attribute
extraction technique, BERTAttr, which integrates spatial and texture features to
accomplish two-phase attribute categorization. The model combines image features
with BERT attributes, offering improved accuracy and a comprehensive method
comparing the performance of conventional and deep learning artists.

This introductory guide is aimed at providing essential background knowledge and practical advice to help researchers working on network-related projects get started and navigate their work. Specifically, it outlines the fundamental mathematical and algorithmic principles behind network research, along with tips for effectively communicating results and managing large networks. The guide also offers holistic networks research inspiration and perspective. It was created by two researchers from the KTH Royal Institute of Technology and has already been used in their teaching and network research community outreach activities. It is now available in the hope that it will be useful to many more researchers and students.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics has primarily focused on individual and coupled timescales of ecological and evolutionary changes. Yet, variations in duration and intensity have received relatively little attention. This work reveals that eco-evolutionary dynamics exhibit a wide range of timescales and amplitudes that can be categorized into three distinct groups: slow, fast, and rapid ecological and evolutionary transformations. The research finds that evolutionary changes occur consistently over extended periods, whereas rapid, batch-driven ecological shifts influence the dynamics within minutes to hours, and rapid, continuous changes occur over a period of hours to days. This new framework uncovers three distinct patterns of eco-evolutionary dynamics and highlights the significance of duration and intensity in shaping complex and multifaceted evolutionary and ecological interactions.

Self-supervised learning methods for speech processing are increasingly successful across speech recognition, training data, and related tasks. However, the underlying principles of speech remain unclear. Previous attempts to investigate these principles through contrastive learning have been hindered by inconsistent negative sampling techniques. We introduce a new method for speech processing self-supervised learning that provides insight into the antagonistic susceptibility of natural sounds. We develop contrastive learning criteria that pinpoint unnecessary similarities within sounds and propose an efficient training strategy and a simple layer to facilitate fast experimentation. Our approach, called ReLearner, enables self-supervised learning with minimal data and fast processing, outperforming existing methods and achieving state-of-the-art outcomes on analogous tasks.

As the cryptocurrency market continues to grow, so have the alternatives to Centralized Exchanges (CEX), which have a history dating back to the early days of cryptocurrencies and initial coin offerings (ICOs). Decentralized Exchanges (DEX) have emerged as the more secure option, even though they come with their own set of challenges, particularly regarding order management and liquidity. With DEX's inherent issues in mind, this research sets out to explore the possibilities of spreading DEX's transaction orders across the network and increasing liquidity by applying the concepts of the Jester protocol, a truth-telling mechanism designed to enhance participation in societal polls. The proposed protocol, which can be applied to DEX, involves participants committing to their orders in exchange for "commitments" that can be later converted into "transactions." The conversions are facilitated through a bonding curve mechanism that ensures consistent and fair prices for market makers and liquidity providers. Our results show that this protocol encourages more users to participate in DEX by offering incentives in the form of discounts, while equally benefitting both market makers and liquidity providers with tailored profit margins. The former gains from reduced costs, the latter gains from increased demand for their services. Analysis of the DEX order book reveals an increased liquidity which benefits both parties as it results in taller order book which allows for greater flexibility in transactions. Our protocol has been shown to improve DEX's capabilities as it opens up new opportunities for both market makers and liquidity providers to participate and profit from DEX

In computational modeling, it's very frequent that some data is missing, yet we often neglect to account for this absence in parameter estimation. This study employs the E-value as a measure to assess the impact of absent information and develops a Bayesian approach to evaluate sensitivity. We primarily explore the E-value within a Bayesian framework but also present a frequency-based equivalent. A Bayesian E-value analysis for normal and log-normal distributions is presented along with a method to quantify the uncertainty associated with this evaluation. This methodology is demonstrated through a parameter estimation case involving a distribution with censored data. Furthermore, we present an empirical example showcasing the utility of the E-value in presenting results.

The study of the quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[\mathbb{P}^1\big]$ raises the intriguing question of determining its Laurent series expansion on the unit circle $S^1$ and constructing the associated C*-algebra $C^*_q\big[\mathbb{P}^1\big]$ through a series of complex matrix transformations. Utilizing the principles of the Yang-Baxter equation allows the development of a new method for expressing the Yang-Baxter drift as a product of two isomorphisms. Furthermore, this approach leads to a comprehensive analysis of the drift's connection to quantum group symmetries, which results in the formation of a regular C*-algebra $C^*_q\big[\mathbb{P}^1\big]$. Building upon this, it is possible to establish an isomorphism between $C^*_q\big[\mathbb{P}^1\big]$ and the C*-algebra associated with the two-dimensional torus $T^2$ equipped with a suitable $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry.

The global network of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) has brought about transformations in daily life along with societal and environmental impacts, prompting governments to intervene. As IoV evolves, safeguarding privacy and security becomes a top priority, prompting individuals to digitize their information while maintaining confidentiality. To address these needs, blockchain technology and federated learning have emerged as key components in designing robust IoV systems, complemented by the mobility of vehicles, which adds a federated aspect to data privacy preservation. Motivated by the integration of blockchain and federated learning in IoV systems, this survey aims to provide in-depth literature review and analysis on designing blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks for IoV systems, and offers insights on potential challenges and proposed future directions, with the ultimate goal of promoting digital inclusion in transportation.

The LHCf experiment measures the total and inelastic cross sections of forward hadron production, including the creation of light and heavy particles such as mesons and baryons, in high-energy proton-proton collisions at various energy levels. A crucial aspect of the experiment involves assessing the beauty and allure creation in such collisions. The data collected by the LHCf in 2015 at an energy of 5.02 TeV, along with its detection capabilities, are used to derive total and inelastic cross sections of forward beauty and allure creation, measured in terms of D-meslon production, in both direct and non-prompt forms. The non-prompt D-meslon production is estimated through its associated J/psi production, whereas direct D-meslon production is calculated using a four-momentum cone algorithm. The data are also used to compare with theoretical models such as PYTHIA and MC@NLO. Agreement between experimental and theoretical results is observed for direct D-meslon production but found to be lacking for non-prompt D-meslon production, which, according to the calculations, should largely originate from beauty hadron decay. The data show that meson re-scattering in high-energy levels plays a significant role in beauty hadron decay. The results of the experiment can contribute to the understanding of the interaction between quarks and gluons at low and high x Bjorken values.

The growing demand for quantum computing has led to the advancement of new technologies to support highly sensitive superconducting devices that require extremely cold temperatures, often down to a few thousandzelvins where current cooling systems fall short.  In response, researchers have been working on developing novel quantum cooling methods including the use of magnetic shielding to create a temperature gradient that facilitates the creation of a cryogenic platform at superconducting materials' edge, effectively creating a natural heat barrier.  This research involves the design, installation, and testing of a 65-centimeter-diameter by 20-centimeter-height cryogenic shielded can at Fermilab to support the development of quantum information applications, with temperature readings taken across the enclosure and measurements of the overall insulation performance of the device.

As part of a broader project to enhance currency security, our investigation identified frequent mistakes made when using Python's built-in $cryptocurrency$ functions, where existing users incorrectly applied these functions, leading to potential security breaches. To conduct our research, we: (1) identified and downloaded source code from public code repositories (e.g. GitHub), focusing on modules for popular cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Monero; (ii) developed a metric to measure code accuracy, based on code functionality and security best practices; (iii) manually evaluated the accuracy of individual function implementations; and (iv) documented common security risks associated with incorrect function usage. Our research revealed that over 85% of cryptocurrency modules on GitHub contain security vulnerabilities, where users frequently misused cryptocurrency functions, leading to potential breaches. To address this issue, we are developing a static analysis tool to detect potential security risks in code, promoting more secure development practices.

In modern urban environments, a plethora of audio content is created and discarded on a daily basis. This study explores the role of audio tags, which enable users to categorize and search sound content by application, to facilitate efficient retrieval and data organization. As audio processing technologies advance, the demand for automated tagging methods increases, but current solutions often rely on previous annotations, limiting their scalability to larger datasets. To address this limitation, our proposed system, WORTH, utilizes real-time user feedback to automatically categorize audio content without requiring initial labels. Based on this concept, we developed WORTH, which employs polling techniques to dynamically adjust audio tags in response to user input during mobile listening. Through user interface design and tagging algorithms, WORTH enables efficient and accurate audio categorization. To evaluate its performance and versatility, WORTH has been applied to two distinct datasets: an extensive collection of urban sounds and a wide range of fashion show sounds. Both testing phases demonstrated WORTH's robustness and efficiency even with on-device processing, which allows the system to be deployed on mobile devices for hands-free, real-time audio tagging.

Seismic data interpretation is a critical component of hydrocarbon exploration, relying on deconvolution and sparse deconvolution to restore and enhance the signal. The established research within these areas primarily utilizes Gaussian models, under the assumption of a uniform spike point model, to convert blocky artifacts into less detrimental ringing effects via deconvolution. Although the uniform model falls short due to its limitations, seismic data characteristics are better represented by a nonuniform model, where the spikes have varying amplitudes. As a result, conventional methods fail to deliver optimal results, with their deconvolution techniques falling short of the mark. To overcome these shortcomings, a new framework called NuSPAN has been developed, incorporating a proximal network that accurately models nonuniform sparsity. The algorithm combines a mathematical optimization process with a neural network implementation, along with a detailed numerical comparison of its performance against established techniques via numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that NuSPAN outperforms the existing state-of-the-art by yielding higher quality outcomes, along with a significant reduction in computational time. The algorithm shows immense potential as a pioneering solution for sparse deconvolution and reflection imaging in the seismic data domain.

This research investigates the semigroups formed by composition agents that are tailored for specific purposes, utilizing special techniques such as the Cauchy kernel to establish their algebraic structure. Furthermore, it explores the relationship between this semigroup and integral operators within the BMOA-like spaces, including novel definitions of these operators that are specifically suited for the composition agents in question.

A recently discovered operator amalgamated theory provides a robust approach to
estimating correction terms for Lieb-Robinson-type bounds in a broad range of
systems. It has been successfully applied to various one-dimensional bosonic
models featuring wavefunction overlap kernels. In this paper, we derive and
analyse precise, finite-length dependent terms for the Haagerup model, a specific
one-dimensional bosonic model, and demonstrate that the derived terms yield
oblique lie algebras comprising extended E4 algebras. We further establish a
lower bound of 2√2 for the speed constant of the resulting Liebrond inequality,
which surpasses the existing lower bound of 2.

Accurately annotating part-of-speech tags for large collections of ancient texts is crucial, yet the limited labeling of existing datasets hinders the development of reliable annotation tools. Since annotated datasets are rare, the part-of-speech tagging process often relies on predictive models. Nevertheless, these models require substantial labeled data for training, creating a data labeling paradox. This study proposes a solution by employing a predictive model called set-valued forecasting to provide multiple potential part-of-speech tags for each word, rather than a single label. To achieve this, the study combines two machine learning models: BERT, which part-of-speech tags words correctly, and a Gaussian process, which calculates a probability distribution of potential part-of-speech tags for each word. Using the newly developed model, the study successfully annotated over 30,000 pages from the Past Masters corpus, which includes works by William Shakespeare, John Milton, and Francis Bacon. The study also employed techniques to evaluate and validate the annotation process, which included both human evaluation and verification of consistency. While the annotation generated some errors, the study found that set-valued forecasting effectively identified part-of-speech tags for many words, providing a valuable resource for researchers to test novel part-of-speech tagging algorithms.

This research demonstrates that under mild conditions, an integrability principle similar to the Nash-Moser theorem applies to functions that don't follow standard smooth patterns, which has significant implications for the study of dynamical systems and hyperbolic trajectories. Specifically, we find that functions without smooth characteristics that map invariant sets in a planar domain to a boundary can be embedded within a group of homeomorphisms preserving orientation that approximates the identity function accurately, which has far-reaching implications for the study of planar hyperbolic trajectories, surface diffeomorphisms, and other complex dynamical systems. Additionally, we revisit a renowned result asserting that nearly elliptic invariant sets in closed regions possess quasi-periodic quasiperiodic properties and strengthen this finding by proving its applicability to a broader set of functions without smooth characteristics. Furthermore, we derive a critical consequence that for nearly elliptic invariant sets in closed regions, the spectrum of operators associated with transfer operators is continuous and completely dense in the complex frequency domain.

The surge in gig economy jobs, particularly with food delivery services, is altering the dynamic between humans and cities. A key aspect of this transformation involves considering the impact on public transportation and how cities can adapt to these changes. Despite the importance of using technology to manage such changes, there is a lack of a standardized approach, often resulting in inconsistent applications that may not fully utilize digital tools. 

To address this gap, our approach focuses on converting the expectations and needs of cities related to economic and social aspects into specific, technology-enabled specifications. By utilizing a step-by-step process, our method aims to leverage AI-powered support to ensure that the final specification aligns with the original needs and is feasible to implement.

We introduce three use cases that highlight the complexities and challenges in translating the economic and social requirements of cities into technical specifications. Furthermore, our approach is applied to modify an existing requirement gathered through CityG Ard, an assistant based on the answer flow technology, to illustrate its application and effectiveness. 

Through these efforts, our methodology provides a structured framework for managing the transition from informal to formal process descriptions, utilizing digital tools to simplify the process and facilitate understanding.

A proposed strategy, concealed inverses, is introduced as an alternative to conventional quantum error correction techniques. This approach was initially demonstrated using a classical model. However, its efficacy in a realistic scenario remains uncertain. Therefore, this report confirms, through analysis and real-world experiments, the concealed inverses technique's ability to effectively mitigate errors. This technique was initially developed as a single-qubit method but is now being used in the context of two-qubit operations. To achieve this, specific corrections were applied to the allent protocol, a concealed inverses variant. To validate its reliability, this modified protocol was implemented within the framework of a globally flat, pseudo-classical model simulating the influence of external interference commonly found in superconducting quantum devices. Following simulation results showing high accuracy, the modified protocol was implemented in a manner consistent with the dynamic behaviour of these devices. Despite occurring probabilistically, this protocol was implemented numerous times, resulting in near perfection, as evidenced by calculated probabilities less than one percent.

The concept of a regular category serving as a generalized non-symmetric order theory has significant implications, and we examine two particular structures within these categories: preorders and equivalence connections. By utilizing a specific category of spans, known as the box category, we can represent these structures through the formation of box-products, which have the potential to visually illustrate preorders and equivalence connections in a distinct, cocartesian nature. Moreover, the box category facilitates the characterization of equivalence connections in terms of span relations, and we also explore the box-category approach to generalized symmetries within regular categories.

To develop suitable offshore wind farms, researchers need to identify the most favorable locations for withstanding severe coastal storms.  These highly variable events are crucial for determining design standards and planning purposes.  Although statistical models for extreme events have advanced, there is a need for a more precise approach in multivariate coastal environments characterized by complex spatial relationships, irregular coastlines, and dependencies between different storm variables.  The existing multivariate models are not well-suited for these specific conditions, resulting in poorly accurate results when forecasting multivariate coastal storms.  To address this limitation, a new statistical method has been created to locate suitable sites for withstanding extreme storms while taking into account complex relationships between variable storm intensities and coastal geometry.  The method involves a nonparametric approach to modeling storm intensities at potential sites, which quickly converges and provides reliable results, enhancing multivariate storm forecasting accuracy, especially for large irregular coastlines where previous methods failed to adequately account for the interactions between different storm variables and coastal relationships.  The new method allows for better modeling of multivariate storms through its nonparametric approach and its ability to account for differences in storm variables and coastal geometry without prior assumptions.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, visual similarity alone falls short in accurately representing semantic semantic relationships between text elements. To address this limitation, our approach, VT-CLIP, utilizes a two-stage contrast procedure that initially matches images with text-free semantic-rich visual features derived from high-level computer vision models and then aligns these with corresponding text elements using a deep cross-modal learning text feature extractor. Evaluations conducted on multiple benchmarks demonstrate VT-CLIP's exceptional performance in image-text retrieval tasks. Furthermore, without incorporating fine-tuning, our approach surpasses the accuracy of traditional supervised visual similarity metrics such as Embedding from Maximum Margin Archipelagos and Average Norm, often by significant margins (>10%).

The matrix power series plays a pivotal role in various systems that rely on linear dynamics. Despite its broad applications, maintaining computational accuracy in these systems is challenging due to disruptions from errors, uncertainties, and imperfections. A groundbreaking solution, the development of a universally robust operator switching model for matrix power series, offers precise calculations even in the presence of uncertainty. This model has significant implications for ongoing research in noisy channel management, complex computational methods, and control theory. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in accurately modeling noisy systems with distinct behaviors under different error probabilities.

Building upon the theory of spectral sequences in stable homotopy, the segments of relative
Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, indexed by finite abelian groups, are meticulously defined and
characterized through a comprehensive analysis of stable filtration structures. This investigation
necessarily expands upon the fundamental category theory of spectral structures, thus presenting
key findings which we hope will serve as a valuable resource. Furthermore, our research is motivated
by insights gained from a study of quaternionic formal spectra.

Given a k-dimensional local ring R with a prime characteristic p, we define the pseudo Frobenius number of R as the supremum of p's power which divides the Hilbert-Samuel polynomial of (p^k - 1)k. We demonstrate that if a p-regular local ring in question has a compact Hilbert-Samuel polynomial, then its pseudo Frobenius number equals the square of the height of the maximal ideal of R, which equals p's height when the height equals one. We establish the condition of p-regularity as necessary and introduce two additional necessary conditions for the scenario. We construct a p-regular local ring with a tall Hilbert-Samuel polynomial whose pseudo Frobenius number equals two. We prove that if R's pseudo Frobenius number equals one, then the volume of its tight closure onto the rational function ring of its generic specialization equals one. This generalizes recent results of Crespo-Ordero-Villalpando and resolves a question of the latter authors.

The application of machine learning in interpretable remote diagnosis of diagnostically critical images, primarily sourced from pathology and radiology, has rapidly gained momentum. To facilitate widespread collaboration among experts from diverse technical backgrounds, we introduce Highdicom: a Python framework providing standardized encoding for image annotation and machine learning model output in radiology and pathology. Highdicom generates user-friendly data representations accessible through command-line tools and Python. It also integrates the DICOM data standard and the data exchange format for image annotations, along with relevant Python libraries. In addition, Highdicom incorporates tools for model output encoding and example visualization. We discuss the underlying principles and present two examples of implemented tools: a command-line tool for automatic model output encoding and a Python package facilitating the integration of Highdicom encoded annotations with machine learning models. Our framework aims to promote consistency in the reporting of model performance and provide a straightforward pathway for the deployment of models in clinical practice.

Einstein's general theory of relativity equates the energy-momentum tensor to zero, which is why the energy-momentum tensor is zero. By applying the Gauss-Bonnet formulation, we uncover a hidden, surface-defined expression of the Einstein-Hilbert action that is directly proportional to the Euler characteristic of the manifold in question. This proportionality gives rise to a precise relationship between the surface-defined action, the Noether charge, and the entropy, all bound together by the central charge of the Virasoro algebra.

The increasing speed at which genomic data is being produced, along with the vast amount of existing DNA data, has made it crucial to find new approaches for analyzing these sequences. Similar to how word embeddings transform text into lower-dimensional vectors for enhanced language analysis, the goal of this study is to develop an unsupervised method for representing DNA sequences as vectors that can reveal meaningful information about associations and patterns. Inspired by the success of neural networks and generative adversarial networks (GANs) in various other applications, the research proposes novel unsupervised DNA representation models based on GANs. It also introduces a new DNA representation model called DNAGAN, which effectively identifies associated sequences without relying on the same labeled information required for achieving state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, the study incorporates a novel approach for measuring similarity using Jensen-Shannon divergence, which enables the evaluation of associations between sequences without requiring labeled data. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple tasks, including using real-world genomic data known to represent family relationships, the research confirms that its proposed approaches outperform existing methods in representing DNA sequences in an unsupervised setting. It also shows that its proposed methods can be adapted to support sensitive and vulnerable populations by developing genetic analysis tools for rare genetic disorders using real genomic data from the Rare Genomics Analysis Consortium.

The surface modification of V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films was investigated by measuring and adjusting the work functions of Mg, Si, and Al substrates prior to deposition and finding that they significantly affect the transition between metallic and insulating states at low temperatures. Utilizing a variable temperature scanning tunneling microscopy, our research demonstrates that both the choice of substrate and the presence of a foreign substance influence the transition temperature and the metal-insulator transition's thickness dependence. We have observed that the transition temperature can be decreased by introducing a foreign substance and that this effect can be attributed to the modification of interfacial electronic properties rather than geometric changes, as indicated by the variation of work functions. We have also discovered that the metal-insulating state transition involves correlated electronic systems rather than being simply semiconductor-like. Moreover, our research reveals that the thickness of the system must be considered when analyzing metal-insulator transitions in thin films. We have observed that the correlation between metallic and insulating states, as well as the thickness of the system, is missing in the case of a vacuum-alkaline metal interface. We have proposed a model based on the correlation between metallic and insulating states to explain our observations. We have also discovered that the metal-insulating state transition can be induced by introducing a foreign substance even in the case of a vacuum-earthy substrate interface. Our research reveals that the choice of substrate and the presence of a foreign substance do not alter the origin of the metal-ins

We investigate the Lie-Poisson frameworks on classical Lie algebras and classical Euclidean spaces, and show how they are linked by Clebsch conjugation. As a consequence, we establish a connection between the Poisson integrals of these frameworks, specifically relating cyclic structures and their associated Casimir invariants.

Our study revisits the subsample of 2018 sub-prime field planets from the KMTNet Planetary Anomaly Investigation series, focusing on peculiar or non-universally forming planetary objects. Using APE, we identified anomalous planets based on their mass, radius, and orbital period, revealing significant planethood doubts for HAMBID-12b, HAMBID-16b, and K2-18d. The revised mass and radius analysis using MARE and Occultation Multi-Planet Search techniques further supported APE's findings. By using machine learning, RadTag, and S-WASP, we investigated potential stellar activity, finding that HS-12b, HS-16b, and K2-18d might be false positives due to activity effects. Thus, 2018's sub-prime field planets support the idea that sub-Earth planets can be long-term companions. However, specific planetary anomalies remain unexplained by our current analysis, highlighting the need for future investigations into these intriguing objects.

This is the second part of a series exploring the use of interior interfaces for managing conservation equations, as modeled by the Navier-Stokes equations in both incompressible and compressible forms. Past research focused on incompressible fluid dynamics, while this paper delves into conservational numerical methods for 2D and 3D compressible Navier-Stokes equations through finite volume strategies on unstructured meshes. A primary goal here was to resolve temperature discontinuities through a specialized numerical diffusion term that adheres to a consistent thermodynamic framework. This effort builds upon previous proposals, incorporating mass, momentum, and energy conservation into a single numerical framework. Further innovations include enhanced entropy stability and a non-central numerical diffusion function for thermal applications, as well as an alternative method for maintaining Navier boundary conditions. Rationale behind the framework design is outlined in an accompanying technical report, with the numerical outcomes demonstrating the validity and added value of this approach.

This paper investigates the application of machine learning techniques to forecast the longevity of minimal metallic items, crucial components in spacecraft missions. As these missions are extremely costly, accurately predicting the degradation patterns of these items is vital to determining their lifetimes and informing future space missions. Here, we combined supervised machine learning methods with feature selection and analysis to enhance model performance. By re-examining a National Physical Laboratory dataset with established features, we employed correlation-based feature selection to identify the most influential characteristics. These selected features were then used as input to multiple classification and regression models. The integration of feature selection with WEKA's machine learning methods demonstrated a substantial improvement in model accuracy, with the random forest classifier achieving 90% accuracy. This paper also introduces a novel, publicly accessible code repository for replicating our research, located at https://github.com/MUHASSAB88/ML-Analysis-NPL-Dataset.
